a-b-c-vom-stein-der-weisen-1778: A, b, c. vom Stein der Weisen, 1778. The philosophers' stone ABC. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
a-breviary-of-alchemy-1678-1678: A Breviary of Alchemy, 1678. The alchemical breviary. This book preserves that work. Future scholars will discover it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The library keeps the document safe.
a-history-of-modern-europe-1792-1878: Charles Alan Fyffe's history carries Europe from the French Revolution through the unification of Germany — the age of Napoleon, nationalism, and empire. Clear narrative and sound judgment made it a standard English textbook for decades. Students meeting the making of modern Europe for the first time will find it a reliable guide.
a-new-illustrated-hand-book-of-phrenolog: A New Illustrated Hand-Book of Phrenology, 1878. The handbook. This book preserves that manual. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1878 the eighth volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica came off the press. The set was nearing its end, yet the method never thins: full proving records, sorted by remedy and region. Allen's wide net caught symptoms from famous provers and obscure ones alike, all filed in order.

Working doctors used the volumes when a case turned on some small, strange sign. The odds were good that Allen had filed that sign somewhere in the ten volumes. Volume VIII, like its mates, asks patience and pays it back in depth, a reference shelf that later short guides could never replace.

Volume IX of Allen's Encyclopaedia, dated 1878, stands one step from the end of the ten-volume record. Its remedy entries hold the same wealth: every prover's symptom, placed by body region, with its source named. The alphabetical march of drugs across the whole set continues through these pages.

Allen's restraint as an editor is the set's quiet strength throughout. He lets contradictions stand, since real provers differ, and leaves judgment to the prescriber at the desk. Students of the school's history read these volumes to see drug pictures whole, before later authors boiled them down to keynotes.
arxiv-2510-00178:
Carmen Frias-Ruiz and four colleagues published this 2025 clinical study on a trap in vitamin B12 testing. Some patients carry MacroB12, bulky antibody-bound forms that inflate lab readings. A high reading can then mask a true B12 deficiency. The team asked whether the raw B12 level and routine patient data can predict this interference.

They studied 875 people whose B12 readings topped the normal range, filling gaps with imputation. MacroB12 was confirmed by a chemical precipitation test in the lab. Older age and autoimmune or rheumatologic diagnoses raised the odds of MacroB12 notably. Higher hemoglobin and cell volume also pointed toward it, against intuition. The raw B12 level alone sorted patients only moderately well, the authors report. They conclude that the lab confirmation test remains essential before trusting any high reading.
arxiv-2510-00478:
Jing Wang and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on adapting image classifiers to new domains without ever seeing the source data. Privacy rules often bar sharing the original training set, yet a trained model may be shared. Their framework also accepts an auxiliary latent diffusion module trained once on the source side. That module becomes the bridge for transferring knowledge safely.

Each source feature's label is baked into its latent neighborhood with a Gaussian prior over nearest neighbors. The diffusion network learns to drift noisy samples back toward label-consistent representations. At adaptation time, target features are sampled, cleaned by the frozen module, and aligned with a contrastive loss. Standard source-free benchmarks showed the method beating leading rivals. Bonus tests found the same module lifts source-domain accuracy and domain generalization too. The authors recast diffusion models as explicit, privacy-preserving knowledge couriers.
arxiv-2510-00778:
Hong, Son, Lee, and Woo present DIA in this 2025 arXiv paper, a defence that sabotages diffusion-based image editing. DDIM inversion lets anyone map a real photo back to its latent code and then synthesize edited versions, a pipeline easily abused for deepfakes. Existing immunization methods such as AdvDM and Photoguard perturb images, but their objectives ignore the actual inversion trajectory, so disruption at editing time stays weak. DIA attacks the integrated trajectory itself.

Its two variants, DIA-PT and DIA-R, fold the differentiable DDIM path into the attack objective. Maximizing trajectory deviation corrupts the latent code that any later edit must start from. Across a range of editing methods, DIA disrupted results more strongly than previous defences, measured by drops in semantic similarity. The authors frame the method as practical immunization for the research community and industry. Code is released with the paper.
arxiv-2510-00978:
Barroso-Laguna, Cavallari, Prisacariu, and Brachmann localize a camera in one feed-forward pass in this 2025 arXiv paper on computer vision, presenting FastForward. Estimating where a photo was taken normally needs a visual map of the scene, and building that map takes minutes to hours even when mapping photos come with known poses. The authors ask whether competitive accuracy can arrive almost instantly instead. Their map is strikingly simple: a collection of image features anchored in 3D space, sampled from the mapping images.

FastForward reads that feature set and predicts image-to-scene correspondences for the query photo directly. Standard pose estimation then recovers the camera position. Coupled with image retrieval to choose the mapping set, the system matched state-of-the-art accuracy with minimal map preparation. It also generalized robustly to unseen domains, including large-scale outdoor scenes. More mapping images steadily improved the estimates in their tests.
arxiv-2510-01178:
Luo and Deshwal pick the example prompts that teach a language model a task, but they grade on honesty as well as accuracy. Most selection methods chase correct answers alone and ignore whether the model's confidence matches its real chances. A confident, wrong model is dangerous exactly where trust matters most.

Their method, COM-BOM, treats selection as a two-goal search over answer quality and calibration error. A Bayesian optimizer explores the trade-off frontier while spending very few model calls. On hard professional-level test questions, it matched or beat rivals at balancing both goals. The frontier view lets deployers choose their own compromise instead of accepting one. Expected calibration error is the yardstick for the honesty goal. Combinatorial search matters because exemplar sets interact as wholes. Unsaturated benchmarks keep the comparison honest at the frontier. Fewer calls mean cheaper tuning for small teams.
arxiv-2510-01378:
Song and co-authors refine the story of why diffusion models create new images instead of photocopying their training data. A perfect score model would memorize, so generation requires selective failure to fit. Earlier accounts blamed uniform underfitting caused by training biases.

The new claim is geographic: good models fit the score precisely in supervised regions and underfit elsewhere. The team characterizes those regions and tests the picture with targeted interventions. Where the model extrapolates freely is exactly where novelty comes from. This selective picture yields testable predictions about generalization and sampling quality. Supervision and extrapolation regions name the two territories. Inductive biases of training decide where the freedom lives. The score function is the object being selectively approximated. MIT and Harvard share the author list on this one. Generalization has an address now. Regions matter more than averages.
arxiv-2510-01478:
Matisan and many co-authors generate images by flowing through a quantized latent space while keeping clear odds over the discrete codes. Quantizing crushes images into codebook tokens, but making them then splits into smooth or discrete camps. Their variational flow matching hybrid keeps smooth transport dynamics with category supervision.

Scores over codebook indices gauge doubt about plausible codes at each step. Temperature control steers sampling variety directly. On ImageNet tests, training converged faster than both pure flow baselines. Image quality scores stayed close to the state of the art. Token geometry stays visible to the velocity field throughout transport. Euler steps sample the learned flow when images are made. Faster convergence means cheaper trials for image researchers. Discrete guidance shapes the smooth dynamics clearly. Doubt over codes is a feature, not a bug.
arxiv-2510-01578:
You and Liu replace the hard cutoff of gradient clipping with a smooth, per-layer shaping of training updates. Clipping guards deep networks against explosive steps, but one fixed threshold ignores how gradient sizes drift during training. Their framework, SPAMP, watches each layer's own statistics and adjusts its limits continuously.

Power-based transformations then soften or sharpen updates in a fully differentiable way. The same lens unifies clipping and warmup as two dialects of update-size control. Experiments on image and language tasks showed steadier, faster, more robust training than standard clipping. Flexible shaping beats rigid rules as networks grow more varied. Update magnitude, the paper argues, is the hidden variable behind several folk tricks. Per-layer treatment respects that early and late layers live different gradient lives. Differentiable shaping lets the optimizer learn its own guardrails. Stability gains showed up across architectures.
arxiv-2510-01778:
Motie, Zayyani, Salman, and Abu Hilal locate a radio emitter with a single drone in this 2025 engineering paper. The drone listens to the emitter's signals as it flies. Doppler shifts reveal motion-related information, while time-of-arrival readings add range clues. Doppler-only methods usually lead to non-convex problems that are hard to solve exactly.

Adding the arrival-time data reshapes the least-squares cost into a friendly quadratic form. Its minimizer lies on a line, which the authors exploit with the extra measurements. A constrained least-squares step then yields the emitter position in closed form. The team also designs the drone's flight trajectory, again with a closed-form solution. That path improves how well the emitter can be tracked over time. Simulations showed the method beating several published alternatives for this localization task.
arxiv-2510-01878:
Rajabi, Nonta, Vajpayee, and Rambhatla cut the memory cost of training large language models in this 2025 paper. Optimizer states, not the model weights, dominate the memory footprint during training. Projecting gradients into small subspaces is a known saving trick. The authors first study how those gradient subspaces actually behave over training.

They found a small core subspace holds most gradient energy early on. Its grip fades over time and in deeper layers, leaving much signal in the residual bulk. The gradient space also shows nearly flat curvature, which algorithms should respect. Their randomized methods, GrassWalk and GrassJump, roam and leap within the subspace accordingly. On LLaMA models with one and seven billion parameters, the methods matched top memory savings. They also improved training performance over prior state-of-the-art approaches.
arxiv-2510-02078:
Yuan, Zhang, Wei, and Fan model games where players cooperate inside groups but compete across them in this paper. Classical Bayesian games treat every player as a lone actor with private information. Real organizations negotiate as blocs, which changes what equilibrium means. Their multi-group Bayesian game formalizes that middle ground.

Two equilibrium notions split the cases: one for groups whose members play cooperatively, a stronger one for groups whose members still compete internally. A transformation converts any such game into a normal-form agent game. The authors give a necessary and sufficient condition for the converted game to be a potential game. When that condition holds, all equilibria can be computed through the potential structure. Algorithms then recover the multi-group equilibria of the original game. The machinery suits coalition settings from supply chains to political blocs. Group behavior in strategic analysis gains a tractable formal home.
arxiv-2510-02578:
Cremer and co-authors build a foundation model that designs drug like molecules inside protein pockets. Their 2025 computational chemistry paper presents a system called Flowr.root. The model generates 3D ligand shapes with flow matching. It respects the geometry of the binding pocket throughout. Affinity prediction and confidence scores come built in. Several design modes share one architecture. Fresh molecules can grow from nothing at all. Existing fragments can be elaborated into fuller candidates. Interaction patterns can steer the generation. Training mixed ligand libraries with protein complex data.

Curated crystal structures refined the model afterward. Project specific fine-tuning adapts it to new targets. Benchmarks showed realistic, low strain generated structures. The affinity module beat recent rivals on standard test sets. It also led on a respected free energy benchmark. Drug hunters gain design and scoring in one tool. Hit finding through lead polishing fits one workflow.
arxiv-2510-02778:
Zhang and co-authors pick keyframes from long videos by balancing query relevance against visual diversity. Their 2025 computer vision paper presents a sampler called AdaRD-Key. Language models answer questions about hours long footage. Uniform frame sampling misses the decisive moments. Rigid spacing rules suppress frames near key events. Pure diversity picks ignore the question entirely. AdaRD-Key scores frames on both axes at once. A max volume objective merges relevance with a diversity term. A scale module adjusts the balance by video length. A gate falls back to diversity when query alignment is weak.

No training or fine tuning is required. Benchmarks on long video question answering showed consistent wins. Gains grew on the longest videos tested. Captioning under tight frame budgets improved too. The module runs on a single GPU. Frame choice is the silent bottleneck of video understanding. Smart sampling raises accuracy without touching the model.
arxiv-2510-02878:
Bernaschi, Celestini, and D'Ambra measure the energy cost of sparse matrix math on GPU clusters. Sparse matrices drive many large science codes. Solving huge sparse systems can exceed one node's memory. The team's library spreads the work across many graphics cards. Earlier work showed it outruns rival libraries at scale. This study asks a greener question. How much energy does each approach burn to finish?

The authors built careful tools to meter energy during runs. They profiled the library's core steps one by one. Smart GPU use plus less data movement cut both time and energy. Head-to-head tests used standard benchmark problems. Their library, BootCMatchGX, beat Ginkgo and NVIDIA AmgX on energy in key kernels. The clearest win came in preconditioned solving. The results argue that energy belongs beside speed as a design target. Sustainable supercomputing needs software built with that mindset.
arxiv-2510-02978:
Ó Ciardha, Buckley, and Portnoff examine the harms of AI-generated abuse imagery of children. New tools can now produce synthetic abuse material with ease. Some voices claim such material harms no one directly. The authors reject that claim as far too narrow. They map a wider web of risks from production and use alike.

Synthetic images can depict real children who were never abused. Known survivors can be revictimized through copies of their likeness. The material can aid grooming, coercion, and sexual extortion. It can also normalize the exploitation of children in wider culture. For some users, it may lower the barrier into offending. Repeated use may dull restraint and feed escalation. The authors warn against calling it a harm reduction tool. Such claims, they argue, hide real risks and stall response. The paper serves as a primer for policy and protection work.
arxiv-2510-03178:
Le and co-authors strip the names out of code to see what language models really grasp. Code speaks through two channels at once. Structure dictates what a program actually does. Names whisper what the programmer meant it to do. The team built obfuscations that erase the second channel. Behavior stays identical while names turn to noise. Models then faced summarization and execution tasks again.

Summaries collapsed into line-by-line narration without names. That was expected, since intent lives in naming. Execution scores also fell, which was not expected. Running code should depend on structure alone. The drop exposes memorized naming patterns inside benchmarks. High scores partly reward recall, not reasoning. The authors release an obfuscated benchmark, ClassEval-Obf, in response. It suppresses naming cues while preserving behavior throughout. Score gaps between models shrank under the new test. Memorization shortcuts lost much of their power there.
arxiv-2510-03278:
Landgren dissects how each physical constraint bends the uncertainty landscape of a Bayesian physics-informed network. Such networks blend data with governing equations under uncertainty. Their confidence can look excessive for subtle reasons. A dominant constraint can shrink the solution space by design. That shrinkage mimics miscalibration while being fully warranted. His framework splits the posterior curvature by constraint. A matrix-free Laplace method keeps the split scalable.

Each constraint's share of the Hessian becomes measurable. Metrics then rank the constraints' true influence on geometry. The Van der Pol oscillator served as the test system. Turning one loss weight reshuffled dominance across all others. Curvature interactions make influence non-proportional to nominal weights. An over-weighted equation term could still lose to data curvature. That inversion explains many confusing tuning experiences in practice. Honest uncertainty needs this bookkeeping before any calibration claim.
arxiv-2510-03478:
Nguyen, at the University of Victoria in Canada, presents a 2025 arXiv paper on how to set the two momentum knobs of the Adam optimizer. Adam trains most large neural networks today, yet theory for its twin decay rates has lagged practice. Earlier work recast Adam as an online learning method, but only when the two rates obey one strict relation. Real training rarely respects that relation. Nguyen derives fresh analyses that cover rates on both sides of it.

The new bounds strictly widen the older results and are tight in the worst case. One finding says the classic linked setting is best against an adversary that cannot adapt. Against an adaptive adversary, that same setting falls short of optimal. Trainers gain firmer ground for a choice they once made by folklore. The work also sharpens how online learning theory speaks to deep learning practice, where Adam remains the default workhorse.
arxiv-2510-03578:
Li and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on learning the dynamics of physical systems from scarce measurements by exploiting symmetry. Sensors in grids and robots often report slowly, while key events flash by in milliseconds. Their model, Latent MoS, mixes several symmetry governed factors inside a latent space instead of assuming one global symmetry. Stacked blocks extend that respect for symmetry across long time spans. The design keeps transformations intact at the local level while the dynamics are learned.

Across varied physical systems, the model beat leading baselines on both filling gaps and forecasting beyond the data range. Its latent factors stay readable, which helps safety and geometry checks. Systems often hold symmetries only locally or roughly, and the mixture design fits that reality. Power grid and robot controllers could learn models from thinner data streams. The authors next want the model to pick its symmetries from validation evidence.
arxiv-2510-03678:
Song, Xie, and Zhou present a 2025 arXiv paper building sampling data structures that make attention computations feasible on streaming data. Attention sits at the heart of language models, but its cost grows quadratically with sequence length. In the turnstile streaming model, data arrives as updates that can add or remove entries. The authors define an attention sampler, modeled on importance samplers, that picks out the entries that matter. They analyze its space and update time across dynamic settings.

Efficient polynomial time samplers exist whether the input matrix, the weight vector, or both change over time, they show. Space lower bounds mark where no sampler can do better. One lower bound shows exponential samplers need linear space in general. Streaming attention would let models run on devices that cannot hold a sequence. The framework isolates which parts of attention need computation. Sparse attention schemes can now be tested against limits.
arxiv-2510-03978:
Sun and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a simple waste in biomedical vision-language models. These models pair medical images with text, but their encoders accept only very short captions. Real biomedical captions often run far longer, so most content gets cut off in training. The authors ask what happens when models are allowed to read the full captions.

They built a dataset of one million image-caption pairs, enriched with context from the full articles. Their model, BMC-LongCLIP, stretches the text window to five hundred twelve tokens. Token waste fell from over half of all caption text to a small remainder. On long-caption retrieval tests, the model posted large gains in top-hit recall over short-context rivals. Classification scores improved modestly as well, and training converged faster. Even so, the results argue context length, not model size, was the binding constraint.
arxiv-2510-04078:
Hu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on discovering which Android permissions each framework API actually requires. Android's permission system guards sensitive data, but the official documentation is chronically incomplete about required permissions. Developers guessing wrong ship apps that crash or over-request access. Earlier mapping tools used static or dynamic analysis and missed many mappings in a huge, evolving codebase.

Their tool, Bamboo, scans every Java method in the Android SDK with a large language model. A dual-role prompting strategy cross-checks the model's judgments, and generated code enables dynamic verification. On Android versions 6, 7, and 10, Bamboo found thousands of API-permission mappings, beating the Dynamo and Arcade baselines by wide margins. It also exposed over three thousand missing permission declarations in official documentation across several versions. Accurate permission maps help developers write safer apps and help auditors spot over-privileged software.
arxiv-2510-04278:
Yang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on a model predictive control toolkit for robots whose states live on curved manifolds rather than flat Euclidean space. Attitude and constrained motion problems suffer from singularities, redundant coordinates, and poor convergence when forced into ordinary vector formulations. FactorMPC represents dynamics, constraints, and objectives as modular factors in a sparse probabilistic graph. Manifold-valued states remain native to the optimization, while Gaussian uncertainty is modeled in local tangent spaces.

The toolkit includes velocity-extended on-manifold control barrier factors for obstacle avoidance in safety-critical settings. Quadrotor simulations and experiments showed stronger trajectory tracking and obstacle avoidance than baseline methods, at control rates comparable to custom implementations. Their longer-term goal is to insert learned dynamics and neural policies as graph factors, connecting geometric control with data-driven components inside one optimizer.
arxiv-2510-04478:
Hongli Zhao, Mihai Anitescu, and Sen Na wrote this 2025 paper on solving optimal control problems in continuous time. Such problems pick a control path that minimizes cost while obeying a differential equation. Big time spans make them costly to solve as one block. The team split the time span into overlapping intervals and solved each piece apart. Their frame comes from the Pontryagin minimum principle of control theory.

Each interval carries a Hamiltonian system, solved in continuous time rather than after discretization. Updating the boundary conditions between neighbors in the right way makes the pieces agree. The key proof shows that a fading sensitivity property, known in discrete time, survives in continuous time. That decay is what makes the overlap scheme converge instead of drifting apart. The method can mix different numerical integrators on different intervals, including adaptive ones. A test problem showed the scheme works in practice.
arxiv-2510-04578:
Varro wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on algebra models of sex linked inheritance with sterility. Gonosomal algebras encode how genes on sex chromosomes pass through a bisexual population. Those models assume every genetic type can reproduce. Populations include sterile types, and the older algebra cannot express that fact. Varro defines gonosomic algebras, a class that builds sterility in from the start.

The paper gives conditions under which an algebra is not gonosomal, so the extension holds. It supplies several constructions that produce gonosomic algebras from simpler data. Each algebra carries an evolution operator that gives the offspring population state at birth. An operator then gives the frequency distribution of genetic types in that population. The paper shows that stability of equilibrium points carries over from the first operator to the second. The work gives genetic algebra a language for a common biological fact it had skipped.
arxiv-2510-04778:
Ming Ming Long, Kirill Melnikov, and Andrey Pikelner wrote this 2025 paper on a calculation needed for precision particle physics. Collider predictions at next to leading order rely on subtraction schemes that cancel infinite terms. Extending one scheme to heavy quarks needs an integral. It is the integrated emission function for two massive particles radiating at an angle between them. The authors compute that integral with a strategy.

All divergent parts come out in analytic form. The finite remainder is arranged so a computer can evaluate it without any regulator. The trick rests on how the soft and collinear peaks of the function can be subtracted. Integrals existed for other schemes, and a back to back case was known for this one. The angle case was the missing piece. With it, the nested scheme can handle processes with heavy quarks. Top quark and bottom quark physics at colliders gain theory.
arxiv-2510-04878:
Xiangyang Xu and Hongyang Gao wrote this 2025 paper on polishing the three dimensional shapes that generative models propose for molecules. A drug candidate molecule folds into many shapes, and the low energy ones decide how it behaves. Diffusion and flow models can sample such conformers, but errors pile up during sampling. The errors creep in during the low signal steps that are hard to train. The authors add a refiner stage built on flow matching.

The refiner starts from the shapes an upstream model produced. It reschedules the noise scale so sampling skips the troublesome low signal phase. The generator plus refiner pipeline then cleans shapes without starting over. Tests ran on two benchmarks of small molecules and compounds. Quality improved while the number of denoising steps fell. The variety of shapes, which chemists need for ensembles, survived the cleanup. Refiners that rescue output could upgrade many generative chemistry tools.
arxiv-2510-04978:
Kun Xiang and a large team of co-authors survey the young field of physical AI in this 2025 arXiv paper. Physical AI tries to give machines a real grasp of how the physical world behaves. Perception of the physical world and symbolic physics reasoning have mostly grown up apart. No shared framework yet joins them.

The survey sorts recent work into four abilities. They are physical perception, physics reasoning, world modeling, and embodied interaction. Across all four, most systems still lean on pattern matching rather than true understanding. The strongest progress comes from hybrid designs that mix learned models with explicit physics. The authors argue that such grounding is key to safe and general AI.
arxiv-2510-05078:
William Fleurat develops a transfer principle for random geometric structures in this 2025 arXiv paper. Large random discrete objects often hide a big component of a simpler type. Results about the whole object do not automatically pass down to that component. Fleurat proves sandwich theorems and a Tauberian theorem for spaces of metric measure spaces.

The method shows how scaling limits descend from a host model to its components. As a proof of concept, he applies it to random planar maps. Irreducible quadrangulations, rescaled, converge to the Brownian sphere in the Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov topology. The proof leans on known limits for general quadrangulations and on couplings that grow maps by opening faces. The approach should adapt to triangulations and other map families.
arxiv-2510-05278:
Paloma García-de-Herreros and three co-authors test whether popular language model designs can learn physics simulations in this 2025 arXiv paper. Decoder-only models dominate natural language processing and scale beautifully. Cross-modal adaptation work, though, mostly uses encoder-only models. The team compares both architectures on time-dependent partial differential equation tasks.

With existing methods applied unchanged, decoder-only models performed far worse than encoders. Scaling the decoders up did not close the gap. One-way attention is the culprit: decoders cannot condition on the full data at once. The authors propose Parallel Flipping and Sequence Doubling to fake bidirectionality. Both tricks improved every task and adaptation method. Sequence Doubling gained the most, nearly matching encoder performance.
arxiv-2510-05378:
Reza Habibi and seven co-authors study how people and AI build shared meaning together in this 2025 arXiv paper. Humans read symbols through social interaction and personal values. AI systems often miss the shifting interpretations that emerge in conversation. The team draws on symbolic interactionism, a theory of how meaning is socially made.

Two studies watched participants negotiate meanings with conversational AI agents. Participants shifted their initial definitions in response to the AI's suggested symbols. The AI's influence grew substantially when social context accompanied its suggestions. Participants also projected personal and social values into the exchange, refining meanings over time. Productive disagreement, not instant agreement, drove the deepest meaning construction. Future assistants should act as partners in sense-making, not repositories of fixed definitions.
arxiv-2510-05578:
Sheng extends a famed correspondence in algebraic geometry to nonlinear objects. The nonabelian Hodge correspondence matches Higgs bundles with flat connections in characteristic zero. Ogus and Vologodsky built a positive-characteristic version of that bridge. Sheng's 2025 article constructs the nonlinear version of their equivalence.

The nonlinear Higgs bundles come from earlier work on nonabelian Kodaira-Spencer maps. Sheng abstracts the matching notion from nonabelian Gauss-Manin connections. Those yield a class of nonlinear flat bundles. Under suitable settings, the two classes become equal in positive characteristic. Lambda-connections supply the common language, joining foliations and Higgs fields. Positive characteristic geometry often behaves unlike the complex world, so each step is hard-won. The paper builds on the author's joint work defining nonlinear Higgs bundles. Curvature zero marks flatness on both sides of the bridge. The equivalence deepens the bridge between geometry and their kin.
arxiv-2510-05678:
Yoo and colleagues help language models reason across languages by mixing them. Models lean on English internally, creating a translation barrier for other languages. When that hidden translation fails, non-English answers collapse. Their 2025 prompting strategy, CSICL, code-switches gradually toward English inside the examples.

Demonstrations and instructions transition step by step from the target language to English. That scaffold bridges the model's latent reasoning into its strongest language. Experiments span four models, six datasets, and ten languages. Accuracy rose by about three points in target languages over standard cross-lingual prompting. Unseen languages gained about two points as well. Low-resource settings improved most, gaining nearly fifteen points in target languages. No extra training or resources are needed at inference time. Code-switching becomes a principled lens on cross-lingual alignment, not a hack.
arxiv-2510-05778:
Kramer and Johnston argue that many millisecond pulsars broadcast from beyond their light cylinders. Their radio profiles often split into components separated by silent gaps. Slow pulsars almost never show that disjoint pattern. Their 2025 technique separates genuinely disjoint components from contiguous ones.

About thirty-five percent of millisecond pulsars show disjoint components, versus three percent of slow pulsars. The authors read this as two emission sites working together. One sits above the polar cap, as convention holds. The other lies in the current sheet beyond the light cylinder, co-located with gamma-ray emission. Some pulsars show only the light-cylinder component. A simple geometric picture predicts when outer emission appears and aligns with gamma rays. High polarization and flat position-angle swings mark those outer components. The beaming fraction of radio millisecond pulsars then exceeds earlier estimates. Coherent emission that far out needs explaining.
arxiv-2510-05878:
Šmite and colleagues trace a resignation wave to remote onboarding during the pandemic. Ericsson Sweden's HR records span 2016 to 2025 across work modalities. Remote work is usually linked to higher satisfaction and retention. Their 2025 analysis finds the opposite pattern for pandemic-era hires.

Resignations rose markedly from summer 2021 to summer 2023. Employees with under five years of tenure drove the increase. Those onboarded remotely resigned significantly more within their first three years. The effect persisted even after everyone returned to the office. Exit surveys blame weak organizational attachment and belonging. New hires need in-office presence from teammates and senior mentors, not just themselves. Selective return-to-office mandates gain support from the evidence. Relationship building and cultural integration are the mechanisms that matter. Retention later recovered to pre-pandemic rates under differentiated policies. Hybrid models anchored in mentorship can sustain retention long term.
arxiv-2510-06178:
Hem applies poset cocalculus, a functor calculus, to multipersistence modules in a 2025 algebraic topology paper. Multipersistence modules track topological features across several parameters, and researchers want to split them into simpler parts. Decompositions are understood for one parameter but stay hard for two or more.

He shows a pointwise finite-dimensional bipersistence module is middle-exact exactly when it matches the homology of a homotopy degree one functor. From that he derives a new, more synthetic proof that middle-exact bipersistence modules decompose into intervals. He also proves a decomposition theorem for multipersistence modules over a finite poset. Any middle-exact such module splits as a direct sum of projective, injective, and bidegree one modules. The theorem holds even without pointwise finite-dimensionality. For topological data analysis, cleaner decompositions clarify what multiparameter summaries can capture. The functor calculus viewpoint may unify results that needed separate ad hoc arguments.
arxiv-2510-06578:
Wensi Wu and four colleagues work on measuring strain in heart valves without surgery. Their 2025 paper tackles valvular heart disease, a major cause of heart failure. The thin leaflets of a valve flex with every heartbeat, and their strain hints at coming damage. Measuring that strain from ordinary clinical images has been hard.

The team presents a feature-tracking method that follows points on the leaflets through 3D ultrasound images. It needs no parameter tuning and handles very different valve shapes. Against a finite element benchmark, it beat other point-based methods on accuracy. It was tested on valves from both children and adults. One clear pattern emerged from the data. Valves with higher median strain and wider strain spread tended to show leaflet billowing. With more validation, such measures could help doctors judge disease and predict how long a repair will last.
arxiv-2510-06778:
Aparna Komarla and Max Hill model product markets the way biologists model predator and prey. Their paper, presented at the INFORMS 2024 meeting, uses ordinary differential equations for market dynamics. Traditional econometric tools track correlations in sales data. They rarely explain the mechanisms that move market share between rival products.

Their framework treats market segments as interacting populations that grow or shrink. Competitive advantage drives flows of customers between segments. The flows include new product adoption, refresh cycles, and products going obsolete. A scoring system quantifies each product's appeal from its attributes and consumer tastes. Demand allocation rules can then mimic outcomes from winner-take-all to split markets. The authors argue such models can beat classic autoregressive forecasts in accuracy. Just as valuable, the equations support scenario analysis for managers. A firm can ask what happens if a rival improves, before the market answers for real.
arxiv-2510-06878:
Daria Ozerova and Ekaterina Trofimova teach language models to debug their own code more stubbornly. Their 2025 paper improves iterative refinement, where a model fixes its answer over several rounds. The search space of possible fixes is enormous. Fixed rules for exploring it cannot learn from which fixes worked before.

Their framework, TGPR, couples reinforcement learning with a tree search guided by Thompson sampling. The search explores failed and successful fix attempts alike. That generates denser, more varied training stories for the model to learn from. A custom hybrid reward scores the debugging trajectories. On the MBPP code benchmark, first-try accuracy rose by up to 4.2 percentage points over a strong baseline. On the harder APPS benchmark, success within ten tries rose by up to 12.5 percentage points. HumanEval gains pointed the same way. The approach treats debugging strategy itself as something a model can learn.
arxiv-2510-07178:
Ziv, Lan, Chemla, and Katzir test whether language models share the built-in biases that shape human language. Their 2025 paper asks a sharp question. Humans find some invented languages impossible to learn naturally. If models learn those as easily as real ones, their biases differ from ours. Earlier work claimed models do favor real languages. This team checked that claim across more languages and more distortions.

The authors trained a mid-size model on real languages and scrambled counterparts. In most cases, the model learned both kinds with equal ease. They also tested whether the model set real languages apart as a group. Across several measures, no clear separation appeared. It matters for debates about what large models can teach us about the human mind. Their learning seems broad and even, where human learning is picky.
arxiv-2510-07278:
Baker, Saxena, and Kyaw remove a bottleneck in quantum simulation by preparing starting states in a universal way. Their 2025 paper uses the first-quantized picture, where particles occupy positions in a chosen basis. Simulations need starting states that respect particle symmetry. Building them case by case is slow and error-prone. The authors map occupation-style configurations directly into the first-quantized form. A classic algebra homomorphism, named for Jordan and Schwinger, supplies the dictionary between the two pictures.

The recipe encodes a superposition of symmetry labels, then undoes a quantum Schur transform to finish. Its cost grows only polynomially with system size and desired accuracy. It works for fermions, for bosons, and even for exotic paraparticles. Resource estimates fit inside leading simulation pipelines for chemistry and materials. A universal loader simplifies the front end of many simulation workflows.
arxiv-2510-07378:
Arora, Ranjan, Moitra, and Mallik argue that a thin hydrogen sky on a rocky exoplanet betrays active volcanism below. Their 2025 paper models close-in worlds on eccentric orbits around their stars. Tides flex such planets and heat their interiors strongly. Hydrogen atmospheres should escape quickly, so keeping one demands a powerful source. The authors couple an interior model to an atmosphere model. Outgassing from a magma ocean must outpace energy-driven escape for at least a billion years to win.

Three ingredients prove necessary together: strong eccentricity, a water-rich basal magma ocean, and chemically reduced melts. The team maps an outgassing zone where the balance works. A specifically thin hydrogen layer signals present-day magmatic supply rather than a leftover primordial blanket. Observers can test the idea by pairing precise mass, radius, and orbit measures with space telescope estimates of atmospheric weight.
arxiv-2510-07578:
Zong, Bierly, Boker, and Eldardiry review liquid neural networks against the recurrent networks they aim to succeed. Their 2025 paper compares the families on three axes: accuracy, memory efficiency, and generalization. Recurrent networks and their gated descendants, LSTMs and GRUs, are the mature standard for sequence data, with a vast ecosystem. Liquid networks are a biologically inspired, continuous-time alternative whose neurons follow differential equations, letting them adapt their dynamics to irregular, noisy, non-stationary streams.

The surveyed evidence favors liquid networks on out-of-distribution generalization, the failure mode that haunts deployed sequence models. Some liquid variants also beat recurrent baselines on parameter efficiency and computational speed. The incumbent's advantages are maturity and scale: recurrent architectures are proven at sizes liquid models have not reached.
arxiv-2510-07878:
Sayed, Reddy, Toomey, and Gleyzer wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on simulating gravitational lensing with learning. Lensing bends light from distant galaxies around massive objects, revealing dark matter. Simulators trace rays accurately but too slowly for surveys. The authors train FlowLensing, a flow-matching model with a diffusion transformer backbone. It generates lensed images directly, conditioned on dark matter model choices and continuous parameters.

Against those simulators, FlowLensing ran more than two hundred times faster on demanding dark matter models. Its images kept high fidelity. The model handles both discrete cases, such as dark matter scenarios, and settings like subhalo abundance. It can also recover parameters that distinguish cold dark matter from axion models. Fast synthesis could let surveys like Euclid probe small dark matter structures statistically. The authors plan to build lensing equations into the model for still deeper fidelity.
arxiv-2510-07978:
Jain and five coauthors at Krutrim AI wrote this 2025 paper introducing VoiceAgentBench, a test suite for voice assistants that act as agents. Speech models can now take spoken requests and run multi-step tasks with tools. Older speech benchmarks mostly grade transcription or single questions. Agentic work also demands cultural grounding and resistance to trickery. It holds over five thousand synthetic spoken queries rooted in Indian contexts.

Tasks range from single tool calls to multi-tool workflows, multi-turn dialogues, and safety probes. Seven languages are covered: English, Hindi, and five other Indian languages. A sampling method diversifies the synthetic speakers by their voice embeddings. Scoring covers tool choice, structural consistency, and invocation correctness, including under attack. Models showed big gaps in orchestration, Indic languages, and robustness. The authors hope the suite pushes speech agents toward capability that survives real accents, languages, and misuse.
arxiv-2510-08078:
Chen and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper naming and fixing a failure of video-to-audio generators: they invent sounds that are not in the video. Models add speech or music with no visual source, a flaw standard metrics never check. The authors call it insertion hallucination and blame dataset bias. They built an evaluation framework using a voting ensemble of audio event detectors and two new metrics.

Their fix, Posterior Feature Correction, works at inference with no retraining. The model generates audio once, hallucinated segments get flagged, and a second pass regenerates with matching video features masked. Across mainstream benchmarks, hallucination prevalence and duration fell by over half on average. Quality and synchronization scores did not degrade. The paper gives the field its first definition, measurement, and remedy for the problem.
arxiv-2510-08178:
Schmidt and Stober wrote this 2025 machine learning paper fixing a hidden flaw in how image classifiers are protected against rotations and scaling. Fine-grained tasks like insect identification turn on subtle cues, yet photos arrive at arbitrary poses. Canonicalization networks rotate each sample into a standard pose before classification. They are usually trained assuming the dataset is already aligned, which real datasets never are. The authors' bootstrapping algorithm re-aligns the training data gradually during training itself.

The process repeatedly reduces the dataset's pose variance while the canonicalizer learns. They prove convergence guarantees under mild conditions for arbitrary compact transformation groups. On four fine-grained benchmarks, the method beat equivariant architectures and ordinary canonicalization baselines. It also matched heavy data augmentation without its compute cost. Biodiversity monitoring motivates the work, where field photos are uncontrolled by nature.
arxiv-2510-08278:
Fevziye Irem Eyiokur and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv method that helps robots find the object a person means. The task, called embodied reference understanding, mixes spoken words with a pointing gesture. Scenes often hold several similar objects, so words alone can point to the wrong one. Depth maps, which record how far each part of the scene sits, add a helpful extra clue.

Their framework joins three parts: extra training data made with a language model, depth map input, and a depth-aware choice module. The module weighs language, gesture, and distance together before picking the target object. Tests on two data sets showed clear gains over earlier baseline systems. The authors report more accurate and more reliable picks of the intended object. The gains held in cluttered scenes where similar objects sit close together.
arxiv-2510-08478:
Ramin Golestanian studies how tracer particles wander in driven electrolytes in a 2025 arXiv paper in statistical physics. Electrolytes are fluids full of ions, driven here by an applied field. Hydrodynamic fluctuations, the random flows of the solvent itself, push tracer particles around. Using a self-consistent field theory, he works out the resulting motion in all dimensions.

The theory reveals a rich set of scaling regimes, including two distinct forms of anomalous diffusion. Anomalous diffusion means spread grows at a rate unlike ordinary random walks. Crossovers between regimes are mapped in terms of the system's tuning parameters. A short-time ballistic regime, where motion is nearly straight-line, appears beyond two dimensions. A long-time diffusive regime exists only at four dimensions and above. Long-ranged hydrodynamic interactions dominate despite Debye screening, which usually hides electric effects.
arxiv-2510-08778:
Fernández–Sarmiento and Martínez–Rodríguez build a theory of gravity from a broken symmetry, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their starting point is Weyl invariance, a freedom to rescale lengths that the theory holds at high energy. When that symmetry breaks on its own, a field called the dilaton appears and plays a bookkeeping role. Through it, the field tied to the symmetry gains a mass near the largest scale in physics.

The resulting interactions fit inside a known healthy family of vector field theories, free of the instabilities that ruin many rivals. The authors also show the new field can be traded for a moving twist in spacetime itself, a quantity called vector torsion. Their construction lists every allowed term in an orderly way, with no leftover terms in four dimensions. At low energy, the theory settles back into Einstein's general relativity with small, controlled corrections.
arxiv-2510-08978:
Wang and colleagues take aim at a notorious flaw of AI image generators: mangled hands, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text-to-image models now render scenes convincingly, yet fingers still come out fused, missing, or bent in impossible ways. Oddly, no standard tool graded hand quality on its own, so generators had no clean signal for fixing the problem and detectors missed a telltale sign of forgery. The team defines hand quality assessment as its own task.

They first built a training set of forty-eight thousand images arranged as matched high- and low-quality hand pairs, which supplies supervision cheaply without human labeling. On it they trained HandEval, a judge that combines a multimodal model's visual understanding with knowledge of hand keypoints. On a human-graded test set from leading generators, it matched human opinion better than rival tools. Used in generation and forgery detection, it improved both.
arxiv-2510-09278:
Jiuheng Lin and four co-authors published CLARity in 2025, an arXiv paper on training expert language models in fields where data is scarce. Their tool is reinforcement learning, which trains a model by rewarding good answers. Training often rests on multiple-choice questions, and the team warns that plain rewards can raise accuracy while harming the quality of reasoning.

To fix that risk, CLARity rewards answers that stay logically consistent, using only a small general model as the guide. Training runs in two stages that first refine and then monitor responses, and the data is reshaped as training proceeds. The authors report consistency gains of sixteen and a half percent and accuracy gains of seven and a half percent over rival methods. Human judges also rated the answers as more coherent and more professional.
arxiv-2510-09378:
Natalie Abreu, Nikhil Vyas, Sham Kakade, and Depen Morwani ask how much speed approximate training methods leave on the table, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Training large language models uses optimisers, and second-order methods use curvature information to take better steps, but they are usually replaced by cheaper approximations. The team establishes a practical ceiling by running full Gauss-Newton updates, an exact curvature method, on transformers up to one hundred fifty million parameters.

Full Gauss-Newton cut the number of training steps more than fivefold compared with strong baselines such as SOAP and Muon. A layerwise version that ignores links between layers nearly matched the full method. The authors conclude that the Gauss-Newton approximation captures what matters for fast convergence. They also note a wide gap between current approximate methods and an ideal layerwise method, marking room for better optimisers.
arxiv-2510-09478:
Sina Beyraghi, Javad Shabanpour, Giovanni Geraci, Paul Almasan, and Angel Lozano plan where to place smart radio surfaces in a 2025 arXiv paper. A reconfigurable intelligent surface, or RIS, is a panel that reflects wireless signals in controlled directions to fill coverage gaps. Cities differ so much that good placement has to be site-specific rather than generic.

The team built a digital twin of a United Kingdom city with the Sionna ray tracing tool and calibrated the scene against measured data. Their automated method chooses placement, orientation, and configuration of each surface, plus the base station beamforming, across 4G, 5G, and possible 6G frequencies. Candidate sites come from scattering-based rays, and clustering users keeps the planning cost down. The results carry a warning: meaningful coverage gains need dense deployments of large panels, which raises hard questions about cost and practicality.
arxiv-2510-09578:
Yuqian Huo, David Quiroga, Anastasios Kyrillidis, and Tirthak Patel improve how variational quantum algorithms are scheduled in a 2025 arXiv paper. These algorithms are leading candidates to show quantum utility on near-term machines. Users usually run them on the highest-fidelity qubits available, which gives good results but leaves the rest of the machine idle and throughput low.

Earlier work showed an algorithm can start on weaker qubits and move to stronger ones later without losing much quality. The authors' technique, Nest, varies the fidelity map of the algorithm carefully across its whole run. That scheduling not only reached near-optimal results but also converged faster than fixed assignments. Nest also co-locates several algorithms on the same computer at once, raising total throughput. The paper frames the three gains, performance, speed, and throughput, as one balancing act solved together.
arxiv-2510-09978:
Liang, Jian-Fu Zhang, Na-Na Gao, and Nian-Yu Yi study turbulence driven by magnetic reconnection in this 2025 arXiv paper in plasma physics. Reconnection is the snapping and rejoining of magnetic field lines, a process that frees energy in plasmas across space. It almost always comes with turbulence, and how the two shape each other is still poorly known.

The authors work in a frame where the reconnection drives its own turbulence. They measure the bulk traits of that turbulence, the patterns that stay stable when the chaos is averaged out. Such traits test which theories of turbulent reconnection match real plasmas. The results bear on solar flares, fusion machines, and other places where field lines reconnect in a stirred plasma.
arxiv-2510-10078:
Ahn and co-authors improve speech emotion recognition in this 2025 arXiv paper on affective computing. Recognizing emotion from speech needs large, well-labeled training sets, which are scarce. Data augmentation helps, and generative models have recently done well at it, creating extra training samples.

The authors add mutual information regularization to the generative model. Mutual information measures how much the generated samples share with the emotional content they are meant to carry. Regularizing on it steers generation toward samples that keep the emotion clear, not just plausible speech. The aim is better recognition when labeled voices are few. Reliable emotion recognition supports call analysis, assistive tools, and mental health screening.
arxiv-2510-10178:
Linton embeds free-by-cyclic groups into larger ones in this 2025 arXiv paper in geometric group theory. A free-by-cyclic group is built from a free group, where words cancel only trivially, together with a cyclic twist given by a mapping torus construction. Feighn and Handel proved broad results about subgroups of such mapping tori.

Linton refines those results for the free-by-cyclic case. He shows that every finitely generated free-by-cyclic group embeds inside a group of the same kind built from a finitely generated free group. When the original group is hyperbolic, meaning it has negative-curvature geometry, the embedding can be made quasi-convex inside a hyperbolic host. Such embeddings transfer properties between groups.
arxiv-2510-10278:
Chiu, Silviu Pitis, and Mihaela van der Schaar simulate oral medical exams for language models in this 2025 arXiv paper on clinical AI. Real clinical reasoning is hypothesis-driven: doctors refine a diagnosis from limited information by asking targeted questions and ordering tests step by step. Current medical benchmarks instead give all information at once in single-turn questions.

The authors build viva voce simulations, spoken-style exams where the model must gather information actively. That format tests whether a model can decide what to ask next, not just recall facts. A model that reasons like a clinician should narrow hypotheses as evidence arrives. The benchmark aims to expose reasoning gaps that knowledge tests hide.
arxiv-2510-10378:
Kyem and co-authors detect pavement cracks without manual labels in this 2025 arXiv paper on infrastructure monitoring. Pixel-level crack annotation is slow and costly, which limits how far automated road inspection can scale. The authors ask whether effective pixel-level segmentation is feasible with no manual annotation at all.

Their self-supervised multi-scale transformer learns from unlabeled road images, with attention-guided fusion combining features across scales. Attention directs the model to the thin, branching patterns that cracks form. Removing the labeling bottleneck would let road agencies survey whole networks from camera footage. The study tests the feasibility boundary of label-free crack mapping rather than assuming annotation is unavoidable.
arxiv-2510-10878:
Zheng Cao and three co-authors build a model that scores how bubbly a stock price looks, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their Hyped Log-Periodic Power Law model detects and quantifies financial bubbles. Labels come from a log periodic power law fit, sentiment scores, and a hype index the team developed in earlier work on forecasting volatility with language models. A dual stream transformer trained on market data turns these ingredients into a time series of confidence values, the Bubble Score.

A distinctive feature is that one framework captures both extreme overpricing and underpricing, positive and negative bubbles. In backtests on United States equities from 2018 to 2024, the approach earned an average annualized return of 34.13 percent in the reported results. It generalized remarkably well across industry sectors. Its conservative bias in calling bubble periods keeps false positives low, valuable for market signaling and decision making.
arxiv-2510-11778:
A. T. Barnes leads the PHANGS collaboration in cataloguing glowing gas clouds across nineteen nearby galaxies. These nebulae shine in hydrogen-alpha light where young stars ionize surrounding gas. The catalogue, presented in a 2025 arXiv paper, rests on sharp Hubble Space Telescope images matched to a fixed physical resolution of ten parsecs. Spectroscopy from the MUSE instrument adds the gas physics.

The catalogue holds 5,177 nebulae. The team robustly classified 4,882 as H-two regions, nurseries of massive stars, and separated out planetary nebulae and supernova remnants. They measured electron densities for more than half of the regions. The typical cloud spans about twenty parsecs, and roughly a third are complexes holding several bubbles at once, a pattern stronger in galactic centers. A size relation calibrated on the Hubble sample then extends size estimates to over thirty thousand fainter nebulae.
arxiv-2510-11878:
Anastasiya Pechko and six colleagues present GS-Verse, a way to grab and deform virtual objects in virtual reality with realistic physics. Today's VR tools often wrap objects in crude tetrahedral cages, which cheapens both looks and physical accuracy. GS-Verse instead welds an object's ordinary 3D mesh directly to a Gaussian splatting representation, the fuzzy-blob rendering style prized for realism. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds the whole system to work with any physics engine.

Because the splats ride on the mesh surface, deformations stay precise and surfaces look right while users stretch, twist, and shake things. Reusing existing mesh assets also simplifies content creation. The team validated GS-Verse against the leading method that couples VR with Gaussian splatting. In a study with eighteen participants, GS-Verse proved significantly better for physics-aware stretching. It was also more consistent across other manipulations. Further tests confirmed high, reliable performance.
arxiv-2510-11978:
Jusheng Zhang and three colleagues stabilize the preference tuning of vision-language models. Such tuning teaches a model to favor good answers over bad ones, but obviously wrong negative examples inject useless gradient noise that can wreck training. Their 2025 arXiv paper rethinks the process as managing learning dynamics, and proposes Cooling-Weighted DPO.

The recipe has two stages. First, supervised training with gentle negatives, lightly weighted wrong answers that curb overconfidence without harsh penalties. Second, a preference stage where each negative's influence is scaled by a cooling weight. The weight comes from the model's own average token probability on that negative, muting easy or off-distribution examples while keeping hard ones loud. Across varied vision-language tasks, the method trained more stably, calibrated better, and won more pairwise comparisons than plain supervised tuning or vanilla DPO. It also converged in fewer steps, and ablations credit the cooling weight itself.
arxiv-2510-12178:
Abdulhady Abas Abdulla and seven colleagues survey Meta's LLaMA herd and the lightweight saddles that tame it. Their 2025 arXiv review traces the LLaMA family from the first generation through LLaMA 4, models spanning seven billion to two hundred eighty-eight billion parameters, including multimodal and mixture-of-experts variants. The second thread is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, adapting giants by training only a sliver of their weights.

Five methods receive detailed treatment: LoRA, the two LLaMA-Adapter generations, LLaMA-Excitor, and quantized QLoRA. For each, the survey explains the mechanism, counts the parameter savings, and gives applications from instruction tuning to multimodal tasks. Structured comparisons include cases where tuned LLaMA models beat larger baselines. Real-world deployments in legal and medical domains ground the catalog. The authors close with open challenges, from longer contexts to robustness.
arxiv-2510-12278:
Ciacco and co-authors apply quantum annealing to a real staff scheduling problem in schools, in a 2025 arXiv paper. A public school in Calabria, Italy must distribute collaborators across kindergartens, primary schools, and secondary schools at several sites. Assignments must respect availability, competencies, and fairness, a mix that makes manual scheduling slow and contentious.

The authors formulate the allocation as an optimization model and solve it with quantum annealing, a quantum method that seeks low energy configurations matching good schedules. To their knowledge this educational staffing problem has not been tackled this way before. Experiments on real world data from the school show that the annealer produced balanced assignments in short runtimes. The results suggest quantum optimization can be useful for educational scheduling. They also point toward value in other complex allocation tasks with many competing constraints.
arxiv-2511-00378:
Yongyang Cai reviews how integrated assessment models handle uncertainty. These models link climate science, economics, and policy to test how human activity and the climate system affect each other, and officials rely on them when weighing climate strategies. Both halves of the system, the physical climate and social behavior, carry deep uncertainties that can swing the advice a model gives.

The review sorts the kinds of uncertainty these models face and surveys the modeling approaches used to manage them. It highlights recent methodological advances, including newer computational methods, and traces what they imply for policy. For model builders and policy readers alike, the overview maps where confidence is earned and where caution is due.
arxiv-2511-00478:
Robert Anderson, Haosui Duanmu, M Ali Khan, and Metin Uyanik prove that competitive markets with harmful byproducts can still reach equilibrium. Their setting is a measure-theoretic general equilibrium model, the benchmark formal picture of perfect competition, enriched with production, bads such as emissions that harm agents, and wide-ranging externalities. A famous counterexample by Hara had shown equilibrium can fail once bads enter, leaving a foundational gap.

When bads and externalities are modeled in an economically natural way, the authors show, equilibrium exists after all. Their result is the first existence theorem with bads for this class of models. The proof leans on nonstandard analysis, which supplies a systematic bridge from finite economies to infinite ones, a technique with reach beyond this problem.
arxiv-2511-00578:
Krishna Tewary, Sanjoy Biswas, and Shivam Verma explore a portal extension of the standard model built around a heavy vector-like lepton, and ask what a future multi-TeV muon collider would see. The hunting ground is associated production: a Higgs boson created together with a vector boson, either the familiar Z or a dark photon, the messenger of a hidden sector.

Producing a Higgs with a Z stays close to the standard prediction across wide parameter ranges. Producing one with a dark photon can surge instead, because the heavy lepton's interaction does not decouple. The dark channel can dwarf the Z channel by up to a hundredfold within safe theory limits. A detailed analysis of the bottom-quark plus missing-energy signature sets exclusion reach for the dark photon's mass and coupling, tied also to dark matter and muon measurements.
arxiv-2511-00878:
Ahmed Magbool, Vaibhav Kumar, Marco Di Renzo, and Mark Flanagan propose a stacked flexible intelligent metasurface for future wireless networks. A metasurface is a sheet of tiny elements that can shape radio waves. Stacking several sheets lets the system process signals in the wave domain itself.

Their new element is flexibility: each layer can be physically morphed, bent into a better shape for the channel at hand. They build transmit, receive, and channel models, then pose the task of maximizing the total data rate under power, morphing distance, and element response limits. An alternating optimization method based on gradient projection solves it, and simulations show clear gains over the rigid stacked version.
arxiv-2511-01078:
Qinwei Huang and colleagues add predictive side tasks to multi agent reinforcement learning, where several agents must cooperate while seeing only part of the world. Most systems train policies from reward alone, even though observations, messages, and other agents' behavior carry useful signal.

Their framework, BEPAL, trains each agent's policy alongside a belief model that predicts hidden state information, such as other agents' rewards or directions of motion. Training is centralized while execution stays decentralized. The extra prediction work enriches the agents' internal representations and steadies learning. On a predator prey task and on Google Research Football, BEPAL improved performance metrics by about sixteen percent on average and converged more stably than baselines.
arxiv-2511-01178:
Ming Tang and colleagues release BzScope, a Python package that computes absolute cross sections for neutron phonon scattering in crystal powders. Such calculations predict how neutrons bounce off the vibrations of a crystal lattice, and older histogramming methods struggle to reproduce sharp features and to converge over large ranges of momentum and energy.

BzScope uses an adapted integral method for one and two phonon scattering in ideal powders, staying numerically robust out to very large momentum transfer. Higher order scattering is handled through an established thermal neutron package, NCrystal, with a plugin for Monte Carlo codes. Benchmarks against nickel, lithium hydride, and beryllium readings confirm it works, and it improves accuracy for low symmetry materials by avoiding an isotropic shortcut.
arxiv-2511-01278:
Takashi Tsuboi studies bounded domains: the shapes of compact, connected three dimensional solids in ordinary Euclidean space whose boundary is one smooth connected surface. Because every such surface bounds a unique solid, the objects match compact connected surfaces, and the question is how to recognize their shapes.

Tsuboi projects the solid onto lines and studies the Reeb graphs of those height functions, summaries that track how the level sets connect and split, for both the solid and its boundary. He introduces weighted and indexed versions of those graphs. When the weights stay below a stated threshold, the solid can be deformed by isotopy into an embedded handlebody. The work is driven by a visibility question: can the solid be reshaped so every boundary point sees infinity along some ray?
arxiv-2511-20378:
Agarwal and colleagues review efforts to pin down matter at extreme densities. Their 2025 article concerns the equation of state of dense nuclear matter. Such matter fills neutron stars and forms in heavy-ion collisions. Lab experiments probe it under controlled conditions. Telescopes now probe it through combined astronomy signals too. Each source alone leaves the picture incomplete.

The review traces methods for both settings separately. It then surveys frameworks that combine the sources of data. Bayesian approaches named NMMA and BAND merge data with statistics. The MUSES engine integrates equation-of-state modules directly. Combined analyses yield mass-radius curves with 95 percent credibility bands. Pressure versus density gets the same treatment. Nuclear symmetry energy values are constrained jointly as well. Open challenges include consistent handling of doubt across regimes. The authors argue precision datasets now demand combined analysis. A coherent picture across all densities is the end goal.
arxiv-2511-20578:
Cui and colleagues print a fingertip-free glove that lets hands feel virtual worlds. Their 2025 paper presents an untethered electro-haptic device for the hand. Touch feedback makes virtual interaction feel real and grounded. Most current devices are wired, bulky, or too coarse. This one is ultra-thin, flexible, and sized to each user.

A photo of the user's hand generates the fitted pattern. Soft materials and printable liquid metal ink form the device. Fifteen electrodes deliver finely controlled electrical pulses to the skin. Those pulses evoke a wide range of touch sensations. Waveform shaping varies the feel across many scenarios. User studies found the device comfortable for long wear. Hand movement stayed natural with minimal interference. Feedback was precise and tunable in the trials. Task performance in virtual reality improved with the device. Immersion and realism ratings rose in most scenarios tested.
arxiv-2511-20678:
Kamal Paykan tests in 2025 whether learning machines can manage a cryptocurrency portfolio better than a classic finance formula. Crypto prices swing wildly and break the calm-market assumptions behind the Markowitz mean-variance model, his benchmark. His trading agent watches daily open, high, low, and closing prices plus volume for four coins (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, and Dogecoin) and resets the portfolio weights each day.

Paykan trained two actor-critic algorithms, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient and the entropy-regularised Soft Actor-Critic, both strengthened with LSTM memory networks that help spot patterns over time. In his evaluations both agents beat the Markowitz benchmark on total return and on risk-adjusted measures such as the Sharpe ratio, which weighs profit against volatility. The Soft Actor-Critic agent did best of all, nearly tripling the starting investment over the test period. The Markowitz portfolio, by contrast, grew more slowly and steadily.
arxiv-2511-20778:
Tatsuhiro Misumi and Cihan Pazarbaşı extend in 2025 exact WKB to general one-dimensional potentials. Exact WKB upgrades the semiclassical method with analytic continuation and resurgence theory, the mathematics of completing divergent series. In this second paper they make the energy parameter complex and track how the exact spectrum moves between sectors of a potential, with false and true vacua at different levels.

Some transitions are continuous. The discontinuous ones are governed by Stokes phenomena. They force different exact quantisation rules, hence different series, per sector. Two examples verify this: a lopsided triple-well, whose trans-series organises like the cluster expansion of a bion gas, and a tilted double-well, where the analysis predicts a neglected complex saddle. For genus-1 systems they derive rules linking any P-NP pair of cycles. All such data transform through classical parameters alone, explaining the S-duality transformations found earlier.
arxiv-2511-21478:
Alexis Metz-Donnadieu studies random family trees with height labels, in a 2025 probability paper. In these models, each edge changes the label by minus one, zero, or plus one, covering cases like branching random walks, Cayley trees, and plane trees. His object is the vertical edge profile: at every label level, a count of the edges stepping up to the next level and those stepping back down.

Metz-Donnadieu proves the profile evolves as a time-homogeneous Markov chain, meaning its future depends only on its present, for a wide class of such trees. Conditioning on the tree's total size preserves the property, provided the profile is enriched with the mass hanging below each label. He computes the transition rules explicitly for incomplete binary trees. The proof chops trees into excursions above and below fixed levels, and a companion paper links the rescaled profile to Brownian motion's local time.
arxiv-2511-21678:
Weihao Bo and eleven coauthors give multimodal AI a memory that learns from its own mistakes, in 2025. Multimodal language models solve each problem from scratch, repeating the same errors, because their usual memory stores past trajectories that suffer brevity bias and keep only one modality's trace. Human semantic memory works differently, holding visual and abstract knowledge in coordinated streams.

Their framework, ViLoMem, mirrors that design with dual streams. One encodes visual distraction patterns, the other logical reasoning errors, so the model can spot both kinds of failure separately. A grow-and-refine update cycle accumulates this knowledge incrementally, preserving stable strategies while sidestepping catastrophic forgetting. On six multimodal benchmarks, ViLoMem consistently improved first-try accuracy and sharply cut repeated visual and logical errors, with the strongest gains on mathematical reasoning. Ablations confirm both streams are necessary, and that separating distraction from hallucination is what makes the memory work.
arxiv-2511-22178:
Ashrafi and Kabir, researchers, classify autism spectrum disorder from brain scans with a graph neural network built to respect how the data are structured. Diagnosis still rests on subjective behavioral assessment, so an objective imaging-based aid matters. They use the ABIDE I collection, resting-state and structural MRI plus phenotypic records for 870 individuals. They build a population graph linking similar participants, then process each data modality in its own branch before fusion, with 5,206 features per person.

Two ingredients do the heavy lifting: Chebyshev polynomial spectral filters, which learn localized patterns on the graph cheaply, and graph attention layers, which weight neighbors by relevance when updating each person's representation. Under stratified five-fold cross-validation the model reaches 74.82 percent test accuracy and an AUC of 0.82. It beats conventional graph networks, autoencoder networks, and multimodal CNN baselines, with ablations confirming the attention component and tuning both contribute.
arxiv-2511-22378:
Pazola and colleagues test two deep learning strategies for filling gaps in environmental data, using groundwater storage in Bangladesh as case study. Sensors give values only at scattered points, yet planners need continuous maps over space and time. One strategy first builds grids from the inputs and predicts gridded targets. The other predicts at the measured points first and then fills the map by kriging, a standard method that weighs nearby points by correlation.

Filling the map turned out to be much harder than forecasting over time. Nearby wells were not always the most similar ones, and unknown geology strongly shaped each point's behavior. Both routes lost accuracy at measured locations once interpolation was added. Even so, the team's models beat the widely used GLDAS 2.2 estimates for Bangladesh by a substantial margin. Grouping locations by time-series behaviour could improve interpolation, they propose.
arxiv-2511-22778:
Navarra and Qureshi survey a field where combinatorics shapes algebra: polyomino ideals. A polyomino is a finite union of unit squares joined edge to edge, like a Tetris piece. Its ideal is generated by the inner 2-minors, small determinants, of the grid of variables over its cells. Whether that binomial ideal is prime, radical, or otherwise well-behaved depends delicately on the polyomino's shape.

The review unifies recent advances on two themes. First, the characterisation of prime polyomino ideals, settling which shapes yield prime ideals, alongside radicality, primary decomposition, and levelness. Second, an emerging bridge to classical rook theory, placing non-attacking rooks on boards: the coordinate ring's Hilbert-Poincaré series, and whether it is Gorenstein, connect to rook numbers of the board. They also present PolyominoIdeals, a Macaulay2 package implementing the theory, making the survey a working reference for newcomers.
arxiv-2511-22978:
Tou and colleagues built ShoppingComp, a real-world test for AI shopping agents, the kind now being added to chatbots to find products and write buyer's guides. Earlier e-commerce tests used simulated shops with fixed catalogs. So the team instead used real products and multi-constraint requests. It added a safety dimension: an agent must also spot when a product would be unsafe for the buyer's situation.

The benchmark holds 120 tasks and 1,026 scenarios curated by 35 experts, grading agents on finding the right product, writing a complete and sound report, and passing safety checks. The results were poor: the best model, GPT-5, scored only 11.22 percent overall under their grading.
