Gemini-2.5-Flash managed 3.92 percent on the same scale, with failures that included missing unsafe product uses and trusting promotional misinformation, which the authors say shows agents are not yet ready for real shopping carts.
arxiv-2511-23078:
Čertík and colleagues study ordered graphs, ordinary networks whose vertices also carry a fixed linear order. They ask how hard it is to decide whether one ordered graph maps into another. Such a map, an ordered homomorphism, must send edges to edges while respecting the vertex order, a stricter requirement than the usual graph homomorphism behind coloring problems in computer science.

They prove a reduction showing that homomorphism questions for unordered structures can be encoded with ordered bipartite graphs. So the ordered problem inherits their difficulty. And they establish that deciding ordered homomorphisms is NP-complete, the standard class of hard search problems. Parameterized by the size of the target graph, the problem is W[1]-hard, meaning no fast algorithm is expected even for small targets. The authors also identify classes of ordered graphs where polynomial-time algorithms do exist.
arxiv-2511-23478:
Maaz and colleagues diagnose a trust problem in leading video reasoning models. Whose written reasoning often sounds convincing while contradicting its own final answer or ignoring the video entirely. They formalize the failure with two proposed metrics, Think-Answer Consistency, checking whether the answer matches the reasoning. And a Video Attention Score, measuring how much reasoning leans on visual rather than textual cues, across 11 benchmarks in the study.

The analysis shows current models rely heavily on language priors over visual content. So the team post-trains Video-R2 with timestamp-aware supervised fine-tuning plus reinforcement learning guided by a new Temporal Alignment Reward. Trained on 15,271 samples from 11,816 unique videos, Video-R2 scores consistently higher on both diagnostic metrics and on overall accuracy across multiple benchmarks. Showing that temporal alignment and reasoning coherence buy more trustworthy video understanding in practice.
arxiv-2512-00078:
Finding single cells in brightfield microscope images matters for much biological research, yet labeled training data is scarce. Mario de Jesus da Graca, Jörg Dahlkemper, and Peer Stelldinger study whether synthetic images can help, in a 2025 study. They use diffusion models, a kind of generative AI, to create artificial microscopy images.

The team generates images with unconditional diffusion models and tests how they affect object detection performance. Hand annotation is slow and costly, so realistic synthetic data could ease that bottleneck. If the added images improve cell detection, labs could train better tools without months of manual labeling. Their study tests the idea with object detection as the measuring stick.
arxiv-2512-00278:
The Anderson model is the standard toy model for how disorder traps electrons in a material. Oluyinka Lindblad and Ezra Guerrero study its eigenvalues and eigenvectors on a finite grid in 2025. The model combines a discrete Laplacian with a random potential whose strength can vary.

The authors focus on simple eigenvalues and on eigenvectors that do not vanish, two properties that shape how the spectrum behaves. Such results support the theory of localization, which explains why some materials insulate instead of conducting. The work is mathematical physics, tightening the proofs behind a model used across condensed matter theory. The finite grid keeps the model computable while the disorder stays fully random.
arxiv-2512-00378:
Semantic search ranks documents by meaning, and witness-based systems are one way to build it. Nikit Phadke establishes a mathematical equivalence between such systems and Shannon's information theory in 2025. The system studied is called REWA, built on similarity witnesses.

Phadke proves that witness overlap is mutual information, a core quantity in information theory. REWA's bit complexity bounds are shown to arise from channel capacity limits, and ranking-preserving encodings obey rate-distortion constraints. Grounding a practical search method in classic theory clarifies its capacity limits and tells builders what no encoding can beat. Shannon's theory also sets the ceiling that no search encoding can exceed. Equivalence proofs like this one turn engineering intuition into settled mathematics.
arxiv-2512-00478:
Thermistor systems couple temperature and electric potential, and their mathematics mixes two parabolic equations. Miguel Nuñez-Chávez, Luis Yapu, and Juan Límaco establish existence, stability, and controllability for the parabolic-parabolic thermistor model in 2025. A single control force acts on just one equation of the system.

The authors prove well-posedness and energy estimates first, then local null controllability. Carleman estimates and an inverse function theorem drive the controllability proof. Thermistors protect circuits and measure temperature everywhere, so rigorous control results support devices that must steer heat and current together. Carleman bounds are the heavy tool behind most such proofs. One control for two equations is the economical case the authors aim for. For folks who steer heat and charge in one part, the gain is a proof they can cite. One push, in one place, can in time bring the whole part to rest.
arxiv-2512-00578:
Hyperquot schemes parametrize sequences of quotient sheaves of a vector bundle on a curve. Riccardo Ontani, Shubham Sinha, and Weihong Xu study the virtual intersection theory of these schemes in 2025. Their results generalize a classical formula known for ordinary Quot schemes.

The authors provide a closed formula for virtual counts of maps from the curve to a partial flag variety. Such counts belong to enumerative geometry, where intersection numbers answer how many maps satisfy given conditions. Extending the formula from Quot to Hyperquot schemes widens a tool used across geometry and mathematical physics. Quotient sheaves parametrize ways a bundle can map onto simpler bundles. Flag varieties are the targets whose map counts the formula delivers.
arxiv-2512-00678:
Braden Scherting, Otso Ovaskainen, Tomas Roslin, and David Dunson wrote a 2025 ecology paper on how to track biodiversity. Good policy needs good counts of species, yet field surveys are costly and often rest on rough choices. Groups of species and their habitats are often defined by habit, and indicator species are picked in ad hoc ways.

The team presents a model-based method that learns sub-communities from survey data itself. It also picks indicator species tied to those groups, in terms of both habitat and species. They show the idea on large-scale arthropod survey data. A firmer method could make monitoring cheaper and easier to repeat.
arxiv-2512-00878:
Chunlin Tian, Xuyang Wei, Huanrong Liu, Zhijiang Guo, and Li Li present a leaner fine-tuning method in a 2025 paper. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, is a popular way to fine-tune large language models cheaply. Instead of changing every weight, it trains small add-on matrices, yet it still costs a fair amount and can suffer interference on complex data.

Newer variants split LoRA's update matrices to exploit asymmetry, but training stays pricey. The team's resource-efficient version pushes the savings further. Cheaper fine-tuning matters for groups that must adapt big models on limited hardware, a common real-world constraint.
arxiv-2512-00978:
Mircea Merca studies a family of q-series in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Q-series are series built from a base variable q and appear across number theory and partition counting. MacMahon pioneered many such series, and recent work by several authors extended his ideas to higher-order partition counts.

Merca studies a class of q-series that arise from nested divisor structures, where divisors inside divisors shape the terms. These are called MacMahon-type series. Results here connect divisor sums with partition generating functions, two classic themes in number theory. Such identities often reveal that two very different counting problems are secretly the same.
arxiv-2512-01078:
SimWorld, a 2025 project, builds an open-ended simulator for AI agents that must live in a realistic world. Language and vision agents now shine at math, coding, and computer use. Complex physical and social environments remain much harder for them.

Acting in the real world, for example by earning income or running a business, demands interaction, reasoning, training, and evaluation across many embodied scenarios. SimWorld aims to supply that massive-scale testbed. A shared simulator would let researchers train agents on survival and work skills safely, and compare systems on the same hard, open-ended challenges.
arxiv-2512-01178:
Zihua Liu, Hiroki Sakuma, and Masatoshi Okutomi present VSRD++ in a 2025 computer vision paper. Monocular 3D object detection finds objects and their 3D boxes from a single camera image, a fundamental task in scene understanding. Most methods need extensive 3D annotations, usually drawn from LiDAR point clouds through labor-intensive labeling.

VSRD++ is a weakly supervised framework that removes the need for 3D annotations. It uses neural-field-based volumetric rendering, guided by weak two-dimensional supervision only. Cutting the labeling burden matters for cars and robots, where cameras are cheap but annotated 3D data is scarce and expensive.
arxiv-2512-01378:
Qiyue Zhang and Jingtao Shi study how to pick a stock mix that balances gain and risk. Their setup adds sudden jumps in prices, modeled as Poisson events. It also uses recursive utility, where taste for risk is built from a backward equation with jumps.

Two classic tools are used to solve the task. One is the maximum principle, the other is dynamic programming. The pair apply both and then study how the two answers link. That link matters since each tool gives a distinct view. A clear link lets users cross-check results in jump-heavy markets.
arxiv-2512-01478:
Omer Sela, Michael Chertok, and Lior Wolf model motion in pro basketball from body data. Their frame, CourtMotion, reads skeletal tracks of players. It learns to spot and forecast plays as they form. A good forecast needs more than raw motion.

Plays gain sense from game context, like score and clock. The model links motion traits to that sense. Coaches and analysts could use it to tag plays fast. Broadcast tools could call out a forming play live. The work treats motion and meaning as one joint task. Skeletal input keeps the model light, since it skips raw video and works from joint tracks that tracking tools already produce.
arxiv-2512-01678:
Anubhab Rupesh Nasre and Rupesh Nasre speed up graph neural network training at scale. Such nets fuse two unlike workloads. Graph walks are irregular and memory-bound. Dense matrix work is regular and compute-bound. Popular tools favor ease of use over that split.

Their system, Morphling, fuses and schedules both parts with care. It aims for fast training on large graphs. Large graphs sit behind social, commerce, and biology tools. Faster training lets teams iterate on bigger data without a matching rise in cloud cost. Scale here means graphs with billions of edges, the size behind fraud rings and web graphs that small test setups cannot mimic.
arxiv-2512-01878:
Knowledge graphs store facts as entities joined by links, and reasoning over them means deciding which entities belong together. Gaganpreet Jhajj and Fuhua Lin propose in 2025 that this reasoning can be steered by surprise: entities close together in the graph should surprise an observer less than entities far apart.

The idea borrows the Free Energy Principle from neuroscience, where brains are said to act to keep surprise low. Here the knowledge graph plays the role of the agent's inner model of the world, and graph distance becomes a stand-in for expected surprise. The framing offers a fresh, principled way to guide inference across large linked datasets.
arxiv-2512-02178:
Drug makers must promise that nearly all units of a product meet quality standards, and tolerance intervals are the statistical tool behind that promise. Seokjun Choi studies in 2025 how to build such intervals using Dirichlet processes, a flexible Bayesian method that avoids assuming a fixed distribution shape.

A tolerance interval must contain a set share of the whole population with a stated confidence. Parametric methods work with small samples but suffer if the assumed distribution is wrong, while older non-parametric methods have their own limits. Choi's approach targets nonclinical pharmaceutical development, where samples are small and quality guarantees carry regulatory weight.
arxiv-2512-02378:
The random phase approximation is a standard way to work out how electrons in a material react as a group. Making it agree with itself step by step gives it better physics. Yue-Hong Wu, Xinguo Ren, and Ning-Hua Tong derive that self-agreeing form in 2025. They start from a broader scheme for Green's function work.

Their route works at all heats, not just near zero. At zero heat it lands on Rowe's classic form, as it should. More than a tidy proof, the frame gives a path to stretch the method still more. Sharper response maps feed straight into forecasts of how new materials act with light and charge.
arxiv-2512-02478:
Thomas P. Steele and David J. Warne study chemical reaction networks inside cells, where random noise matters. Standard models treat each reaction as memoryless, a Markov view with well developed simulation tools. Some biology breaks that view: gene transcription and translation carry delays, so the past shapes what happens next.

For such history dependent systems, both simulation and inference get harder. The authors present methods that handle non-Markovian dynamics, where waiting times are not simple exponentials. Better tools here help biologists fit models to real cell data and predict how noisy gene expression unfolds over time. Cell data with long tails in time is now the rule in labs, not the rare case it once was.
arxiv-2512-03078:
Some losses matter more when they are rare and large. Vahid Ramezani and Benjamin Englard study a risk tool built for that case in this 2025 work. The tool reshapes a base loss so rare, high-loss events count more, while the math stays workable.

The authors ask how that risk tool fits flow matching, a way to train models that turn noise into data. Their reading links risk ideas from statistics to this newer learning method. Such links could help builders train models that stay safe in rare cases. That matters in fields like health and finance. Risk-aware training could matter most when rare events carry the greatest cost of failure.
arxiv-2512-03178:
Lensed quasars can measure how fast the universe expands. Eric Paic and a large team report a new measure in this 2025 work, part of the TDCOSMO series. Light from a quasar split by gravity arrives at different times, and that delay gives the expansion rate.

The team focuses on a quasar lensed into two images, HE 1104-1805. Past milestone results leaned on quads, with four images, to pin down mass profiles. Adding doubles widens the sample. A firm rate helps test whether current cosmic models are complete. Doubles are more common than quads, so each added system strengthens the method's base.
arxiv-2512-03278:
False claims can often be checked against hard records. Michael Theologitis and Dan Suciu build a system for that check in this 2025 work. Politicians, media, and public figures make claims about crime, growth, and health that records can test.

Their system, called Thucy, uses language model agents that work together. The agents query relational databases, the structured stores behind most official data. A tool that cites records could help journalists and citizens judge claims fast. It also shows where a claim has no support in the data. Claims about budgets or crime rates suit the tool best, since records there are structured and public.
arxiv-2512-03678:
Hao-Run Cai and Han-Jia Ye tackle tabular data whose meaning drifts with time, in this 2025 paper. A feature's relationship to the label evolves as the world changes, so static models stale and adaptive ones chase noise. Their analysis identifies shifting feature semantics as the core difficulty.

They propose conditioning each feature's representation on its temporal context, adjusting properties like scale and skewness. This feature-aware modulation realigns what features mean across periods without heavy machinery. The design deliberately balances staying general against adapting to the present. Benchmark evaluations across temporal shifts validated the approach against both static and adaptive rivals.
arxiv-2512-03978:
Some diffusion equations degenerate, meaning their smoothing power fades or vanishes in places, and proving their solutions behave is delicate work. Khalid Baadi establishes well-posedness for a family of them in a 2025 analysis preprint. They are second-order and parabolic, with a rough, time-dependent fading part and lower-order terms that may grow without bound.

Baadi works with weak ones under minimal assumptions, allowing the troublesome terms to live in mixed space-time Lebesgue or Lorentz spaces. He proves a fundamental solution exists and is unique. It matches the evolution family of the source-free problem and represents each one. Off-diagonal decay estimates and Gaussian upper bounds follow. The approach is purely variational, avoiding smooth approximations. Two tools carry the proof: inequalities for fractional powers of the operator, and embeddings restoring time continuity.
arxiv-2512-05378:
Peng Gao and Xiaosheng Wu bound the average size of twisted sums built from the Fourier coefficients of a modular form. Modular forms are highly symmetric functions whose coefficients encode deep arithmetic information, and twisting those coefficients by Dirichlet characters — periodic multipliers — probes how the values distribute. The authors study moments: averages of the absolute value of character-twisted partial sums, raised to a range of powers, over all characters modulo a large prime.

For moments up to the first power they prove a sharp upper bound in the full range of the summation length. A consequence is an average-case estimate showing the normalized twisted sum is little-o of the square root of the length once both quantities grow — cancellation stronger than trivial bounds deliver. Estimates of this kind feed the analytic theory of L-functions, where understanding moments is tantamount to understanding the forms themselves.
arxiv-2512-05578:
Zheng Sun and four co-authors give a robot eyes that see chemistry. Hyperspectral imaging identifies materials by their full light spectrum, far beyond colour, but marrying it to robotic grasping has been blocked by cost and integration complexity. Their system pairs two pieces. PRISM is a polyhedral reflective scanning mechanism that captures distortion-free hyperspectral images with simplified hardware. SpectralGrasp is a framework that plans grasps from both the spatial and spectral content of the image.

In tests the system recognizes textiles better than human sorters and sorts objects more successfully than RGB-camera methods, with comparative experiments backing each component's contribution. Materials that look identical to an ordinary camera — the bane of recycling and textile handling — separate cleanly by spectrum. The authors present the work as evidence that hyperspectral guidance can move robotic grasping from appearance-based guessing toward material-aware handling in messy, dynamic settings.
arxiv-2512-05878:
Dominique Unruh and José Manuel Rodríguez Caballero bring the theory of bounded operators on complex spaces into the Isabelle proof assistant, where every step must check out mechanically. Bounded operators are central to quantum theory. Isabelle's library handles real vector spaces thoroughly, but the complex side, where physics lives, was thin. Their formalization builds the missing ground: complex normed spaces, Banach spaces, and Hilbert spaces.

On that ground they define the type of bounded operators between complex spaces and grow the theory around it. It covers unitary maps, projectors, adjoints, the extension theorem for bounded linear functions, the Loewner order, and closed subspaces. For finite dimensions, they connect operators to matrices, so verified operators can generate code. Quantum information, the first author's home field, leans on exactly these operators; having them machine checked turns a library of lemmas into trusted infrastructure.
arxiv-2512-06078:
Rathindra Nath Das and three co-authors build a finite dimensional toolkit for a young idea: entanglement in time. Timelike entanglement links moments, through correlations between time slices. They recast it as a generalized response tensor. A spacetime density kernel extends it to higher point correlations.

The payoff is unification. These functions reproduce the spectral form factor's moments. The kernel's own correlations yield the same form factor with rescaled times. Scrambling diagnostics and spectral statistics, two literatures that evolved separately, land on the same footing, and the fine grained dynamical information in exotic time orderings becomes legible. A common language lets one diagnostic testify about the other.
arxiv-2512-06178:
Georgiana Haldeman, Peter Ohmann, and Paul Denny bring measurement to a skill courses preach but rarely grade well: splitting code into meaningful pieces. Teachers need exercises whose difficulty they control. Their framework grades structuring tasks on repetition, code pattern, and data dependency.

An interactive tool generates tasks at chosen levels. It targets introductory courses. Instructors get a design space with dials, not a drawer of uneven exercises. Sound frameworks keep the reshuffle honest. Teachers can start small and raise the level step by step. Students learn to see structure before writing code from scratch.
arxiv-2512-06478:
Madhu Sudan surveys how algebra powers the codes that keep digital messages intact. Error correcting codes add smart redundancy to data so that noise in transit can be spotted and fixed. Sudan traces the history of these codes and the algorithms that make them work in practice, from early basic designs to modern ones.

Much of the survey is given to constructions and decoding methods that rest on fairly simple applied algebra. That algebra's part in building codes is widely known from textbooks. Its part in designing the algorithms that encode and decode, Sudan argues, is just as deep but far less widely understood. The survey works to close that gap, giving readers a path from the basic ideas to the modern frontier of algorithmic coding theory.
arxiv-2512-06778:
Federico Dell'Anna, Matteo Grotti, and Vito Giardinelli solve a classic network puzzle with cellular automata, grids of cells that update by local rules. The puzzle, maximum independent set, asks for the largest set of nodes in a graph with no two linked. It is notoriously hard in general, and it models tasks from scheduling to network design.

Their probabilistic automaton updates all cells at once and drifts toward sets that are maximal, hard to grow further. In simulations the chance of landing on a true maximum climbs steeply as the activation probability nears one, and they chart how the time to settle scales with graph size and connectivity. A quantum version then alternates a settling phase with a unitary shuffle that respects the constraints, concentrating weight on the maximum sets over repeated cycles. Tensor network simulations support the picture.
arxiv-2512-07078:
Bo Gao and co-authors rebuild a real-time object detector around the needs of very small objects, the first thing ordinary detectors lose. Their diagnosis names three flaws in the baseline design: attention spread evenly regardless of a scene's complexity. Feature pyramids whose signal strength drifts when images are enlarged, and stacked filters that steadily rub out the fine edges small objects depend on. Each proposed module answers one named flaw.

The resulting detector refines features iteratively in the frequency domain and aggregates them dynamically. It was tested on two very different benchmarks: surface defects on steel and tiny objects in drone footage. On both it reached strong accuracy scores while staying small and cheap to run, with parameters and operations well within real-time budgets.
arxiv-2512-07278:
Sanghoon Lee and Jiewon Park study when a curved space that satisfies Einstein's equations with no matter, a Ricci-flat or Einstein manifold, is forced to be completely flat. Their spaces curve less and less at infinity, with curvature decaying quadratically. The probe is the Green function, a basic potential attached to the space. The authors show that if the slope of that potential stays uniformly bounded away from zero, flatness follows.

A second result says that on Ricci-flat spaces with quadratic decay and orderly volume growth, the curvature is integrable to every power from two upward. Combining the two with deep results of Cheeger and Tian and of Kröncke and Szabó. The spaces must be of a special asymptotically flat kind, ALE spaces, with the best possible decay rate.
arxiv-2512-07478:
Jianghao Su, Zhuoran Zhuang, and their co-authors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on tool-using agents. Language models with tools can plan, call software, and fold the answers into their reasoning. Training such agents with rewards is slowed by two problems.

First, right-or-wrong rewards say nothing about the steps in between. Learning then crawls, because good and bad moves earn the same silence. Second, a group method can waste samples when every try earns the same reward. The authors answer the first flaw with Progressive Reward Shaping. It gives stage-wise feedback, rewarding clean tool calls first and correctness later. Short and long answers each get a scoring style that fits them. Their second method, VSPO, swaps useless samples for prompts chosen by task value. A smoothing rule steadies the training updates. Across question-answering benchmarks, the pair trains faster and finishes stronger than rival methods.
arxiv-2512-07678:
Franco Rabec, Jérôme Beugnon, Jean Dalibard, and Sylvain Nascimbene wrote this 2025 physics paper on ultracold atomic gases. Their subject is a binary mixture of Bose-Einstein condensates, clouds where two components share one trap. The interesting regime sits right at the threshold of miscibility.

At that threshold, the two clouds are poised between mixing and separating. The authors show the mixture's dynamics collapse into a single nonlinear equation.  Stable soliton solutions then appear in both one and two dimensions. Solitons are self-keeping waves that hold their shape as they travel. Binary mixtures also reach beyond the standard nonlinear Schrödinger story. They can mimic the Landau-Lifshitz equation, which governs spin chains in ferromagnets. One platform thus serves several classic equations. The experiments show how a tuned mixture becomes a flexible stage for soliton physics.
arxiv-2512-07778:
Sen Ye, Jianning Pei, Mengde Xu, Shuyang Gu, Chunyu Wang, Liwei Wang, and Han Hu wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Image generators usually squeeze pictures into a latent space first. Diffusion or autoregressive models then work inside that compressed world.

Standard encoders quietly constrain that space without shaping it on purpose. Nobody knew which latent distributions actually serve generation best. Their Distribution-Matching VAE aligns the encoder's output with any chosen reference distribution. The classic Gaussian prior becomes just one option among many. References can come from self-supervised features or from diffusion noise itself. With that freedom, the team compares latent shapes systematically. Distributions drawn from self-supervised features strike an excellent balance. They reconstruct images faithfully while staying easy to model. Strong generation quality arrives after strikingly few training epochs. Choosing the latent structure deliberately, they conclude, beats inheriting a fixed prior.
arxiv-2512-07978:
Jun Kimura, Ryusei Satoh, Kentaro Terada, and Sho Sasaki wrote this 2025 planetary science paper. Icy planetesimals seeded the outer solar system and may have watered the rocky planets. Their inner temperatures, though, seem to have varied wildly from body to body.

Samples from asteroid Ryugu speak of a cold, water-altered past. Iron meteorites from similar material instead record serious heating. Direct exploration samples only spots, so models must explain the diversity. The team builds one that grows a planetesimal from the outside in. Impact heating, water's phase changes, and chemical alteration all feature. Structural differentiation is tracked alongside the thermal story. Final size, growth timing, and growth style are varied systematically. Bigger bodies generally run hotter, but history matters as much as size. Early, fast growth can push interiors toward iron melting thresholds. Ryugu's cool material likely formed near a hydrated layer's surface. Convection sheds heat efficiently there.
arxiv-2512-08578:
Subhajit Barman and K Hari study three linked quantum probes that start together in a shared entangled state. The probes sit in flat spacetime and are taken as either still or moving at steady speeds. The authors ask how the light the probes emit, and the loss of their shared state, depends on how they are arranged.

Different layouts, motion directions, and switching patterns lead to clearly different emission behavior. The study also adds a warm background to mimic more real conditions, and traces how heat, motion, and switching each change the outcome. A practical aim runs through the work. By mapping which setups suffer least from loss of coherence, the results can help design probe systems that stay useful for longer.
arxiv-2512-08778:
Stefano Profumo and Kally Wen search short gamma ray burst catalogs for signs of exploding primordial black holes. Theory predicts that a black hole in its final evaporation stage would produce a very short, hard burst whose brightness rises steadily, with little or no afterglow. Such a backwards burst would look unlike normal bursts.

The authors build templates from full evaporation models, including detector response, and compare them with standard burst shapes. They test a set of well characterized short bursts from the Swift satellite that have faint or missing afterglows. Every event shows the usual fast rise and slow decay, which conflicts with the black hole prediction. Formal model comparison favors the standard fits for all bursts. No candidate is found, so the team sets an upper bound on the local explosion rate. Their template method can scale to larger catalogs.
arxiv-2512-08978:
Ruud Huijts and Koen Suilen report a six month pilot of an institutional artificial intelligence platform at Fontys, a university of applied sciences in the Netherlands. Fragmented adoption of commercial tools had created unequal access, high cost, and compliance risks from opaque processing and hosting outside Europe. Banning those tools was seen as unrealistic, so an accountable alternative was needed.

Their solution is a governed gateway with three layers. A familiar chat front end ties access to institutional identity and makes model choice explicit. A gateway core enforces policy, controls budgets, and routes traffic to European infrastructure by default. A provider layer wraps commercial and open models in institutional model cards for clear governance. The pilot ran reliably with no privacy incidents and strong adoption. The authors recommend a formal AI Officer role and argue that AI must be governed as strategy, not as a support function.
arxiv-2512-09078:
Anmay Raj presents an unsupervised analysis of stellar motions in the solar neighborhood using Gaia data. The study covers stars within a small distance of the Sun and uses full six dimensional position and velocity information. Its goal is to find stellar moving groups without assuming their membership in advance.

A density based clustering algorithm is applied in velocity space to locate overdensities blindly. The method recovers the kinematic cores of major local moving groups, including the Hyades and Pleiades streams. No prior assumptions about membership or spatial layout are used. The author analyzes velocity spread and structure of the recovered groups. Results show automated clustering is a robust tool for mapping the dynamical history of the local galactic disk. The substructures confirm a hierarchical pattern in local stellar kinematics. A catalog of high probability members is provided for future spectroscopic follow up work.
arxiv-2512-09478:
Igor A. Ostanin describes a framework that couples two methods to model granular and particulate systems across scales. The discrete element method tracks single particles and their mechanical contacts, but long-range forces between many particles are expensive. The kernel-free fast multipole method computes those long-range interactions well without depending on their exact form.

The combined code, built on the MercuryDPM discrete element software, handles problems where fine-scale particle mechanics meet coarse-scale long-range effects. Examples include electric forces in powders and clays, magnetic interactions in ferromagnetic granulates, and gravity in asteroid clouds. The framework also supports rigid clumps, letting non-spherical particles with any charge pattern interact over long distances. Several examples show the technique at work. The author presents the coupling as a way to address a large class of problems across scales that neither method handles well alone.
arxiv-2512-09678:
Alexey Kravatskiy and colleagues explore matrix norms as the engine of optimizers for training neural networks, going beyond the spectral norm behind the Muon update rule. Optimizing functions of weight matrices is central to deep learning, and the choice of norm shapes the update geometry. Their work builds families of algorithms from the duals of the Ky Fan norms.

The resulting Fanion family of linear minimization oracle algorithms sits close to Muon and to related methods like nu-SAM and Dion. Mixing Fanion updates with normalized or sign-based gradient updates by convex combination gives two families, the F-Fanions and S-Fanions, whose lead members are F-Muon and S-Muon. In an empirical study across tasks and settings, F-Muon and S-Muon matched Muon's performance and beat it on a convex problem. The authors present the families as a menu for matrix optimization in machine learning.
arxiv-2512-09878:
Sandhya Sajith Menon leads a team presenting GFH-v2, an improved pipeline for hunting long lasting gravitational waves from newborn magnetars. A magnetar is a neutron star with an extreme magnetic field. Just after birth, such a star may spin down mainly by radiating gravitational waves, producing a signal that lasts far longer than a chirp. The search builds on a generalized Frequency Hough transform, a technique for finding faint tracks in time frequency maps, and sharpens sensitivity and speed.

The authors describe what changed from the original implementation and how they choose the region of parameter space to search. They compute the method's theoretical sensitivity two ways: from formulas, and by injecting fake signals into real data from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detectors' fourth observing run. The two estimates back the improved performance. The pipeline is a firm base for directed searches after supernovae and other transient events.
arxiv-2512-09978:
Francesco Iacovelli, Jacopo Tissino, Jan Harms, and Emanuele Berti assess what a gravitational wave detector on the Moon could do. The proposed Lunar Gravitational Wave Antenna would listen in the decihertz band, between space and ground based instruments. The authors check detectability against events already recorded up to the latest catalog, and against simulated populations matching current reconstructions of the black hole population.

They find the lunar antenna alone would have caught more than a third of events seen so far. Each year it could see dozens of binaries that later merge for ground detectors, enabling early warning and joint analysis. Third generation ground detectors would catch most of those mergers, making hundreds of multiband events routine. A case study modeled on the most massive detection yet shows decihertz data alone can measure chirp mass superbly and locate the source well, even from one observatory.
arxiv-2512-10078:
Jingyao Ren, Eric Ewing, T. K. Satish Kumar, Sven Koenig, and Nora Ayanian map out a research agenda on why some multi agent pathfinding problems are hard in practice. Pathfinding for many agents on a shared map, with no collisions, is provably hard in the worst case. Yet real instances vary enormously in difficulty, and theory does not explain the variation. The authors call this empirical hardness and pose three challenges. First, algorithm selection: predicting which solver will win on a given instance. Second, identifying the instance features that drive difficulty.

Candidate features include phase transition structure and backbone or backdoor sets, small structures that control solvability. The third challenge is generation: using hardness knowledge to create genuinely hard instances and diverse benchmark sets, rather than accidental ones. The paper is a position and agenda piece, published at a leading multi agent systems conference.
arxiv-2512-10478:
Yumeng Zhang, Huayan Guo, and Vincent Lau design a cheaper way to estimate channels in extra-large massive MIMO, the antenna systems heading toward future wireless networks. Their arrays are so wide that users far apart are simply not visible to the same antennas, an effect called spatial non-stationarity. Instead of fighting that effect, the authors put it to work.

Their pilot scheme groups users whose visibility regions differ and lets each group share the same frequencies for channel sounding, so more users fit with less overhead. Inside a group, users are separated by shifted cyclic codes. The array itself is built from sub-arrays, each locally steady, with channel structure modelled by a two-dimensional Markov random field. A low-cost turbo Bayesian estimator using that model beat alternatives in simulation while serving more users.
arxiv-2512-10578:
Pierre Auclair-Desrotour and co-authors build an analytical model of atmospheric tides on rocky planets, the first of a planned series. Starlight heats one side of a planet more than the other, and the resulting thermal tide can speed up the planet's spin, fighting the slowdown from ordinary gravitational tides. That tug of war may explain Venus's odd rotation and a resonance in Earth's deep past.

Working in linear theory, the authors solve for the atmosphere's response to both gravitational and thermal forcing, under two bracketing temperature profiles: one uniform in temperature, one uniform in potential temperature. Cooling is included through Newtonian relaxation. Both cases fall under one closed-form solution, giving explicit three-dimensional fields for pressure, temperature, density, and wind through the whole atmosphere, ready for the torque formulas promised next.
arxiv-2512-10778:
Zitong Lan and co-authors build digital twins you can hear as well as see. Today's twins of real rooms are almost purely visual, yet acoustics carry much of a space's realism and usefulness. Their system, AV-Twin, claims to be the first practical way to construct an editable audio-visual twin using nothing but ordinary smartphones.

Phones capture the room impulse response, the fingerprint of how sound rings in the space, while a visual-assisted acoustic field model reconstructs the room's acoustics efficiently. Differentiable acoustic rendering then recovers what each surface is made of, acoustically speaking, by working backward from the recordings. With materials, geometry, and layout in hand, a user can remodel the room, swap a wall's material or move furniture, and both the picture and the sound update together. The result is a twin meant for real environments, not just laboratory scenes.
arxiv-2512-10878:
Xuan Zhao and co-authors turn explanations into a way to copy a classifier. A counterfactual shows the smallest change that would flip a model's decision, and such points hug the decision boundary. For rebuilding a target model with a surrogate, counterfactuals are informative but lopsided samples, and naively training on them shifts the surrogate's boundary away from the original.

Their method blends original samples with counterfactuals to estimate a prototype for each class as a Wasserstein barycenter, a kind of average that respects the shape of the data spread. Training the surrogate around those prototypes keeps the class structure intact and counters the boundary shift. Across several datasets, the rebuilt surrogates matched their target models more closely than with naive use of counterfactuals. The work, presented at an ICML 2025 workshop, links explaining a model and stealing its behaviour in one framework.
arxiv-2512-10978:
Xueqi Ma and co-authors study what different attention heads inside large language models actually do during reasoning. Models perform well on many tasks, but their inner workings remain hard to see. Drawing on ideas from human cognition, the team built a framework to map heads to specific mental functions.

They created CogQA, a dataset that breaks hard questions into step by step subquestions tied to functions like retrieval and logical reasoning. Probing several model families, they found sparse heads that specialise in these functions and interact in ordered ways. Removing such heads hurt reasoning, while boosting them improved accuracy. The findings suggest practical routes for designing, training, and fine tuning future models.
arxiv-2512-11178:
Takuya Kurihana and colleagues build a framework for learning from the messy, mixed data that cities generate. Transport, safety, and environmental decisions depend on information gathered by separate agencies in different formats and standards. National datasets are broad and standardised, yet still varied in type and structure, making joint analysis hard.

Their pipeline fuses data across domains over datasets that vary in space, in time, or in both, drawing on more than fifty sources. A graph learning module builds in homophily, the tendency of nearby places to behave alike, using the spatial data. Five demonstrations on public data such as ride sharing, traffic crashes, and crime reports from several cities showed strong predictions. The framework also moved to new cities and problem domains with little reconfiguration, supporting scalable smart city analytics.
arxiv-2512-11578:
Gabriel Michelena, Christoph Ernst, and Pablo Bertin measure what the 2025 tariff clash does to jobs around the world. The United States raised tariffs under its America First plan, and other nations hit back. The team uses a world input and output model tied to a trade model, so prices, demand, and trade shares can all shift.

They run three cases: tariffs with no reply, tariffs with replies, and a calmer path where tensions ease. In the worst case, world job losses pass 23 million. Low skill and informal workers take over 80 percent of the losses. Rich and middle income nations also see sharp drops in exports.
arxiv-2512-11978:
Suman Chatterjee and co-authors describe the pipeline behind the MeerKLASS on the fly continuum survey with MeerKAT. The survey maps huge sky areas for cosmology with hydrogen intensity mapping, while also making sharp interferometric images. On the fly mode records data during fast, level scans, imaging hundreds of square degrees per night.

Fast scanning in the current correlator mode smears sources, so the pipeline corrects with time based phase rotation, direction aware point spread modeling, and wide band faceted cleaning. Pilot data reach noise of 35 and 33 microjanskys per beam in the two bands. The full survey will cover 10,000 square degrees. It doubles as a technical pathfinder for SKA-Mid.
arxiv-2512-12178:
Mohammad Taghi Dabiri and four co-authors tackle a hard sensing task for light based links in a 2025 paper. Free space optical links send data by laser through air. To judge a link, users must measure pointing error, arrival angle wobble, and turbulence fading, all mixed in one signal.

The team designs a receiver with many lens openings to spread the effects apart. A layered deep learning system then reads the three values in order: angle, pointing error, then turbulence. Tests reached near best possible accuracy at far lower cost than standard methods. The system also beat end to end learning on accuracy and on new cases.
arxiv-2512-12378:
Junqiao Fan and eight co-authors present M4Human, a radar benchmark for rebuilding human body meshes, in a 2025 paper. Cameras struggle with blocked views, poor light, and privacy limits. Millimeter wave radar can sense people indoors without images, but past radar data sets were small and labeled only sparse skeletons.

M4Human holds 661K frames, nine times the prior largest set, with radar, RGB, and depth data. It covers 20 subjects and 50 actions, from still poses to sports and rehab moves, with motion capture meshes and paths. Both raw radar tensors and point clouds are included. Benchmarks cover radar alone and fusion with RGB-D, and fast free motion stays hard.
arxiv-2512-12678:
Fatimah Zohra, Chen Zhao, Hani Itani, and Bernard Ghanem present beta-CLIP for fine grained vision language alignment in a 2025 paper. CLIP links images and text well at a global level, but it lags on fine grained tasks even after fine tuning on long captions. Matching a phrase to the exact image region it describes needs alignment at many scales at once.

Beta-CLIP aligns text at three granularities, full captions, sentences, and phrases, with their visual regions, using cross attention to pool image patches per level. A new loss balances strict query matching with relaxed context from the same image. Results hit 91.8 percent text to image and 92.3 percent image to text recall at 1 on Urban1K, plus 30.9 on FG-OVD Hard.
arxiv-2512-12778:
Zaid Tahir and four co-authors present VeBPF, a many core architecture for network functions on FPGA based SmartNICs and IoT devices, in a 2025 paper. SmartNICs offload packet processing from servers, and FPGAs offer reconfigurable hardware, but existing FPGA designs lack a configurable many core layout specialized for packets. Their cores implement the eBPF instruction set in Verilog, so they plug into existing FPGA blocks.

Many VeBPF cores run eBPF rules in parallel for low latency packet processing. Core and rule counts scale with the application and the available FPGA resources. Rules can be updated at runtime with no FPGA reconfiguration, enabling adaptive processing. The design, software libraries, and test frameworks built with Python and Cocotb are released as open source.
arxiv-2512-13178:
Katharina Ledebur and co-authors use product space analysis to predict where electric vehicle industries will emerge. Making electric cars draws on electronics, batteries, and software more than on classic mechanical skill. Regions and firms must build on what they already do well.

The team built product spaces for all industries and for over 900 car components, grouping parts that are exported together. Closeness centrality in the country-level space, not simple proximity, best predicted new strengths. Vehicle and aluminum strengths in Europe were projected to spawn far more EV strengths than other sectors. South Korea, China, the US, and Canada showed strong potential to diversify into EV products.
arxiv-2512-13278:
Jiaru Zou and co-authors present AutoTool, a training framework that teaches language model agents to pick their own tools as they reason. Most agents get a fixed tool set, which fails when tools change or new ones appear. Real work needs agents that adapt mid-task.

Training runs in two phases: first stabilizing reasoning with tool use, then refining multi-step tool choice with a ranking method under a regularization limit. The team built a 200,000 example data set with stated reasons for tool choices, spanning over 1,000 tools. Across ten benchmarks, AutoTool beat prior agents, with gains of 6.4 percent in math and science and 7.7 percent in code tasks.
arxiv-2512-13478:
Kei Saito specifies Non-Resolution Reasoning, a framework that keeps competing readings alive instead of forcing an early single answer. Language systems that rush to one resolved output can lose the open doubt that later context would have settled correctly. His design makes the delay explicit and controlled.

The framework tracks context indexed options with separate weights, declared retention and commitment operations, and non-destructive projection to outputs. Proposed parts include multi-vector embeddings and non-collapsing attention. In a small test two-turn task, one gated version held entropy at 0.91 bits before context arrived, near the maximum, then resolved correctly once context came. The author notes this does not validate the full design.
arxiv-2512-13678:
Ziqi Ma, Hongqiao Chen, Yisong Yue, and Georgia Gkioxari present Steer3D, a feedforward method to edit 3D assets with text. Image-to-3D models now serve design, augmented reality, and robotics, but their outputs are hard to edit. Steer3D adds language steering to a pretrained image-to-3D model in one forward pass.

The design adapts ControlNet ideas to 3D generation, backed by a scalable engine that makes training data automatically. Training pairs flow matching with Direct Preference Optimization, on 100k data items. Against rival methods, Steer3D followed text instructions more faithfully and kept the source asset more consistent. It was also 2.4 to 28.5 times faster, showing a new modality can steer a pretrained 3D model.
arxiv-2512-14078:
Da Zhang and co-authors present FusAD, a unified framework for general time series analysis across finance, health, industry, and weather data. Tasks include classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection. Past deep models were often built for one task or data type, and real series add noise and multi-scale patterns that complicate feature extraction.

FusAD fuses time and frequency views with an adaptive mechanism using both Fourier and Wavelet transforms, capturing global, local, and multi-scale dynamics. An adaptive denoising mechanism senses and filters varied noise types, highlighting key sequence changes. Masked pre-training supports transfer of multi-granularity representations. Experiments show FusAD beats state-of-the-art models on mainstream benchmarks for all three task families, while staying efficient and scalable.
arxiv-2512-14478:
Paolo Malgaretti and Emanuele Locatelli study active polymers, chains that push on themselves and so never settle into equilibrium shapes. Their question is what happens when the push varies along the chain in a wave pattern rather than acting uniformly. They model a semiflexible chain with the continuum Rouse model and work in the limit of weak activity.

The pattern decides the shape. Gentle, low-wave forcing squeezes the chain into a compact ball, while higher-wave forcing stretches some segments and compresses others, swelling the chain overall. A chain can even end up compact by one measure yet extended by another. Computer simulations matched the theory closely.
arxiv-2512-15078:
Tushar Singh and two coauthors introduce a new class of rings in commutative algebra. A ring is Noetherian when its ideals cannot climb in endless chains, a finiteness trait that makes rings workable. Their S-J-Noetherian rings blend two earlier generalizations: J-Noetherian rings, tied to a chosen ideal J, and S-Noetherian rings, tied to a multiplicative set S.

The authors develop the basic properties of the class and give several ways to recognize its members. They prove a Cohen type theorem for these rings, the kind of test that reduces a global property to prime ideals. They also show that S-primary decomposition exists in such rings. That result extends the classical Lasker-Noether theorem, which splits ideals into simpler primary parts, into the S-J setting.
arxiv-2512-15178:
Jun Song and two coauthors map where soft particles come from in high energy collisions, using the sideways spread of the particles produced. When protons or nuclei collide at RHIC and the LHC, the hadrons that emerge have a spectrum in transverse momentum. The authors study the curvature of that spectrum's logarithm and find two special points in it.

Below the first point lies the soft region, fed by a soft parton system. Above the second lies the hard region, fed by energetic partonic jets, with a transition zone between. They measure both points for kaons, K*, phi mesons, and baryons like protons, Lambda, Xi, and Omega, across collision types and energies. The first point tracks each hadron's average momentum in a pattern that differs for baryons and mesons, explained by how quarks combine. The study calls that point a sensitive probe of soft particle production.
arxiv-2512-15278:
Melih Solmaz presents DELight, a planned experiment hunting dark matter particles far lighter than the usual targets. Decades of searches have found no dark matter, and masses below a few GeV remain largely unexplored. Such light candidates demand detectors with lower thresholds and new target materials.

DELight will use superfluid helium 4 as its target, watched by large area microcalorimeters built on magnetic microcalorimeter technology. The setup is optimized for low mass dark matter, where a faint energy deposit is the only sign of a hit. The paper overviews the experiment: its detection technology, its sensitivity goals, and the research and development studies behind it. DELight joins a wave of experiments pushing direct detection toward the lightest dark matter still allowed.
arxiv-2512-15678:
Jorge Poveda and Andrew Teel give a tutorial style introduction to hybrid set seeking systems in a 2025 article. Extremum seeking controllers hunt for the best operating point of a system without a model, using feedback alone. Hybrid versions mix continuous and discrete behavior, which suits digital sensing and switching plants.

The article first reviews perturbation theory for hybrid inclusions, the base for averaging and singular perturbation analysis. It then applies those tools to extremum seeking designs for static and dynamic plants. Examples cover switching rules under fast switching, dwell time limits, and safety constraints, plus momentum based and reset type schemes. The piece was submitted to IEEE Control Systems Magazine.
arxiv-2512-15978:
Anastasia Halfpap studies the rainbow Turan number of broom graphs with length two handles in a 2025 paper. A broom is a short path with several pendant edges at one end. The rainbow Turan number asks for the most edges an n vertex graph can have while admitting a proper edge coloring with no rainbow copy of the target graph.

Johnston and Rombach began this study and claimed an asymptotic value for all brooms of this type. Halfpap corrects an error in that argument, finding two small cases where the claimed value is wrong. In all other cases the original value is recovered. The proof also characterizes the extremal constructions for certain residue classes of n modulo k.
arxiv-2512-16178:
M Oltan Sevinc, Liao Wu, and Francisco Cruz test a camera swap for self-driving in this 2025 arXiv paper, accepted to an Australasian robotics conference. Cars trained on daytime images often fail at night, a mismatch called the domain gap. The authors ask whether event cameras, sensors that report only brightness changes, suffer less from that gap.

Event cameras react to motion and edges rather than full frames, so lighting shifts may matter less. In their tests, event camera systems kept performance steadier across lighting conditions than grayscale frame systems. Their cross-domain penalties were generally comparable or smaller, and their baseline results in shifted conditions were better. The findings suggest event cameras could make driving perception more robust when conditions change, without retraining for each new setting.
arxiv-2512-16378:
Sara Papi and ten co-authors benchmark speech translation in this 2025 arXiv paper. It was accepted by a journal in computational linguistics. Speech language models promise to translate spoken words directly. That skips the old transcribe-then-translate pipeline. Whether this beats strong cascaded systems was an open question.

The team built Hearing to Translate, a test suite for the task. It compares 6 speech language models against 16 direct and cascaded systems. Coverage spans 16 benchmarks and 13 language pairs. Nine hard conditions are included, like noisy or disfluent speech. Cascaded systems stayed the most reliable overall. Recent speech language models matched or beat them in many settings. Speech foundation models alone lagged behind both. The lesson: a language model somewhere in the loop is essential for quality.
arxiv-2512-16478:
Boris Leistedt and a large team plan a sky survey's rhythm in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025, submitted to an astrophysics journal supplement. The Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time will scan the sky for a decade. Its baseline rolling strategy revisits parts of the sky more often, which serves time-domain science like supernova hunting.

The authors check what rolling does to static science, galaxy clustering and weak lensing, which need uniform depth. In mid-survey data releases, nearly half the area could be too patchy to use, cutting the dark energy figure of merit by about 40 percent. They propose uniform rolling, which restores even coverage at key release years without losing time-domain data. Metrics for photometric redshifts and clustering also recover. The strategies were folded into the survey's baseline plan.
arxiv-2512-16578:
Sajad Salami and Arman Shamsi Zargar study Shioda elliptic surfaces given by the curve family y squared equals x cubed plus t to the m plus one. For such a surface over the rationals, they seek its splitting field, the smallest field where all its rational points can be described.

For each whole number m from 1 to 12, the authors find that splitting field in full. They also give a set of independent generators for the Mordell-Weil lattice, the ranked list of rational sections of the surface. The results give concrete data for a classic family used to test ideas about ranks and heights.
arxiv-2512-17578:
Ge Wang, Xing Liu, and Xin Yuan rebuild a whole video from one mashed snapshot. Their camera squeezes many video frames into a single exposure by scrambling each pixel's light over time. A one-hot scheme lights each pixel in exactly one time slice, which cleanly separates the frames in theory. No software had yet cashed in that clean split.

Their method treats the job as filling in a video, guided by a noise process that mirrors the camera's own scrambling. A fast regression pass sketches the frames, then one diffusion pass polishes them, keeping the method quick. A second optical path in the hardware feeds extra detail to patch the spatial softness one-hot capture causes. Tests on fake and real scenes show the frames come back sharp.
arxiv-2512-17678:
Daphné Chopard and four co-authors present YOTO, a system that picks a short list of telling genes while it learns to predict from them, all in one training run. Single-cell data measures thousands of genes per cell, yet a useful biomarker panel needs only a handful. Old pipelines pick genes first and predict second, so the picking never hears what the predicting actually needed.

YOTO welds the two jobs: the prediction error steers which genes survive, and the surviving genes shape the prediction in return. A sparsity rule forces the final model to use only the chosen genes, no leftovers. Trained across related tasks at once, it beat leading baselines on two single-cell data sets. The gene lists stayed small and biologically meaningful.
arxiv-2512-17878:
Herlock Rahimi studies a math problem behind AI image makers: how to draw samples from a complex target shape. Standard diffusion methods wander slowly when the target has several separate humps. A richer geometry, named Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao, lets mass grow or shrink as well as move, which could speed the search.

Rahimi shows how to add the needed correction terms through weighted random equations, using a classic Feynman-Kac form. The study is early and careful rather than a finished tool. It maps the shape and operator structure of these flows, giving later work a firm base for faster samplers.
arxiv-2512-18078:
Francesco Fanelli, Young-Sam Kwon, and Aneta Wróblewska-Kamińska study a squeezed flow model for magnetized gas. Their reduced system describes a compressible gas with magnetic forces in two dimensions, kin to models of two mixed fluids. They ask what the flow becomes as one dial, the magnetic pressure scale, is turned toward zero.

Even with the gas still moving at a healthy Mach number, the limit lands on an incompressible flow. The proof works for rough starting data and for the case of strong spin, as in a rotating planet. A transport law hidden in the system lets them track the small leftover terms exactly, which closes the limit cleanly.
arxiv-2512-18178:
Qijia Zhai of Sichuan University develops a deep learning method for interface problems, equations whose coefficients jump sharply across a boundary between two regions. His 2025 paper covers elliptic and parabolic interface problems in two to ten dimensions. The approach splits the domain and trains two independent neural networks, one per subdomain. The networks are joined through interface conditions placed inside the loss function.

The key device is a multi activation mechanism inside each network. It blends several activation functions, such as tanh and Gaussian type functions, with weights that respond to the interface. That blending helps learning near the boundary, where the coupling demands are hardest. Zhai proves conditional error bounds linking solution accuracy to the trained loss and quadrature errors. Numerical tests across interface geometries from two to ten dimensions confirm the method works accurately. Such solvers matter wherever materials meet, from heat flow to electromagnetics.
arxiv-2512-18278:
Xianming Liu and Xu Sun study how shared random noise can pull restless systems into step with each other. When twin systems feel the same noise, their paths may merge over time, a result called synchronization by noise. Past proofs leaned on a strong reach trait that many systems lack, and they often assumed well behaved bell shaped noise.

The pair give tests for weak merging that are both enough and required, and the tests work for thin, degenerate noise and for noise with other shapes. Their work answers part of an open question left by Flandoli and others in 2017. On the classic Lorenz 63 weather model, weak merging holds when the noise is small, and fails when the noise is large, so a sharp switch sits between the two.
arxiv-2512-18378:
Julian Allagan, Shawn Langley, Weizheng Gao, and Mohamed Elbakary map a family of networks built around a center. Their graphs, called strong central 2-trees, grow by stacking triangles on edges, and the outer tail points are allowed only two or three links each. They sort the family by how many center points it has: one, two, or three.

With one center, a single fan shaped graph is the only option at every size. With two centers, the count of three link tails is always even, and the team gives sharp rules for when the shape is unique. With three centers a divisibility rule appears, and the count of distinct shapes grows at least quadratically for endless sizes.
arxiv-2512-18578:
Yuqiao Li extends a basic quantity of geometry and gravity, mass, to spaces whose metrics are merely continuous rather than smooth. The setting is asymptotically hyperbolic manifolds, spaces that curve away like hyperbolic space at infinity. Classical mass definitions assume smoothness, which excludes rough spaces that arise naturally. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, defines mass through a smoothing flow.

The tool is the normalized Ricci-DeTurck flow, which evens out the metric over time. The mass read off this way agrees with the classical mass whenever the metric is smooth. To make the rough definition sound, he also introduces a scalar curvature lower bound adapted to continuous metrics. The work lets geometers assign mass, and test conjectures like the positive mass theorem, on a wider class of spaces.
arxiv-2512-18778:
Andrés Collinucci and four co-authors construct new five-dimensional superconformal field theories, exotic quantum theories with no weak-coupling description. They build them from abelian orbifolds of a geometric object called Reid's Pagoda. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, reports families of non-toric theories, including an infinite family of rank-one theories that dodge every known classification.

Using the McKay correspondence, they derive each theory's BPS quiver and superpotential. The signature feature is a new sector they name Pagoda matter. Its vacuum values block the Kaehler moduli, freezing the gauge coupling at infinite strength, so the theories are strongly coupled by construction rather than by accident. The authors finally read the constructions as deformations by non-constant flavor backgrounds. The catalog of five-dimensional theories just got stranger and larger.
arxiv-2512-19578:
Cosmologists Alex Edison, Matthew Lewandowski, and Leonardo Senatore tackle a bookkeeping problem in how galaxies trace the unseen matter around them. Their paper builds a systematic galaxy bias expansion inside the effective field theory of large-scale structure. Unlike simpler versions, theirs lets each field contribute from its own separate time in the past, carried up to sixth order.

Working from the general expression for galaxy overdensity, they compute the complete sixth-order set of bias operators and find 57 independent biases, against 46 in the local-in-time version. That gap means detailed clustering measurements can tell local from non-local galaxy formation, and can even sense when galaxies formed, all at one redshift. Recursion relations and soft limits for the kernels round out the results.
arxiv-2512-20078:
Taekyun Kim and three co-authors generalize a classic counting device into the degenerate world. The Euler-Seidel method pulls facts from a difference table built by a plain recurrence. Their version inserts a parameter, lambda, into that recurrence. The result is a degenerate Euler-Seidel matrix for any start sequence. New binomial identities come with it. So do generating-function relations, all in lambda form.

The machinery is then applied to three polynomial families. They are the degenerate Bernoulli, Euler, and Genocchi polynomials. Each already carries a deformation parameter of its own. Several new combinatorial identities fall out. The work extends the classic method as a frame for degenerate special polynomials and numbers. It gives the field a uniform tool for making and sorting such identities.
arxiv-2512-20178:
Chen Zhuang leads an eight-author team cutting wasted chatter from distributed sparse matrix work. Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication backs HPC and deep learning alike. On clusters, its bottleneck is communication. Two flaws feed that cost. Transfers ignore the matrix's sparsity pattern. Layouts waste the network's tiers, pushing data over slow links between nodes for no need.

SHIRO answers with a fine-grained, sparsity-aware communication plan. It sends only what the pattern requires. The plan is mapped onto two-tier GPU network layouts, to keep traffic on fast links. Tests on real data scaled to one hundred twenty-eight GPUs. At that scale, speedups over four top baselines ran from about nine-fold to over two-hundred-fold, in geometric mean. The work was accepted at ICS 2026.
arxiv-2512-20478:
Zepeng Wang and Juan Peypouquet design an optimization method that tunes its own step size. Accelerated gradient methods converge quickly on smooth convex problems, but they need the smoothness constant, which is rarely known. Line searches work around that at extra cost and complexity.

Their method estimates the smoothness constant locally as it runs, adapting the step size without any line search. The iterates converge weakly to a minimizer, and the function values shrink at the fast inverse-square rate characteristic of acceleration. When the objective is strongly convex, the rate improves to linear. The result is a practical accelerated scheme for the common situation where problem constants are unknown in advance.
arxiv-2512-20578:
Amirhosein Ghasemabadi and Di Niu ask whether a language model can feel itself going wrong. Models hallucinate confidently, and existing checks cost extra compute or match correctness weakly. Their mechanism, Gnosis, listens to the model's own internal activity while it generates.

Gnosis passively reads hidden states and attention patterns, packs them into fixed-size digests, and predicts whether the output is correct. The host model stays frozen; the add-on carries only about five million weights and ignores sequence length. Across mathematics, question answering, and academic benchmarks, and backbones from small to twenty billion parameters, Gnosis beats internal benchmarks and large external judges on accuracy and tuning. It even flags failing generations early, enabling compute-aware fixes.
arxiv-2512-20778:
Moshe Rafaeli Shimron and Vadim Indelman study teams of agents that must act as one while each sees the world in its own way. Each agent holds its own belief about what surrounds it, shaped by the data it has received. Most planning methods assume all agents share the same beliefs. That idea breaks when the team can barely talk to each other.

Their framework plans joint actions while openly allowing for mismatched beliefs. It gives guarantees, framed as probabilities, for both consistent action and performance. Agents share data only when they must. The authors also ask when sharing data after an act improves later inference. In tests, their method beat the leading rival approaches.
arxiv-2512-20878:
SenYuan Su, Chunling Tong, and Yuansheng Yang settle an open problem in graph coloring. Their target is a family of circulant graphs, networks where vertices sit on a ring and each connects to neighbors at fixed jumps. A total coloring assigns colors to both vertices and edges so that nothing adjacent or incident shares a color, and the total chromatic number is the fewest colors that suffice.

For the four-regular family C_n(1, 3), where each vertex links to its nearest and third-nearest neighbors, they determine the number exactly for every ring size. It equals six for the five exceptional sizes seven, eight, twelve, thirteen, and seventeen, and five for all others, closing a question that had resisted many earlier efforts.
arxiv-2512-21278:
Some first-order theories are as simple as their subject allows: every formula can be rewritten using only existential, positive statements. Manuel Bodirsky, Bertalan Bodor, and Paolo Marimon study such model-complete core theories and the core companion each theory may possess, a simplest partner whose models map into the original's and back.

Companions are unique when they exist, and omega-categorical theories always have one. The authors show prized tameness properties survive the move to the companion: stability, NIP, simplicity, and the NSOP hierarchy all carry over. Two natural classes of interpretable theories fail to be closed under the operation, though. A conjecture equating one such class with Lachlan's classic class is supported by a trace-definability result confirming a conjecture of Walsberg's.
arxiv-2512-21478:
Brani Vidakovic brings a classic signal-processing tool, the nondecimated wavelet transform, into quantum computing. The classic transform analyzes a signal at many scales while keeping shifted copies, which makes it stable and shift-invariant. Those qualities are prized in denoising, though redundancy is usually something quantum algorithms avoid.

Vidakovic develops two quantum versions. The first promotes the shift index to a quantum register, applies controlled shifts and then a wavelet operation, producing every shifted transform at once in one process. It also supports denoising through quantum shrinkage. The second version uses the Hadamard test with diagonal phase operators to probe scale-and-shift structure, giving shift-invariant energy maps without rebuilding every coefficient. Uses in denoising and feature work show that extra copies can be an asset in quantum signal processing.
arxiv-2512-21578:
Sudhanshu Garg, Andrew Wang, Srinivasan Manoharan, and a wider team describe how PayPal tuned the language model behind its Commerce Agent, an AI shopping assistant. The retrieval stage, which finds products, accounted for over half of the agent's total response time, so it became the optimization target.

Working with NVIDIA, the team used the NeMo framework to fine-tune a small Nemotron language model for the Search and Discovery agent, replacing the larger base model. They swept learning rates, optimizers, annealing schedules, and LoRA adapter ranks. The tuned small model fixed the retrieval bottleneck, cutting latency and cost while holding or improving quality. The authors frame the work as the first use of the NeMo framework for commerce agent optimization, and a reusable pattern for production multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2512-21678:
Alain Schumacher, Takuji Nishimura, and Makoto Matsumoto report a statistical defect in the Mersenne Twister MT19937, the famous pseudorandom number generator two of them introduced in 1998. The generator is still everywhere in software and passes nearly all standard randomness tests. A birthday-spacings test had raised doubts, but that test is rather artificial.

The authors found a natural test the generator fails: the distribution of run lengths in its output integers. Runs of length six hundred twenty-three appear about forty times more often than expected, while neighboring lengths appear at normal rates, driving the test's p-value essentially to zero. They analyze the phenomenon mathematically and prove a theorem explaining it. Finding the defect takes astronomical effort, so it is not a practical danger for ordinary users. Still, the authors argue the behavior should be on the record for the community.
arxiv-2512-22178:
Chuanting Zhang and four co-authors build TIDES, a system that forecasts wireless network traffic across a city using a large language model. Good forecasts guide resource management in next-generation networks, but earlier language-model predictors mostly ignored how traffic in one district relates to its neighbors. TIDES is designed to capture those spatial links together with patterns over time.

The system first clusters districts with similar traffic habits and trains a personalized model for each group. A prompt scheme converts traffic statistics into structured inputs a language model can read. A DeepSeek module then aligns information across related regions through cross-domain attention, while only light components are fine-tuned. On real cellular datasets, TIDES beat leading baselines in accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2512-22278:
Hussain Alasmawi, Numan Saeed, and Mohammad Yaqub introduce Fetal-Gauge, a benchmark for testing vision-language models on fetal ultrasound images. Prenatal scanning faces a global shortage of trained sonographers, and AI assistance could help, but no standard test existed for this difficult, operator-dependent imaging type. Their visual question answering benchmark is the first and largest built for the purpose.

Fetal-Gauge contains over 42,000 images and 93,000 question-answer pairs. Tasks cover identifying anatomical planes, grounding forms visually, judging fetal orientation, checking view conformity, and making clinical diagnoses. Leading general and medical models were evaluated systematically. The best reached only 55 percent accuracy, far below clinical needs, which the authors take as a call for domain-adapted designs and specialized training.
arxiv-2512-22378:
Donggyun Bae and Jongil Park propose Fourier-Activated Adapters, a way to fine-tune large language models by training only small added modules. Their adapters inject random Fourier features into the model's intermediate representations, splitting them into low- and high-frequency components. The design lets adaptation emphasize whichever frequency bands carry useful information for a task while the frozen backbone keeps its general capacity.

Across GLUE, E2E NLG, and instruction-tuning benchmarks, the method matched or beat current parameter-efficient fine-tuning approaches while keeping computation and memory overhead low. Ablation studies confirmed that both the frequency-aware activation and the adaptive weighting methods contribute to the gains. The authors present the system as a robust, efficient option for post-training large models.
arxiv-2512-22578:
Syed Luqman Shah and Nurul Huda Mahmood cut the cost of learning a wireless channel's state. Next-generation networks need accurate channel state information, but pilots, the known signals used to measure the channel, eat energy and airtime. The authors model the channel as a proper complex Gaussian process spread over the transmit and receive antenna arrays, then treat full channel recovery from partial observations as a Bayesian inverse problem.

Their Gaussian process regression extrapolates from sparse, noisy pilot readings to every unmeasured entry. A new kernel built from the array geometry, proved to be a valid Hermitian positive semidefinite kernel, injects propagation structure into the prior, and hyperparameters are learned online within each coherence block. Simulations cut pilot overhead by up to seventy-five percent and training energy by nearly ninety-four percent.
arxiv-2512-22778:
Muhammad Zain Ali, Bernhard Pfahringer, and Tony Smith work on detecting fake news written in Urdu, a language with far fewer labeled resources than English. A standard recipe fine-tunes a multilingual language model, but such models often stumble over domain-specific words in news text. The team tests whether extra pretraining on Urdu news, called domain adaptation, fixes that weakness before fine-tuning for classification.

They adapt two widely used multilingual models, XLM-RoBERTa and mBERT, on a public Urdu news corpus, then evaluate on four public Urdu fake news datasets. Domain-adapted XLM-RoBERTa beats its plain version consistently across the datasets. The adapted mBERT gives mixed results, sometimes helping and sometimes not. The findings suggest staged training is a practical route for misinformation detection in low-resource languages, though the benefit depends on the base model chosen.
arxiv-2512-22878:
Hasan Faraz Khan, Noor Fatima, and Muzammil Behzad present SwinTF3D, a system that outlines organs in three-dimensional medical scans following a written instruction.
