Most segmentation networks learn only from images and large labeled datasets, so they cannot react when a clinician asks for a different, user-chosen target. Adding language gives that flexibility, but heavy multimodal models are expensive to run.

SwinTF3D pairs a transformer-based visual encoder for the scan volume with a compact text encoder, joining the two through an efficient fusion step. The design aligns phrases with the matching anatomy while keeping computational overhead low. On the BTCV benchmark it reached Dice and overlap scores competitive with much larger systems across several organs, and it generalized to unseen data. The authors pitch the approach as a practical, interpretable route to interactive, text-driven segmentation in clinical imaging.
arxiv-2512-22978:
Hoa Dinh Thi and colleagues simulate the polarized X-ray glow of magnetars, neutron stars with the strongest known magnetic fields. Their surface emission pulses as the star spins, and its polarization encodes the star's geometry. The team's Monte Carlo code tracks each photon's electric field through the atmosphere and magnetosphere. It includes relativistic effects and vacuum birefringence, a quantum effect that splits light by polarization in strong fields.

The upgraded simulation now includes quantum electrodynamic influences on polarization during magnetospheric travel. Fitting recent pulse profile data for a magnetar, the authors constrain the viewing geometry. They estimate the angles among the magnetic axis, the spin axis, and our line of sight, plus the polar cap sizes. Vacuum birefringence turns out to raise the linear polarization degree importantly. A comparison with a weakly magnetized neutron star is included, and the authors note the vacuum resonance effect still needs adding.
arxiv-2512-23378:
Yifan Xuan and co-authors forecast how many giant planets and brown dwarfs the Chinese Space Station Telescope will find by watching stars wobble. The telescope, set to begin operations around 2027, will survey areas away from the Galactic and ecliptic planes. Its astrometric precision, fine even for faint objects, can reveal companions tugging their hosts. The authors generate synthetic catalogs and run injection-recovery simulations with different occurrence rates.

Companions around Sun-like stars look like a poor harvest: the telescope could barely discover giant planets there. The payoff concentrates on low-mass hosts. Over its ten-year mission, the camera is projected to detect tens to over a hundred giant planets and low-mass brown dwarfs around M-dwarfs within three hundred parsecs. It should also find several hundred brown dwarf binaries within six hundred parsecs. Such a haul would grow the sample around the smallest stars.
arxiv-2512-23578:
Yu-Xiang Lin, Cheng-Han Chiang, and Hung-yi Lee document a failure mode of spoken language models, which they name style amnesia. When such a model is told at the start of a conversation to speak with a certain emotion, accent, volume, or speed. It gradually stops doing so as turns accumulate, even though nothing asked it to change.

Testing three proprietary and two open-source models, they found none could hold an instructed style through a multi-turn conversation. Oddly, the models could recall the instruction when asked, yet still failed to express it; explicit recall in later turns partly repaired the problem. Styles given in system messages, which are designed to persist, fared worse than styles in user messages. The study appeared in the ACL 2026 Findings.
arxiv-2512-23678:
Igor Ermakov and Oleg Lychkovskiy present a symbolic version of the recursion method for computing how strongly correlated fermions behave over time. The classic way tracks how an operator grows through nested commutators. Most groups run that track on a computer, one system at a time. Their implementation works directly in the thermodynamic limit and at all time scales.

Applied to interacting spinless fermions and to the Hubbard model, the method confirmed the universal operator growth hypothesis for fermions. It gave current autocorrelation curves at endless heat, the charge spread rate, and the hot conductivity. It also found where weak and strong coupling meet. Because the expensive symbolic step runs once and its output can be reused for any parameters, the authors present the approach as a new computational paradigm for strongly correlated matter.
arxiv-2512-23978:
Tinglong Dai, David Simchi-Levi, Michelle Xiao Wu, and Yao Xie argue that operations research is the missing discipline keeping generative AI safe at work. As GenAI moves from chatbots to agentic systems that sense, decide, and act inside real workflows, a paradox appears. More autonomy demands more formal structure, more explicit constraints, and stronger discipline about rare, costly failures. Random generators left alone are fragile when the data shifts, and in high-stakes conditions.

Their framework for assured autonomy rests on two pillars. Flow-based generative models recast generation as deterministic transport governed by a plain differential equation, enabling auditing and constraint-aware generation. Operational safety is framed adversarially, testing decision rules against worst-case shocks inside stated uncertainty sets. As autonomy grows, they argue, operations research shifts from solver to guardrail to system architect. The article appears in Production and Operations Management.
arxiv-2512-24078:
Junyu Liao, Ashwin Lall, Mitsunori Ogihara, and Raymond Wong work on interactive queries. Such a query learns what a user wants. It shows small sets of options. The user picks a favorite. The query then gradually homes in on the best recommendation.

The catch is scale. Housing and financial datasets can carry hundreds of attributes. Older methods slow down badly at that size. Others pester the user through a thousand rounds or more. The team's framework, FHDR, avoids both failures. It answers in under a hundredth of a second. It needs fewer than thirty rounds of feedback. Experiments compared it with the best known algorithms. FHDR won by at least ten times on running time. On interaction counts, the margin was far larger. The authors call it a new state of the art.
arxiv-2512-24378:
Konstantin Yakovlev, Anna Markovich, and Nikita Puchkin compare two ways to learn a score function. The score, the gradient of the log density, drives modern generative samplers. Implicit score matching and denoising score matching estimate it differently. Data with low-dimensional structure is the setting. Such structure should make estimation easier in principle.

The authors prove implicit score matching adapts to the intrinsic dimension. Its convergence rates match denoising score matching in sample size. Both methods also estimate log-density Hessians by simple differentiation. No curse of dimensionality appears in that step. The result justifies convergence of ODE-based samplers for diffusion models. The proofs rest on Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequalities. Those relate weighted norms of functions to norms of their derivatives. Two estimation traditions end up equally strong on structured data.
arxiv-2512-24478:
Hyunjun Kim formalizes language-model-guided causal discovery with sheaf theory. Finding causal structure from observations is limited by identifiability. Language models hold prior causal knowledge worth using. Earlier integrations of that knowledge were heuristic. HOLOGRAPH gives them a mathematical frame. Local causal beliefs become sections of a presheaf over variable subsets.

A coherent global structure is then a global section. Obstructions show up as nonzero sheaf cohomology. Hidden confounders are handled by an algebraic latent projection. Beliefs are optimized by natural gradient descent on the belief manifold. Benchmarks on synthetic and real data cover fifty to a hundred variables. Performance stayed competitive with rigorous foundations attached. Three axioms held to numerical precision. The locality axiom failed on larger graphs. That failure hints at real non-local coupling in latent projections.
arxiv-2601-06678:
Isabelle Mohr and co-authors propose reflective reasoning for SQL generation in 2026. Robust text-to-SQL over complex real databases remains brittle, they write. Even modern language models stumble on such database questions often.

Iterative refinement often introduces syntactic and semantic drift, they observe. Corrections tend to be non-transferable across queries in naive loops. Naive use of large context windows also scales poorly, they add. Their controlled framework is built around reflective refinement instead. Reflection aims to fix errors without wandering from the original intent. Database users get queries checked against their own logic before running. The work speaks to anyone deploying language models over real schemas. Accuracy there is a business need, not a benchmark luxury.
arxiv-2601-06978:
James Le Houx wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to grade self-run science. Big user labs now move from machines that just log data to machines that find new things on their own. To track that shift, labs need shared words for each stage of the move. The car world has such a scale, the SAE J3016 standard.

Past scales for science tend to assume one owner runs the lab. That view clashes with how large user labs must work. Such labs serve many teams, with strict rules and fixed slots of time. Le Houx sets out a ranked scale built for that world. The scale lets labs state where they stand. It lets them compare their stage with the stage of other labs on the same terms.
arxiv-2601-07078:
Oko Emmanuel Godwin and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers ab initio characterization of c 2 ​ h 4 ​ n 2 \text{C}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{4}}}\text{N}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. This work presents a comprehensive theoretical investigation of key isomers of C 2 ​ H 4 ​ N 2 using state-of-the-art quantum chemical methods.

The objective is to characterize their molecular structures, spectroscopic constants, and electronic energies. And elucidate plausible formation and destruction pathways, providing data critical for astrochemical and atmospheric detection. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07778:
Wen Guo introduces DT-ICU, a digital twin framework for patients in intensive care. A digital twin mirrors a real system and updates as new data arrive. DT-ICU estimates risk continuously during an ICU stay. It combines variable-length clinical time series with static patient information. One multitask architecture handles the predictions together. Their 2026 preprint stresses explainability as well as accuracy.

Doctors need to know why a risk score changed before they act on it. Iterative inference updates predictions as each new observation accumulates. Multimodal inputs reflect how ICU teams actually work, mixing charts, monitors, and background facts. The framework aims at monitoring that clinicians can inspect and trust. The paper speaks to medical AI scholars and critical care teams. It treats explanation as part of the product.
arxiv-2601-08178: Shangqian Li, Tianwa Chen, and Gianluca Demartini study how AI-generated content shapes expert decisions. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that modeling online decision-making must weigh personal traits, topic type, and search behavior. Products like ChatGPT have become a standard part of how people gather information online. Yet how domain knowledge interacts with AI content during decisions stays unclear. The study targets topics that require expertise, where a wrong AI claim can mislead even trained readers. It speaks to designers of search and decision support tools.
arxiv-2601-08778:
Tengjun Jin and three co-authors warn that top test sets for data queries have many wrong labels. These tests ask a system to turn a plain ask into a database query. Staff then grade the query by a stored right answer. If that stored answer is wrong, good systems look bad and bad ones can look good.

The team shows that label flaws are wide spread in these tests. Rank lists built on them can mislead buyers and labs. A fix needs fresh checks of the stored answers by skilled staff. A reader who picks a query tool gets a clear warn. Do not trust a rank list till the test labels have been checked with care.
arxiv-2601-08978:
A. Kurko and ten co-authors report a new sweet spot where atoms stop scattering light into a tight trap. They work with rubidium atoms held near a high grade light trap. At most hues, atoms throw light into the trap. At one hue in a fine split line, that throw stops. Two effects meet to cause the stop.

One effect is wave clash, where waves cancel. The next is the joint pull of many atoms on the trap light. Both must act for the sweet spot to show. A reader in atom light work gets a new tool. A hue where scatter stops can help hold atoms still for tests and clocks.
arxiv-2601-09678:
S. Bini, K. Król, K. Chatziioannou, and M. Isi ask how much to trust the reading of a record gravitational-wave event. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies GW231123, a merger of two massive, fast-spinning black holes. Reading its properties correctly matters for what it says about how such black holes form.

The catch: only a few signal cycles were observed. Different waveform models then give systematically different answers for mass and spin. The authors test how waveform errors and Gaussian noise steer the inference. Their checks show which conclusions about this extreme event are solid and which are model-driven.
arxiv-2601-09778:
Raphael E. Hviding and a large team examine an odd X-ray bright object tied to a new class of galaxies. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether the X-ray dot is exotic dust or a late stage of the so-called little red dots. Those compact red sources, found by JWST, are widely read as active galactic nuclei.

Little red dots look wrapped in dense hot gas rather than dust, judging by their X-ray weakness and spectra. A key open question is how they connect to normal luminous active nuclei. A transitional object would show the change in progress. The team weighs the evidence for each reading of the dot.
arxiv-2601-09978:
Jer Shyuan Ng, Wathsara Daluwatta, Shehan Edirimannage, and Charitha Elvitigala map a new need in shared model work. In this work, many devices train one model. No raw data leaves the device. That guards privacy at the start.

But laws now grant a right to be erased. A user can ask that their data be wiped. Shared training has no built in way to undo one user's part. The wipe task is named unlearning. The paper maps what is known, what is hard, and where the work is used. It ends with open paths for work at the edge of the net.
arxiv-2601-10278:
Hyungkee Yoo bounds the ribbon cost of a class of links. A link is a set of loops tied in space. Its ribbon length is the least ratio of length to width for a folded ribbon form of it. That cost gauges how much stuff a form needs.

Yoo works on links that swap at each cross. Their chart has a dual graph that splits in two parts. For such links, he proves the cost is at most a set factor of the cross count. The factor is the square root of three. Such bounds tie a shape cost to a chart count.
arxiv-2601-10378:
Dian Jiao and co authors pack long text into images to save tokens. New sight and text models can read text from a page image with low loss. That opens a trick. Render text as an image, and the model needs far fewer tokens to take it in.

Fewer tokens cut the cost of attention, which grows fast with length. The team mix sight and text steps in one stream. They call it global context compression. Long files can then fit in one run. The aim is long reads at a cost labs can bear.
arxiv-2601-10578:
Warren E. Pickett writes about superfluid density, a basic quantity in the theory of superconductors. The idea has drawn interest since the field began. Yet papers rarely give an actual number for the density itself. Over time, the term has mostly meant a scaled value tied to the magnetic penetration depth.

Pickett traces how that habit formed, first in cuprate and later in other high-temperature superconductors. He sets superfluid density next to penetration depth and condensate density, three ideas that are often blurred together. Sorting them out matters when lab data are read as densities. The paper serves readers who want the terms used with care.
arxiv-2601-10978:
Nan An and co-authors design delay-aware task offloading for vehicular fog computing. Cars can hand computing tasks to nearby fog nodes to cut delay. That serves the delay-sensitive services of next-generation transport. Classic schemes rely on radio frequency links. Radio struggles in dense traffic, where channels crowd and fade.

The authors build a heterogeneous setup that mixes visible light communication with radio. Light links offer fresh bandwidth where radio saturates. Offloading choices must weigh delay against the quirks of each link. The work targets smart roads where many vehicles compute at once and every millisecond of delay can matter for safety services.
arxiv-2601-11378:
Daniel Campbell and six coauthors build transmons that emit and catch single photons. Their 2026 preprint shows a new circuit called the double transmon coupler. A transmon is a superconducting qubit used in quantum machines. The coupler links it to a waveguide of microwave modes.

The link is compact and can drop into known designs. It can be tuned and picks which transition couples out. Paired units act as emitter and detector for microwave photons. One unit sends a single photon down the waveguide. The other unit can catch that photon at the far end. Such links could wire quantum chips into networks.
arxiv-2601-11578:
Ibrahim Al Azher, Zhishuai Guo, and Hamed Alhoori generate research limitations with agents. Their 2026 preprint names the system LimAgents. Stating limitations is essential for transparent, rigorous science. Readers need to know where a study's claims stop.

Zero-shot LLMs often write superficial limitation statements. Stock lines cite dataset bias or generalizability in vague terms. They repeat what authors said without deeper probing. Methodological issues and contextual gaps go unmentioned. LimAgents uses multiple agents to dig for real limits. A team of models can split the critique by angle. Sharper limitations help readers judge a paper's true weight.
arxiv-2601-11778:
Sheriff Issaka, Erick Rosas Gonzalez, Lieqi Liu, and a broad team tackle a gap in tests for language models. Models claim skill in many tongues, yet true test sets made by humans exist for fewer than 30 tongues. That leaves most of the world's 7,000-plus tongues with no firm check.

They ask if translation can stand in as a scaled proxy for such tests. Hand made test sets face cost, few experts, and leaks of test data into training. A proxy that tracks true skill could guide work on low resource tongues. The study weighs how far that proxy can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-12078:
Linfeng Du, Ye Yuan, Zichen Zhao, and a broad team tune user profiles for personal replies from large models. Retrieval can adapt a model to a user with no retraining. Past tools pick past records by sense match alone.

The team use contextual bandits to pick profile records. A bandit learns which picks pay off from past results. That can beat a fixed match rule as user needs shift. A better profile pick means replies that fit the user with less noise.  Bandit picks learn from each reply the user rates.
arxiv-2601-12378:
G. H. Zheng, S. F. Liu, and a large team from the EXL-50U project work on fusion plasmas. Their test bed is a spherical torus used in work on controlled fusion. A key need is to rebuild the shape of the plasma as it runs, in real time. That task rests on number crunching that must be both fast and exact.

The team puts forward a new way to speed up such math. They use machine learning frameworks, namely PyTorch and TensorRT, to tune the code. These tools are modular and can tune themselves, which lowers the work of setup. Their test case is a program called PTEFIT. It shows the method can be fast, flexible, and easy to use at once.
arxiv-2601-12578:
Eduard I. Vorobyov and four co authors ask how exact our measures of young planet forming disks are. These disks of gas and dust ring newborn stars. Their masses and sizes are basic inputs for theories of planet formation. Yet both values come with large uncertainties, as the team stress at the outset.

A disk mass that is off by a lot can flip what a theory predicts. Sizes matter too, since they set where planets can form and how fast. The team study the accuracy of these measurements head on. Work of this kind tells observers which methods to trust. It also tells theorists how much slack to allow when they test a model against disk data.
arxiv-2601-12778:
Sheng-Chao Zhang and four co authors search for a low lying excited baryon in particle decays. The target state is a Sigma star with spin parity one half minus. Such excited baryons are short lived and hard to pin down directly. The team study a decay of the charmed baryon Lambda c into a Lambda, a neutral kaon, and a pion.

Recent BESIII measurements of related decays motivate the search. Those decays are singly Cabibbo suppressed, a class with small but telling rates. If the Sigma star exists, it should leave a mark in this decay channel. Finding or excluding it sharpens the baryon spectrum. That spectrum tests how quarks bind inside hadrons.
arxiv-2601-12878:
Kevin Schafers and Michael Gunther propose a hierarchical way to split complex differential equations. Splitting methods solve each part of a system in turn, then combine the steps. For systems split into many parts, design choices multiply fast. Their approach builds methods for N split systems by iterating two split methods.

That iterative design principle keeps construction systematic at any N. They analyze the convergence order of the resulting methods. They derive explicit formulas for the leading order error terms. They also investigate self adjointness, a symmetry that often boosts accuracy. Compositions of hierarchical methods get detailed treatment in the work.
arxiv-2601-12978:
Saad Khan, Simon Parkinson, and Monika Roopak work on a weak spot in cyber security research: shared test data. Logs of events from real systems are key for spotting attacks. Some attacks stretch across many events and show only when the events are linked. Teams must study such logs to keep systems safe, yet real logs are hard to share.

The logs also grow fast in size and rate, which strains tools. The team build a test data maker with knobs that can be set by the user. It makes logs with known attack marks baked in. Tools can then be graded on fair, shared tests. That helps the field check if new results can be run again by others.
arxiv-2601-13178:
Joseph Gatto and co-authors build a test set for triage of patient notes sent through web portals. Triage means to sort patients by need and give scarce care first to those who need it most. Portal notes are a new and fast growth form of such calls for care.

Their set is the first large public set for this task. It frames triage as a pair rank task. A tool must say which of two notes is more urgent, not just tag each one alone. Pair ranks fit how staff sort a queue by eye. For health teams, the set gives a fair way to test tools that may one day help sort notes by risk.
arxiv-2601-13278:
Don MacMillen gives a clear tour of a neat quantum case, an electron held between two grounded planes. The case joins two famed toy systems. One is the bit in a box, a free bit in a closed space. The other is the Coulomb pull, the force from a lone charge. The third famed toy, he notes, is the harmonic spring.

Here an electron sits in the gap of an endless capacitor, two flat plates held at zero volts. MacMillen works out the allowed energies and wave forms for that bind. Such toy cases teach how bind shape sets the ladder of states. For physics students, the piece is a bridge from first toys to a more rich real set up.
arxiv-2601-13378:
Lucas Pasquevich, Gustavo E. Romero, and Matias M. Reynoso ask if hid ultra bright X-ray sources in our galaxy beam neutrinos at Earth. Such sources shine in X-rays past the cap for a star mass hole fed at a calm rate. The lead view is that they are binaries fed too fast.

At that feed rate, trap of light puffs the disk thick. A thick disk can hide the core from most views, hence a hid source. The team models if such hid cores can still beam neutrinos, bits that pass through the puff with ease. A find would give a new way to see cores that light cannot leave.
arxiv-2601-13578:
Qian Feng, JiaHang Tu, and co-authors study a hard task for trained AI models in 2026. When users ask for their data to be deleted, the model must forget it step by step. Old methods often block some weights or scramble what the model knows. The team notes that such forgetting can stay shallow, with traces of the data still left to find.

Their method, called FG-OrIU, adds rules at two levels at once. It guides both the learned features and the gradients, the signals used in training. The aim is deeper forgetting that still keeps the rest of the model's skill intact. Weak forgetting, they warn, can risk leaks and harm trust in the model.
arxiv-2601-13878:
Hossein Safi and co-authors show a gigabit Ethernet link sent through open air with light in 2026. The link runs both ways at one gigabit per second over a one-meter free-space path. It uses a VCSEL-PIN pair, a laser source and a light sensor. All parts are commercially available, with no amplification.

The transparent system ran error-free in their tests. Latency stayed under twenty-five nanoseconds, a very short delay. Alignment tolerance reached the centimetre scale, so aim need not be perfect. Simple optical links like this could join boards or racks without cables.
arxiv-2601-14078:
Mathieu Lehaut, Anca Muscholl, and Nir Piterman revisit how to split asynchronous automata across machines in 2026. Zielonka's asynchronous automata model systems whose parts run at their own pace. Distribution splits one automaton into local parts that communicate. The team works in restricted settings with tree-like process architectures.

An architecture is tree-like if a spanning tree underlies it and communications stay local on the tree. They show a simple, quadratic distribution construction for this case. They also revisit synthesis for such automata. Tree-like layouts fit sensor nets and modular robots well. Quad cost is low for a build of this kind. That makes the method fit for large nets with many small parts.
arxiv-2601-14278:
Marc Walden, Jason Liu, Ryan Liu, and Hamza Khan model campus access in this 2026 paper. Their concern is students who use wheelchairs. Stairs and steep slopes make many campus paths hard or barred. The team wants a map of routes that work for all.

They build the campus as a network on a graph whose edges carry time weights. Data come from Strava and other APIs, merged into one model. A depth-first search then walks the graph to find paths. The aim is clear insight into which routes are wheelchair-accessible. Such a map can guide both daily trips and campus planning.
arxiv-2601-14378:
Erin Motherway and seven co-authors describe an odd binary star in this 2026 paper. The system is 2M07515777+1807352, a post-common envelope eclipsing binary. Its orbit takes 10.3 days and is nearly, but not quite, circular. The pair holds a massive white dwarf of 1.08 solar masses. Its partner is a main-sequence star of 0.66 solar masses at 4,400 kelvin.

A white dwarf that heavy should be compact. This one is oversize for its mass, which is why the title calls it a not-so-compact companion. The team gives a detailed characterization of the system. Readers get measured facts on a pair that tests how such binaries evolve.
arxiv-2601-14478:
Sasha Ronaghi and a team of health researchers study AI help for qualitative research in this 2026 paper. Large language models show promise for improving the efficiency of qualitative analysis in large, multi-site health-services research. Yet guidance on how to integrate them into that work is limited. Evidence of their impact on real research methods and outcomes is also scarce.

The team developed a model- and task-agnostic framework for human-LLM qualitative analysis. It is designed to support diverse analytic aims. Their title stresses scale and rigor together. Readers get a method for using language models on interview and field data without giving up the care qualitative work demands.
arxiv-2601-14578:
Naoki Seto studies gravitational waves from double white dwarfs in this 2026 paper. He investigates the detectability of post-Newtonian higher harmonics from Galactic double white dwarfs in the centihertz band, near 0.01 hertz. The quadrupole mode is the main signal such pairs emit. Higher harmonics are weaker overtones that carry extra detail about the orbit.

Using a synthetic population of these systems, Seto reaches a clear verdict. Unlike the quadrupole mode, higher harmonics remain undetectable with LISA, except for rare nearby systems. His title frames the upside: those harmonics could link LISA and DECIGO, two planned detectors in distinct bands. Readers get a sober forecast for a hoped-for signal.
arxiv-2601-14678:
Justin Cheung, Samuel Savine, Calvin Nguyen, Lin Lu, and Alhassan S. Yasin study cancer classifiers in this 2026 paper. Supervised deep learning models often perform excellently within their training distribution. They struggle to generalize beyond it. In cancer histopathology, a convolutional neural network may classify cancer severity accurately for cancer types in its training data. It may fail on related but unseen types.

The team applies transfer learning from one cancer to another via deep learning domain adaptation. Domain adaptation retunes a model so skill gained on one data source carries to a distinct one. Readers get a test of whether a severity classifier for one cancer can be adapted to serve another.
arxiv-2601-14978:
Nilanjana Chatterjee, Sidharatha Garg, A. V. Subramanyam, and Brejesh Lall work on finding a person from a written description. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with text-based person search. Vision-language models drive the field, but the training data stays small.

These models also were not pre-trained for spotting pedestrians. So each dataset gets its own fine-tuned model, shaped to that dataset alone. The authors train one model across many datasets at once. One single unified model then serves all of them well, instead of a whole shelf of separate, narrow, single-use models.
arxiv-2601-15078:
Juan J. Segura turns the study of myth into math. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with structural approaches to story, in the line of Lévi-Strauss. Such readings are strong up close but hard to compare across cultures, media, and scale.

Segura builds a formal frame that keeps the reading clear. Myth variants become typed rewrite programs. Each runs on a two-register state. One register holds the everyday social channel. The other holds the symbolic channel that grants legitimacy. Superhero continuities and long franchise arcs both fit the same formal frame well.
arxiv-2601-15278:
Mingyue Zha and Ho-Chun Herbert Chang read TikTok videos as full messages, not as separate tracks. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with short-form video and mental health discourse. A post mixes text, visuals, and audio into one communicative act.

Past work tends to study those parts in isolation. The authors build a pipeline that joins them. Automated tools extract features from all three modes. Shapley value methods then show how each mode drives engagement. The study scales that joint reading to a large set of real, public TikTok videos on health.
arxiv-2601-15378:
S. Sartori, S. Contarini, and co-authors find cosmic voids by running the universe backwards. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with voids, the vast underdense regions between galaxies. Voids are a powerful probe of cosmology, but they are hard to pin down.

Their size and emptiness make them sensitive to shot noise and redshift distortions. Observational systematics add more trouble, above all for density-based definitions. The Back-in-time Void Finder uses optimal transport reconstruction. It rebuilds the past density field, then identifies the voids in that cleaner, rebuilt early-time picture of the cosmos.
arxiv-2601-15778:
Jiaxin Zhang, Caiming Xiong, and Chien-Sheng Wu study confidence in AI agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents are moving from passive models to autonomous systems. They execute complex, multi-step tasks on their own. Overconfidence in failure remains a fundamental barrier to high-stakes use. An agent that does not know it is failing will not stop or ask for help. Existing calibration methods were built for static, single-turn outputs.

Agent runs break those methods' assumptions. Errors compound along trajectories. External tools inject their own uncertainty. Failure modes stay opaque across long runs. The title names the goal: agentic confidence calibration. Calibrated agents could slow down, verify, or escalate when doubt grows. That behavior is a precondition for trusting agents with real work.
arxiv-2601-15878:
Antonis Kalogirou studies a scalar field's heat effects in de Sitter space in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is Part II of a series. The setting is the Poincaré patch of de Sitter spacetime. He uses the thermo-field dynamics approach to compute semiclassical backreaction. Backreaction means the field's energy reshapes the spacetime it lives in. The resulting bulk equation takes Whittaker form, a known special-function shape.

Two applications follow. At leading order, curvature perturbations match a constant-roll model in its frozen attractor regime. That match gives an ultraviolet enhancement of the spectrum. The spectral index there runs near two. The second application concerns holography, per the title. Early-universe physics uses such models to explain the seeds of cosmic structure.
arxiv-2601-16178:
Luca Di Persio, Matteo Garbelli and Adrian Zălinescu link late growth tasks to back and forth chance maths. Their 2026 preprint deals with growth tasks that rest on the whole past path. Edge terms are of the Neumann type, which set flow at the rim. The chance maths pair a forth path with a back path. The forth path holds a bounce part writ as a Stieltjes sum.

The team shows the pair solves the growth task in the mild sense. Mild means the task holds in sum form, not point by point. Such links let chance tools solve hard path tasks. They also give ways to price path based claims. The work joins two fields that oft sit apart.
arxiv-2601-16278:
Branislav Pecher and five coauthors use large models as makers, not judges, for low stock tongues. Their 2026 preprint deals with text sorts in tongues with scant tagged data. Large models show strong skill in many tongues. Small sort models need tagged data that such tongues oft lack. The team has the large model make fake tagged texts.

Small models then train on the fake set for the sort task. The test checks if fake train beats use of the large model as judge. Fake data may give strong small tools at low cost. That path serves tongues left out of big data sets. The work weighs maker use as the best role.
arxiv-2601-16378:
Bridget Leonard and Scott Murray use mind based tokens to fix self view bias in joint models. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that join pics and words. Such models do well on sense tasks that join the two. They fail on space tasks that need the view of an other. That fail is a self view bias that will not fade with scale.

Tokens drawn from mind study aim to break that bias. The tokens push the model to hold an other view in mind. Gains would show that form cues can fix space thought. Space thought counts for robots and aid tools in real rooms. The work tests a low cost fix path.
arxiv-2601-16678:
Avraham Gal pays tribute to three late leaders in a niche field of nuclear physics. Tullio Bressani, Bogdan Povh, and Toshimitsu Yamazaki all died in the past two years. Each helped shape the study of strange nuclei. These are nuclei that hold a strange quark for a brief span. Gal's 2026 talk text honors their lives and work.

The piece traces the field from its start in the 1970s. Groups at CERN used beams to make the strange nuclei in flight. Later work moved to labs in the United States. Gal also notes the record of Yoshinori Akaishi, who died in 2025. The text serves as a brief past of the field.
arxiv-2601-16778:
Simon Lämmer, Mark Colley, and Patrick Ebel build fake crowds to test travel plans. How folks pick buses, cars, or bikes is hard to gauge. Taste, norms, and faith in new tech all play a part. Old ways use fixed rules and dear field polls. Their 2026 preprint swaps those rules for AI agents that act like folks.

Each agent weighs trips with its own tastes and traits. Crowds of them then show how a town may move. Planners can test new tech or rules in this fake town. That test costs far less than a real trial. It may steer green travel plans with more care.
arxiv-2601-16878:
Tim Johnston and Pierre Monmarché build a safe step rule for chance flows with sharp traits. Such flows drive grain packs in physics and trade. Their drift traits can spike to huge size in spots. Plain Euler steps fail to track such flows. Proof of sound steps was thin on the ground. Their 2026 preprint gives a tamed Euler rule with proofs.

A Lyapunov gauge, a kind of energy cap, tames the steps. The drift's slope must sit below such a cap. That need still lets drift blow up in a fin zone. Tamed steps let sims run where plain steps die. Physics and risk teams gain a tool they can trust.
arxiv-2601-17078:
Aras Bacho, Svetlana Selivanova, and Martin Ziegler ask what fast-compute means for a class of functions. Their class holds functions whose square sums stay fin. Two plain takes on fast compute arise for them. Their 2026 preprint shows the two takes do not match. That split holds short of a famed count-class merge.

One take builds from digit reads of the function. The next builds from mean-square fits by fast nets. If the two takes split, terms in proofs must be picked with care. Such care shapes how real-number compute is taught. It also guards claims in numeric code work.
arxiv-2601-17278:
Wei-Shan Su and four co-authors model what a passing star does to dust in a young planet-forming disc. Stars are born in clusters, so flybys are common. A close pass can warp the gas disc. Its effect on dust is less clear, mostly when dust and gas are weakly linked. The team runs three-dimensional fluid simulations of such passes.

They test flat passes and tilted passes side by side. They track how dust moves and clumps after each pass. Clumping feeds the streaming instability, a step toward planet birth. The results help link disc shapes seen today to past flybys. They also guide hunts for young systems shaped by a near miss.
arxiv-2601-17378:
Mohammad Zare and Pirooz Shamsinejadbabaki test privacy in federated learning. In that setup, data stays on user devices and only model updates move. It sounds private by design. Membership inference attacks test that claim. An attacker asks if one sample was in the training set. The authors present Res-MIA, an attack that needs no training of its own.

Their attack rests on resolution, a trait of how models treat data. If the attack works, private facts can leak from shared models. Health and finance models face the most risk. The work gives defenders a new test to run. It shows where federated claims need proof, not trust.
arxiv-2601-17678:
Zhiyu An and Wan Du study inverse mechanism learning. The task is to recover a hidden incentive mechanism from observed play. Self-interested agents learn and act under that mechanism. Their traces are the data. Past inverse work infers rewards inside a known structure. Here the target can be unstructured, even a neural map.

A differentiable method, DIML, learns the mechanism from trajectories. It works across multi-agent learning paths. Knowing the true incentives helps audit markets and platforms. Designers can check if rules drive the play they see. The work widens inverse game theory to black-box rules. That matches modern platforms, whose rules are learned, not written.
arxiv-2601-18278:
Indrė Žliobaitė asks what a learned model really measures when it is used as an instrument. Her 2026 preprint addresses a shift in how models are used. In science and data work, models now often serve as measurement tools, not just predictors of set labels. When the measurement rule is learned from data, the map from observations to quantities is set by the training mix and the model's biases. Several unlike maps can fit the same data. Žliobaitė examines what that freedom means for trust in the readings.

A measure whose meaning shifts with its training set is a shaky instrument. Naming the problem is the first step to standards for learned measurement. The work speaks to any field that reads nature through a model.
arxiv-2601-18378:
Takahiro Yamamoto studies a space task that aims to hear a faint hum from the young cosmos. The craft, called DECIGO, will listen for waves in space in a band where pairs of dense dead stars make a loud front noise. Those pairs spiral in and merge, and their waves crowd the band.

To hear the faint hum, staff must first strip that front noise away. Yamamoto checks how well that strip can work. He bases the check on what a past run of ground based sensors has taught us about such pairs. The count of pairs and their traits set how much noise is left. If too much noise stays, the old hum stays hid. If the strip works well, the craft could open a new view on the first age of the cosmos.
arxiv-2601-18678:
Eslam Zaher and three colleagues hone a way to tell a user what small change would flip a model's call. Such a tale, called a counterfactual, should be small, close to real cases, and in line with how the facts hang as one. Past ways pick the change by a flat gap count. A flat count can pick changes that look near on the page but could never occur in life.

The team pick the change by a path that rides the true shape of the data. That shape is built from how real cases spread in the model's hid space. A path on that shape keeps the tale in the world of real cases. Such tales could help a user act: to gain a loan, say, by a change they can truly make. Fair tales count for trust in smart calls.
arxiv-2601-18878:
Eugenio Carretta mines an old sky hunt's data to pull fresh counts of four kinds of stuff in a huge set of stars. The hunt was famed for a find that split old star groups in two by their light stuff: each group holds more than one crowd of stars, with un-like mixes. That find set the field's view of such groups for a score of years. Its shots still hold more than was pulled at the time.

Carretta pulls the counts of four mid-weight kinds of stuff for a vast set of red big stars in a score of groups. All counts are made in one way, so group can be set next to group with trust. The four kinds split by how they were made: some in calm burn, some in blasts. A clean, wide set is a gift to that work.
arxiv-2601-18978:
José Ignacio Burgos Gil and three co-authors close in on a stubborn number in number theory. For height functions, which grade how complex a point is, the essential minimum is a key floor value. For many common heights, no one has pinned that floor down in exact terms.

The team pairs two old routes. One is a lower bound method that goes back to Smyth. The other is an upper bound method based on how whole points spread out in the limit. Joining the two with linear programming narrows the gap. Each closed gap sharpens what number theorists can say about the smallest, simplest points of a given kind.
arxiv-2601-19178:
Jingyu Li and seven co-authors share cached memory across steps in sequential recommendation. Models that suggest the next item from a user's history lean on transformer attention. That math grows costly as histories lengthen, which hurts response time for long sequences.

Key-value caching, borrowed from language models, stores past work for reuse. Their method, CollectiveKV, decouples and shares that cached data across the team of computations. Shared caches could let recommenders read long histories at a price that products with strict speed limits can pay. The gain comes from not recomputing the same past steps again and again for each new pick the system must make.
arxiv-2601-19378:
Ziyang Xu and seven co-authors build an open encyclopedia of skin pathology images with an AI run workflow. Clinicians and trainees in dermatopathology often struggle to find high quality open image sets for learning and cross checking. Good sets are scattered, small, or locked away.

Their resource, DermpathNet, aims to be comprehensive and open for teaching, reference, and machine learning alike. An AI based workflow helps gather and organize the images at scale. Open, well ordered image sets lift both training of doctors and training of the models that may one day assist them.
arxiv-2601-19778:
Ahmad Farooq and Kamran Iqbal argue that peer review in software engineering research is in crisis. Submissions keep growing, incentives are misaligned, and reviewers are exhausted. Surveys report that researchers see the process as broken. The authors frame these failures as mechanism design problems, the study of how rules shape behaviour.

If the rules are the problem, better rules can be computed. Their position paper proposes a multi-agent mechanism design approach to reimagining review. Agents could match papers to reviewers and balance loads under clear incentives. The argument is programmatic: it sets out a direction rather than a finished system. It speaks to a debate every research community is having about its own gatekeeping.
arxiv-2601-20078:
R. N. Robert Bush, J. T. John Stefan, and A. G. Alexander Kosovichev investigate shock waves in the Sun's corona that appear without an eruption. A leading theory ties sunquakes to flare-accelerated particles dumping energy into the visible surface. Simulations suggest such events also excite wavefronts travelling through the corona and chromosphere. These resemble the classic Moreton-Ramsey waves and the large-scale fronts seen sweeping the corona.

The puzzle is extreme ultraviolet shockwaves with no coronal mass ejection behind them. If no eruption launched them, something else must. The authors investigate observations to test the flare-driven account. Coronal waves are diagnostics of the Sun's magnetic atmosphere. Explaining the orphan waves would complete a corner of flare physics.
arxiv-2601-20578:
Dimitris Michailidis, Sennay Ghebreab, and Fernando P. Santos ask who benefits when transport networks expand, using congestion games with learning agents. Bigger networks are meant to improve mobility, yet they can also create inequality. The authors show that disparities arise not only from the shape of the network but also from how commuters adapt to it.

Different travelers learn and adjust at different rates and in different ways. Those differences can leave some groups with worse trips after an upgrade. The finding warns planners that a fair network on paper can still play out unfairly in daily use.
arxiv-2601-20778:
Lisa Marquand and Sasha Viktorova construct new families of a classic object in algebraic geometry. Their 2026 paper studies cubic fourfolds, shapes cut out by a cubic equation. The authors focus on smooth cubic fourfolds that contain highly singular hyperplane sections. A hyperplane section is the shape left when a flat cut passes through.

The pair construct five irreducible divisors in the moduli space of such fourfolds. Each divisor parametrizes fourfolds with one of these singular sections. They then prove that none of the five is a Noether-Lefschetz or Hassett divisor. The proof uses a computational method due to Addington and Auel. The result adds new landmarks to the map of how cubic fourfolds can vary.
arxiv-2601-20978:
Omid Khosravi and Mehdi Tatari solve a wave equation with neural networks that respect physics. Their 2026 paper studies the one-dimensional advection equation. Advection describes a quantity carried along by a flow. The hard cases here have discontinuous initial and boundary conditions. Sharp jumps are where physics-informed neural networks, or PINNs, often struggle. Spectral bias makes them favor smooth answers over sharp ones.

The authors stack three techniques against that bias. A Fourier feature mapping layer feeds the network richer inputs. A two-stage training strategy tunes the features first, then the weights. Adaptive loss weighting balances the terms during training. Together the steps help the network honor sudden jumps. The work serves engineers who simulate transport with learned solvers.
arxiv-2601-21178:
Antonio Smecca examines whether a broken symmetry of QCD heals as matter heats up. The 2026 paper studies the axial U(1) symmetry at finite temperature. In the massless QCD Lagrangian, this symmetry is explicit. Quantization breaks it through the anomaly. At some finite temperature, it may be effectively restored. That restoration would carry important consequences. It would bear on the order of the chiral transition and the QCD phase diagram.

Mesonic correlators are the probe. These functions track how quark-antiquark pairs behave in hot matter. Their patterns differ depending on whether the symmetry is restored. Heavy-ion collisions create such heat for an instant. Lattice simulations can compute the correlators directly. Smecca's study helps read those signals. The result feeds the map of matter at extreme temperature.
arxiv-2601-21278:
Mohit Talreja and nine co-authors test whether vision models can explain how they guess where a photo was taken. The best models now rival top human players at naming the place. Yet many give poor reasons for their guess, even when the guess itself is right.

Their benchmark, GeoRC, grades the chain of evidence behind each answer. A model must point to the clues in the image that support its call. Right answers with wrong reasons reveal luck rather than skill. The benchmark pushes models toward answers that people can check, trust, and learn from.
arxiv-2601-21478:
Kang You builds a new way to model causal links in the brain from scalp recordings. Modeling how brain regions drive each other, from tiny circuits to the whole brain, is hard. Group comparisons make it harder, since wiring thousands of neurons cannot be modeled directly at that scale.

The author constructs differential causal networks straight from EEG data. The networks highlight where causal patterns differ between groups. That focus suits studies of illness, where the change from healthy wiring is the signal of interest. A direct route from raw traces to causal maps could speed clinical research.
arxiv-2601-21778:
Zijie Xu and co-authors examine a shortcut that often fails. Spiking neural networks can be made by converting an already trained ordinary network, which avoids costly retraining. That is attractive for reinforcement learning, where training through live interaction is expensive and can be unsafe.

In practice, though, converted networks perform poorly on continuous control, tasks where actions vary smoothly, like steering or balancing. The 2026 preprint studies how errors grow during conversion and what limits the method in these settings. Knowing where the shortcut breaks helps engineers decide when conversion is safe to use. And it points to what a better conversion method would need to fix first.
arxiv-2601-21978:
Shiqi Fan and co-authors work on reasoning over temporal knowledge graphs, networks of facts that change over time. The task is to predict future events by inferring missing entities as the graph evolves. Language model methods for this job tend to favor context over structure.

As a result, they struggle to pull the right subgraphs out of a dynamic graph, lose structural information, and produce unstructured, sometimes hallucinated reasoning. The team's 2026 preprint bridges graph structure with knowledge-guided editing to keep reasoning interpretable. Better temporal reasoning would help forecasting in finance, politics, and logistics. Where events build on chains of earlier facts that a model must respect, not invent.
arxiv-2601-22478:
Khiem Le and six co-authors lift a training method by showing it the same task in fresh dress. Their 2026 preprint notes that models learn by next-word prediction, which makes them pattern matchers at heart. A reworded task can trip them, though the core ask is the same.

Their tweak, Transform-Augmented GRPO, trains on such reworded forms. The aim is to lift Pass@k, the chance that one of a few tries is right. Robustness to wording is key for real use, where no two users ask alike. The work makes training match that fact.
arxiv-2601-22878:
Rajini Makam and four co-authors present DIVER, a method for cleaning up underwater photos. Underwater images fade and blur because water absorbs colors unevenly, scatters light, and lights scenes poorly. These problems shift with water type and depth, so one fixed fix rarely works.

DIVER blends hands-on corrections with a physics-guided model, and it learns without labeled examples. The design aims to work across many waters, not just the ones it trained on. Clearer images help divers, biologists, and robots inspect reefs, wrecks, and pipelines. The method is unsupervised, so it needs no hand-cleaned example images, which are almost impossible to gather underwater.
arxiv-2601-22978:
Jonathan Baumann and co-authors build a verified defense against speculative control-flow attacks. These attacks, of the Spectre family, trick a processor into leaking data while it guesses ahead. Their defense, SpecIBT, joins hardware control-flow checks with compiler-added hardening for risky loads.

The key insight is that hardware checks can flag exactly when a guess went wrong, so hardening applies only then. The whole defense is formally verified, meaning its safety is proved, not just tested. Proved defenses matter for chips that guard secrets. Compiler-inserted hardening is applied with precision, guided by exactly where the hardware protection says speculation went wrong.
arxiv-2601-23078:
Timo Feistl, Severin Schraven, and Simone Warzel prove symmetry-protection theorems for quantum lattice systems. The classic Mermin-Wagner result limits which symmetries can break in low dimensions. Their version covers systems with multipole symmetries, symmetries tied to higher moments of charge.

They show that higher-order symmetries protect lower-order ones from breaking. In particular, charge symmetry needs more dimensions to break when multipole symmetries are present. Such theorems set firm rules for what phases of quantum matter can exist. Higher multipole symmetries raise the critical dimension for breaking the charge symmetry, a concrete, checkable consequence.
arxiv-2601-23178:
Chenxi Kong, Michael Gurnis, and Zachary E. Ross run mantle convection both forward and backward with neural operators. Reconstructing the mantle's past thermal state means reversing convection, which is an important but very costly computation. Those reconstructions link seismic images with what we see at the surface.

Neural operators learn the convection mapping itself, making repeated runs far cheaper. Fast forward and inverse runs let geophysicists test many Earth histories against data. That speed could clarify how plates, plumes, and the deep Earth evolved. Seismic tomographic images supply the observations the reconstructions must respect, tying deep structure to present-day measurements.
arxiv-2603-01578:
Quantum programs must be mapped onto real chips, where each chip wires its qubits in its own layout. Gabrielius Keibas and Linas Petkevicius present a shared test frame for that mapping job in this 2026 work. Many mapping methods exist, but no common frame compared them fairly across chips and circuits.

Their open-source frame, QuMeld, now holds six mapping methods and sixteen chip layouts. Users can score each method with several metrics and swap parts in or out with ease. New methods, circuits, layouts, and metrics plug into the same frame as the field grows. A single yardstick helps teams pick the right mapper for a given chip instead of guessing from scattered claims.
arxiv-2603-01978:
P. Cataldi, V. Cristiani, F. Rodriguez, and colleagues prepare a way to estimate how galaxies fill dark matter halos for a coming survey. Their 2026 work targets the LSST imaging survey from the Vera Rubin Observatory. The halo occupation distribution links galaxy counts to halo mass and anchors galaxy formation tests.

Their method extends background subtraction to use more photometric information from imaging data. An iterative centroiding tool finds group centers, a step the whole estimate depends on. Each pipeline step faces checks for group size, purity, and completeness of the group catalog. Photometric redshift errors and halo mass uncertainty enter as systematics in the tests. On a mock catalog built from a large simulation suite, the method recovers the target distribution across a wide brightness and mass range.
arxiv-2603-02278:
Phil Attard extends a quantum simulation method in classical terms in this 2026 physics paper. Quantum effects can be folded into classical phase space through a special commutation function. That function encodes the uncertainty principle inside an otherwise classical picture. Attard expands it to third order and simplifies it for use in position space alone.

Momentum is integrated out, leaving a real function over positions only. That form fits standard Monte Carlo sampling, a workhorse of simulation. He reports simulation results for liquid helium-4 in a classic pair-potential model. Runs cover temperatures below ten kelvin, deep in the quantum regime for a light liquid. The paper is the second part of a series on this approach.
arxiv-2603-02378:
Alexander Nemecek, Hengzhi He, Guang Cheng, and Erman Ayday expose a clash between two content checks in this 2026 paper. Provenance records claim to certify who made a file, and watermarks tag AI-made content. The two systems run independently and never consult each other. That gap lets a file pass both checks while telling two opposite stories.

Their Integrity Clash is a file with a valid record claiming human authorship and a watermark marking it as AI-made. Standard editing workflows can wash metadata to create such fakes with no cryptographic break. Only one permitted missing field in the current standard enables the trick. Their joint audit, checking both layers together, classified thousands of test images perfectly. The fix, they argue, is simple and overdue.
arxiv-2603-02978:
Bethany Terris asks what an observer is inside one view of quantum theory. That view treats quantum states as facts for an observer, not as fixed traits of the world. Her 2026 paper presses a basic worry: shared checks need observers who last through time and keep stable records.

Terris argues that the bare rule, any system that interacts counts, cannot support that kind of lasting record. She adds a second layer: the capacity to hold records together across many acts of measuring. With that layer, cases where one observer watches another still yield facts both can confirm. The paper shores up the view's account of shared proof.
arxiv-2603-03078:
Siwei Zhang, Yun Xiong, Xi Chen, and colleagues widen the exploration habits of tool-using language agents during training. Agents trained by reinforcement learning usually learn only from their own rollouts, so they rarely discover reasoning styles outside their current habits. Their 2026 method, RAPO, injects retrieved outside experience into the loop.

Training splits into two phases. During rollouts, the agent reasons continuously over retrieved step-level traces from other policies, extending what it can consider. cia-0000015378: A reported sighting of unconventional aircraft fills a CIA file dated September 3, 1955. Reported is the careful word; no one swore to the craft. The fall of 1955 brought a fresh crop of such claims. This file holds one of them, worded with the era's full and careful caution. The September sighting report is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015478: Sightings from January 19 to May 15, 1954, are gathered in a CIA record of unidentified flying objects. The title's own span is used here, since an older summary gave a shorter one. Four months of reports in one bundle let readers judge pace and pattern. Spring brought a fresh crop of claims, and the agency counted them like the seasons before.
cia-0000016878: How well Vietnamese communist forces could keep fighting in South Vietnam is weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1967. Such papers measured troops, supply, losses, and will to fight. In 1967 the war was growing, and sound judgment of enemy strength carried grave weight. The clipped title marks the paper as an original study, a core task of the agency's analysts.
cia-0000042878:
El Salvador: Update on the Jesuit Killings, number 6, is a CIA record dated April 4, 1990. By the sixth update, the case was months old and still open. The series had become the case's public diary in brief form.

Inside, the latest position of the investigation is recorded. Spring updates dealt with courts, custody, and slow legal motion. The file shows the case settling into its long middle passage. Headlines had faded by the spring, yet the numbered briefs kept coming on schedule. Their steady rhythm is itself evidence of how long justice took in this case.
cia-0000044478:
R. Zamora was interviewed on the killing of the Jesuit priests, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The file is a second interview record under nearly the same title. Zamora spoke for the political opposition in El Salvador.

Inside, his account of the case is given again, weeks into the new year. Repetition let the opposition keep its charge before the public. Each interview sharpened the case against the army's account. The file shows that pressure being maintained on purpose, so the murders could not sink from view while the courts moved at their own slow pace.
cia-0000045978: Diplomats commented on a photograph said to show living American servicemen still held after the Vietnam War. A CIA item dated June 6, 1991, kept their reactions. cia-0000049078: El Salvador's chief of staff gave his views on criticism of the military high command in a CIA item from 1984. The criticism, much of it from Washington, blamed the command for abuses it refused to punish. His answer, preserved here, shows the brass defending its honor while the war's record grew darker.
cia-0000049178: The Joint General Staff headquarters in El Salvador evaluated public comments by a former colonel in a CIA item from 1990. cia-0000049278: A House intelligence staffer named Giza sent a follow-up request in 1985 about the Honduran death squad investigation, and a CIA item preserves it. cia-0000075278: Pro-Cominform Communist Party protest of the Rosenberg sentences is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075278, dated October 1, 1952. cia-0000096478: Decision of Balram Singh Rai to lead an alternative East Indian party is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000096478, dated July 4, 1964. cia-0000119578:
An April 1966 special report in the CIA's Current Intelligence Weekly takes up the problems of the Czechoslovak Communist Party. The title trails off mid-phrase in the file, but the subject is clear enough: the party that ran Czechoslovakia was in trouble. The report appeared two years before the Prague Spring.

The party's problems, as the agency framed them, grew out of reform pressure inside a system built on tight control. Analysts were watching for cracks in the Soviet bloc, and Czechoslovakia was showing them early. The report matters because it shows the strain was visible long before the famous reform movement of 1968 made headlines around the world.
cia-0000126878: Dated around August 1968, this CIA document studies the short-run economic effects of the Soviet occupation of Czechoslovakia, the heading breaking off. cia-0000126978: A June 1975 CIA National Intelligence Bulletin covers Angola. cia-0000132178: Situation report 494, from January 1991, covers political developments including Soviets evacuating, the heading breaking off. cia-0000132278: Spanish legislators reaffirming support is the headline of Situation Report 587 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 3, 1991. cia-0000132578: Castro planning a return to the United Nations General Assembly fills item 11 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated September 4, 1960. The short item tracks the early plans for that appearance.
cia-0000132678: Two items share a CIA paper dated March 2, 1961. The first reports Poland keeping up its long-term credits to Cuba. The short paper covers both halves as they were filed together that day.
cia-0000132778: Washington filed a third paper on Cuba and the Caribbean on August 4, 1960, and this briefing is that entry. Three same-day regional papers show a government watching closely, with Cuba at the center of its concerns. The declassified text survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive, cataloged as document 0000132778.
cia-0000135678: Dated 2 November 1960, this Spanish text is one of several 2506 Brigade documents bearing that same date in the declassified release. Read together, the same-day papers suggest a busy administrative period in the camps; read alone, this one is a dated Spanish record of the brigade, preserved through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135978: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 February 1954, covers the trading of a burnt plane, raised as a possibility in a cable from the Lincoln station. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136278: A cable of 1 May 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with Instruction 15 for broadcast, the high-water mark of the numbered script series. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000138978: Russian troop disposition is the subject of this 1946 report. The sample kept here is mostly markings. Distribution stamps limit it to American and British officials. It shows early Cold War order-of-battle reporting. Its substance stays locked in the original file.
cia-03179878: April 15, 1955: the day's intelligence went out. Analysts sent their global roundup to senior officials. The Cold War's tax-day brief. Future scholars will discover it. This declassified bulletin stays. It is archived. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06485478: 1. <SANITIZED> REPORTS THAT THE ASSASSINATION OF DR. MARTIN LUTHER KING, a CIA document. The King assassination file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
cia-06569678: SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC - "FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF YUGOSLAVIA", a CIA document. The Serbian leader's file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
