The title gives the answer: trazodone impairs the cortical plasticity that sleep should bring. A drug taken for sleep that blunts sleep's brain benefit is a poor bargain for some patients. The finding widens the caution beyond one drug class and gives prescribers a reason to weigh brain effects, not just hours slept.
plos-pone-0006178:
Sea cucumbers lack the neat immune organs that backboned animals have, yet their guts still answer attacks. Francisco Ramirez-Gomez and colleagues studied gut tissue in the sea cucumber Holothuria glaberrima for a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used a bacterial product called LPS, a common trigger, to switch the tissue's defences on.

The team catalogued which genes turned on in the gut after the trigger. The results show that organs not built for defence can still join the immune response. That finding widens the picture of immunity in animals without backbones. It may also help explain how sea cucumbers heal and regrow gut tissue so well.
plos-pone-0006278:
The tissue around a tumor usually helps it grow, but fat tissue cells may do the opposite. Beatrice Cousin and colleagues tested adult stromal cells from human fat against pancreatic cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Normal tissue balance depends on constant talk between epithelial cells and their surroundings; cancer breaks that balance.

The fat-derived cells provoked pancreatic cancer cell death both in dishes and in living animals. A cell type from ordinary body fat thus shows anti-tumor action. The finding suggests a possible cell-based treatment route for a hard cancer. It also reframes how the tumor environment can be used against itself.
plos-pone-0006378:
The rails inside cells, called microtubules, are built and taken apart all through the life of a cell. Bernard Piette and his team built a heat and energy model of that build and break cycle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These rails are key to two big tasks: pulling gene bundles apart and the last split of a cell in two.

The model ties the speed of growth to the energy the parts carry. It shows which facts set how fast a rail grows or falls apart. Such rules help make sense of the wild swings seen under the microscope. They also guide drugs that freeze the rails to stop cancer growth.
plos-pone-0006478:
Robert Bradley and co-authors modeled the evolution of non-coding RNAs in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2009. Non-coding RNAs are RNA molecules that work without becoming proteins. Finding their genes in a genome is hard, since they leave faint signals. The team benchmarked prediction methods that use evolutionary grammar models.

They experimented with eight models of structural evolution and two prediction programs. Benchmarks show which model best balances finding real genes against false alarms. Better prediction expands the known RNA catalog in Drosophila, a key model species. The lessons also apply to gene hunting in other animals.
plos-pone-0006578:
Kennedy Matsagas, David Lim, Marc Horwitz, and colleagues tested long-term drug effects in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2009. Small invertebrate animals, such as nematodes and fruit flies, are increasingly used to test candidate drugs. They serve both specific therapeutic purposes and long-term safety testing. The team examined functional side-effects of stimulants and sedatives in Drosophila melanogaster.

Long-term effects are hard to study in short-lived patients trials, but flies live fast. Functional readouts show whether behavior and health suffer over time. The work supports flies as an early screen for drug safety. It may flag problems before mammalian testing.
plos-pone-0006678:
Darryll D. Dudley, Hong-Cheng Wang, and Xiao-Hong Sun examined a protein called Hes1 in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hes1 belongs to a family of proteins switched on by Notch signaling. These proteins repress transcription, turning other genes down. Mice lacking Hes1 had hinted that it matters for normal development. The authors asked what happens when Hes1 stays active in T cells.

Their work shows Hes1 can strengthen T cell lymphomagenesis, the formation of T cell lymphoma. It does so by raising activity in a subset of Notch target genes. That links a single repressor protein to cancer growth in immune cells. The study clarifies how Notch signaling can tip toward malignancy. It may help explain some T cell cancers in people.
plos-pone-0006778:
Elizabeth M. Goebel, Xuqing Zhang, and Eric T. Harvill tested cross-protection between two Bordetella bacteria in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. One species, B. bronchiseptica, infects many mammals and spreads efficiently. It is rarely seen in humans. The other, B. pertussis, causes whooping cough in people. It appears specialized for the human host.

Mice were infected with or vaccinated against B. pertussis. They were then challenged with B. bronchiseptica. Prior exposure substantially protected them, as the title reports. Shared antigens likely explain the protection. The result shows immunity crosses between these related bacteria. It may inform vaccine designs that borrow protection across species lines.
plos-pone-0006878:
Leticia Ochoa-Ochoa and her team weighed two ways to guard land for Mexico's frogs and toads in PLOS ONE in 2009. Land guard plans tend to count just state-run parks. Towns and land owners now guard land in their own ways too. Those grass-roots acts add up to a real force for wild life. Mexico's frogs and toads are rich in kinds and much at risk.

The team set state parks next to grass-roots guard work. They asked how much frog and toad safety each one brings. Town-held land may shield kinds and homes the state parks miss. Put side by side, the two can close gaps that each leaves on its own. Plans should count town-held land with full weight.
plos-pone-0006978:
Yubo Hou and Senjie Lin compared genome sizes across life forms in PLOS ONE in 2009. Predicting how many genes an unsequenced genome holds is a prized skill. It is especially wanted for dinoflagellates, whose huge genomes resist sequencing. The pair used fully sequenced genomes from many branches of life as their base.

They found the link between gene number and genome size differs by group. Eukaryotes follow one pattern, and non-eukaryotes another. Applying the right pattern gave gene counts for dinoflagellate genomes. Those estimates guide genome projects before costly sequencing begins.
plos-pone-0007078:
Caroline Savage and Andrew Vickers audited data sharing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many journals require authors to share their data with other researchers. Authors can deposit data publicly or send it on request. These rules are explicit but had barely been tested. The pair checked authors publishing in PLoS journals.

They asked how well authors actually complied with sharing policies. Empirical checks matter because shared data underpins replication. If requests quietly fail, published findings rest on weaker ground. Their audit gave editors rare hard numbers on a policy most journals simply assume works.
plos-pone-0007178:
Jin Hu, Ola Winqvist, Amilcar Flores-Morales, and colleagues studied human immune cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their focus is dendritic cells, which show foreign material to other immune cells. Labs can grow these cells from blood monocytes and then mature them with a bacterial signal called LPS.

The authors ask how a regulator protein named SOCS2 changes that maturation step. They follow human monocyte-derived dendritic cells as they respond to LPS. Their findings add detail to how the immune system tunes its first response to bacterial infection and inflammation.
plos-pone-0007278:
Paul van Donkelaar, Yu Lin, and David Hewlett studied eye movement planning in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Saccades are rapid eye movements that align central vision with objects of interest. Children often make quick saccades that are poorly planned and fall short of their target, the authors had shown.

The authors test adults on a gap saccade task. They examine frontal oculomotor areas in the cortex, the brain regions that plan eye movements. They report asymmetric contributions from the two sides of the brain. Their work clarifies how the brain plans fast, accurate gaze shifts.
plos-pone-0007378:
Yan Ropert-Coudert, Lisa Brooks, Maki Yamamoto, and colleagues measured koala heart responses to tourists in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Koalas operate on a tight energy budget. They may not show behavioral avoidance even when stressed, because moving costs energy they cannot spare on their low-nutrition eucalyptus diet.

The authors investigate physiological responses of captive koalas at a conservation centre. They record ECG, the heart's electrical signal, as tourists approach. Their preliminary study tests whether hearts reveal stress that behavior hides. Wildlife centres can use such measures to judge visitor distances and handling rules.
plos-pone-0007478:
Anne Beghin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a small molecular switch protein called Arl2 and its role in breast cancer. Earlier work showed Arl2 levels affect how breast tumor cells divide and how their internal skeleton behaves. The open question was whether Arl2 changes how aggressive tumors become in a living body. The team tested that in mice lacking immune defenses.

They grew two different human breast tumors in the mice, with Arl2 levels raised or lowered. Shifting Arl2 changed how aggressively the tumors behaved. That moves Arl2 from a cell-culture curiosity to a driver of tumor character in vivo. A switch that controls aggressiveness is a possible drug target. It is also a candidate marker for judging how dangerous a tumor may be.
plos-pone-0007578:
Erik Hill and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on cocaine methiodide, a charged variant of cocaine. Unlike cocaine itself, this analog cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Researchers therefore use it to study the drug's actions on the body alone. Yet its strength at cocaine's main molecular targets had never been pinned down clearly. The team measured those potencies in mice.

They determined how strongly the analog hits each major target, including the transporters cocaine is known to block. Firm numbers let researchers interpret older experiments with confidence. They also sharpen new ones that separate body effects from brain effects. Cocaine's harms to the heart and vessels happen outside the brain, so the distinction matters. The study is measurement work, the kind that makes other experiments trustworthy.
plos-pone-0007678:
Eduardo Altmann, Janet Pierrehumbert and Adilson Motter published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the timing of words in text. Word counts follow a famous rule: a few words appear often, and most appear rarely. The authors asked a different question, about when words show up.

They tracked bursts, when a word appears many times in a short span, and lulls, when it fades from use. They found that these timing patterns follow scaling laws, much like patterns in nature. The work hints that the rhythm of language carries information that plain counts miss.
plos-pone-0007778:
Thomas Ioerger and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reads the genomes of drug-resistant TB strains from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. That region had suffered an outbreak of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. The outbreak strains belong to the highly virulent KZN family.

The team sequenced strains that resist many drugs, and some that resist nearly all. Comparing their genomes shows how resistance evolved step by step. It also reveals which mutations matter most. Genome clues like these help labs track dangerous strains. They can also guide the search for drugs that still work.
plos-pone-0007878:
Nian Xiong and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It presents a rat model meant to mirror Parkinson's disease more faithfully. A good animal model could reveal what causes the disease. It could also speed the testing of new medicines.

Existing toxin-based models fail to copy the main clinical features. They also miss the disease's slow pathology. The team infused rotenone precisely into rat brains using stereotaxic guidance. They report the model is reliable for research use. A model that behaves like the human disease makes drug screening far more meaningful.
plos-pone-0007978:
Apratim Mitra and colleagues used chip data to compare genomes within a species, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their tool was array-based comparative genomic hybridization, which counts how many copies of each DNA stretch a sample holds. Such copy shifts are a large source of variety.

The team built a way to read those shifts and draw family ties from them. Copy patterns can show how alike two samples are and how groups split over time. The method turns a tool made for disease work into one for basic questions about variety and kinship.
plos-pone-0008078:
Aneta Kotevski and colleagues reported a ghost gene found on mouse chromosome 7 in PLOS ONE in 2009. The look-alike mimics XIAP, a real gene that blocks the cell death program and juggles many partners. Genome scans had flagged the copy as if it were a second working gene.

Close reading showed the copy is a pseudogene, a worn fossil that makes no working protein. Naming it as a fossil matters. Without the label, labs could waste years chasing a gene that does nothing, or misread tests that pick up its echo.
plos-pone-0008178:
Felix Wussow, Helmut Fickenscher, and B. Karsten Tischer described a lab method in PLOS ONE in 2009 for handling cloned herpesvirus genomes. Scientists often clone large viral genomes inside bacteria using bacterial artificial chromosomes, or BACs. These carriers help build test viruses and targeting tools. A cloning carrier must later be removed cleanly.

The team used Red-mediated transposition to move and finally release the mini-F vector part of the clone. Red-based methods let researchers edit BACs inside Escherichia coli with care. A clean final release leaves the infectious viral genome free of carrier parts. That makes the clone safer and more exact for later study.
plos-pone-0008278:
Inés Horovitz, Thomas Martin, and Jonathan Bloch described early marsupial skulls in PLOS ONE in 2009. The early evolution of living marsupials is poorly understood. Early members of the group are known almost only from jaws and teeth. That gap limits knowledge of how living marsupials are related. It also clouds the origin of opossums.

New cranial material fills part of that gap. Skulls reveal far more about diet, senses, and kinship than teeth alone. The authors used the anatomy to place early marsupials on the family tree. Their work clarifies where opossums came from.
plos-pone-0008378:
Song Yang and Philip E. Bourne traced protein domain history in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Protein structural domains are evolutionary units of proteins. Their relationships can be detected over long evolutionary distances. Domain history includes origins, loss, transfer, duplication, and new combinations. Viewing that history through species phylogeny was the authors' approach.

They mapped how domains changed as species diverged. Gains and losses of domains mark key steps in protein evolution. That view helps explain how new protein functions arise. It also informs the classification of proteins across all life.
plos-pone-0008478:
Raghavan Madhavan and co-authors study a protein at nerve-muscle junctions in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. At those junctions, clusters of acetylcholine receptors receive nerve signals. Clustering depends on a muscle receptor called MuSK. A nerve protein called agrin switches MuSK on. That switch starts a chain of signals inside the muscle cell. The team ask where cortactin fits in that chain.

Cortactin helps organize the cell skeleton near the membrane. The authors test if it is needed for receptor clusters to form. Their results place cortactin in the clustering process. The work adds a step to how synapses between nerve and muscle are built.
plos-pone-0008578:
Markus Hilty and co-authors compare airway germs in asthma in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A rich germ environment in infancy protects against asthma. Yet infections also trigger asthma attacks. The team compare airway microbiota in adults with asthma. They also study patients with COPD, a related lung disease, and healthy controls. Samples come from three levels of the airways.

They find the microbial communities in asthmatic airways are disordered. The mix of germs differs from that in healthy airways. Such disorder may sustain inflammation even without a clear infection. The work shifts asthma research toward the whole airway community, not single germs.
plos-pone-0008678:
Toshio Kodama, Kazuyoshi Gotoh, Hirotaka Hiyoshi, and coworkers studied a germ that spoils seafood meals. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article looks at Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a cause of food poisoning around the world. Much of its harm comes from one stretch of DNA called Vp-PAI. That stretch holds toxin genes and a needle-like system for injecting proteins.

The team asked which switches turn those island genes on or off. They singled out two regulator proteins that help drive gut toxicity. Blocking such switches could weaken the germ without killing it outright. The work gives drug hunters a clearer picture of how this pathogen causes illness.
plos-pone-0008778:
Stuart Wilson, Judith Law, Ben Mitchinson, and colleagues modeled how rat brains map whisker movement. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A recent experiment found pinwheel patterns in the rat barrel cortex. Each pinwheel sorts whisker pushes by direction. The layout recalls maps seen in visual brain areas. How such a map builds itself during development was unknown.

The model grew maps from simple activity-based rules. Simulated maps matched the pinwheel layout seen in real brains. Self-organization may thus explain the pattern without detailed wiring instructions. The work links touch maps in rats to broader rules of brain development.
plos-pone-0008878:
Charles Willis, Brad Ruhfel, Richard Primack, and colleagues used Henry David Thoreau's old plant records to judge invasion success. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-native plants often outcompete local ones as climate warms. Thoreau catalogued Concord's flora in the 1850s with unusual care. Modern surveys of the same woods show which species won or lost. Climate response was the suspected edge.

Plants that shifted their flowering with warming fared best, and non-natives shifted more. That favorable response explains much of the invaders' success. The finding warns that warming tilts plant contests toward newcomers. Historical records prove priceless for such century-scale tests.
plos-pone-0008978:
Claudia Kruger and Claudia Kappen studied mice carrying extra copies of two body-plan genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hox genes tell a growing embryo where body parts belong. They also guide cartilage cells as they mature into the tissue that precedes bone. Too much Hoxc8 or Hoxd4 activity badly deforms cartilage in these mice.

The pair measured which cartilage development genes changed under the overdose. Genes that cartilage cells need for orderly growth shifted up or down. The pattern helps explain why the animals' skeletons form wrongly. It also shows how a small dosing error in one gene can ripple across a whole tissue.
plos-pone-0009078:
Pradeep Gupta, Shihui Liu, and Stephen Leppla profiled a mutant hamster cell that shrugs off bacterial toxins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chinese hamster ovary cells are workhorses of cell biology labs. The mutant was found by inserting retroviruses to break genes at random. It survived several toxins that normally poison cells by tagging proteins.

The resistance traced to a fault in elongation factor-2. That factor is a core part of the cell's protein-building machinery. The toxins attack exactly that factor, so breaking it first blocks them. Mutants like this reveal which cell parts a toxin truly needs.
plos-pone-0009178:
Akira Yamasaki and co-authors reported this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject is asthma, a disease where airways swell and tighten. Earlier work had linked a signaling protein called IL-9 to the inflammation behind allergic asthma. The team asked how IL-9 acts on the muscle cells that line the airways.

Working with human airway smooth muscle cells, they traced what IL-9 switches on inside the cell. They found that IL-9 raises production of CCL11, a chemical that draws in allergy-related immune cells. The signal runs through a relay protein called STAT3. That pathway helps explain how IL-9 may feed the long-term airway changes seen in asthma.
plos-pone-0009278:
Elizabeth Selig and John Bruno published this ocean study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reef-building corals are declining worldwide under pressure from human activity. Coral reefs hold great value for wildlife, coasts, and people, so their loss is a global concern. Marine protected areas, where fishing and other uses are limited, are a leading tool to save them.

The authors analyzed evidence from protected areas around the world. They asked whether protection actually slows or prevents coral loss inside the reserves. A global verdict matters because reserves are costly and politically hard to create. Their answer helps conservation groups spend that effort where it works.
plos-pone-0009378:
Maria Christina Shina and co-authors published this slime mold study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dictyostelium is an amoeba that moves and feeds as a single cell. Its genome carries several Sec7 genes, which make proteins that switch other proteins on. Those switch proteins fall into three families found across complex life.

The team characterized a Dictyostelium member of the cytohesin family. Cytohesins were known from animals, where they help run cell traffic and signaling. Finding and describing the amoeba's version shows how far back this family reaches. It also gives a simple organism in which to study what cytohesins do.
plos-pone-0009478:
Francisco Quintana and co-authors looked at immune control in zebrafish in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fish, like people, build a wide set of immune receivers by shuffling gene parts. That power brings a risk: some receivers may attack the body's own tissues. In mammals, regulatory T cells that carry Foxp3 keep that risk in check.

The team found a like system at work in zebrafish. These fish are among the oldest backboned animals with this kind of immunity. So the peacekeeping role of Foxp3 cells is very old. The finding shows that immune self control has deep evolutionary roots.
plos-pone-0009578:
Mikael Lindstrom and Monica Nister silenced a ribosome part in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ribosomes build the cell's proteins. When their work is disturbed, the tumor guard p53 often wakes and stops growth. A small set of ribosome proteins can trigger that alarm. The team turned off ribosomal protein S9 in cultured cells and watched what followed.

Silencing S9 set off a wide set of cell responses tied to p53. Cancer cell growth slowed as a result. The work shows how closely protein making is tied to tumor defense. A ribosome part can thus be a weak point that future cancer research may exploit.
plos-pone-0009678:
Zebrafish are small striped fish that labs around the world use to study hormones and development. In 2010, Gayathri Chandrasekar and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE how much estrogen receptor zebrafish carry at two life stages. They compared embryos with adult fish after dosing with natural and lab-made chemicals that bind these receptors.

Estrogen receptors are proteins that let cells respond to estrogen and similar chemicals in water. Counting them before and after exposure gives a baseline for a widely used test animal. The results help researchers judge how estrogen-like pollutants may affect fish while they are still growing.
plos-pone-0009778:
Sander P. van Noort and co-authors published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study models how the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum varies its surface coats to dodge the immune system. One coat family, PfEMP1, has about 60 variants in each parasite genome and is a prime target of immune attack.

The model joins spread between hosts with rivalry inside one host. It sorts the coats into blocks with set rank, some strong inside a host and some favored by immune pressure across hosts. That split reproduces patterns seen in field data. It predicts two clusters of coat genes, one fit for new hosts and one for hosts with some immunity.
plos-pone-0009878:
Finding where transcription factors bind DNA is a core task in genomics. Xiang Zhou and colleagues approached that prediction from systems biology, using whole-network thinking. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transcription factors are the proteins that switch genes on and off.

A binding site is a short DNA stretch a factor grips to control a gene. Systems biology adds context, like which genes work together, to raw sequence clues. Better predictions save lab time and sharpen gene maps. The approach treats binding as part of a living network, not a lone pattern.
plos-pone-0009978:
Long life, strong immunity, and stress resistance may rise and fall together in tiny worms. Francis Amrit, Claudia Boehnisch, and Robin May measured how those traits covary. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worms live only a few weeks, so aging is quick to study.

Phenotypic covariance means two traits change together across individuals. The animals were Caenorhabditis nematodes, worms widely used in aging research. If the traits trade off, breeding for one may cost another. Shared roots would mean one pathway steers aging, defense, and toughness together.
plos-pone-0010078:
The authors were Ryan Kitko, Jessica Wilks, Gian Garduque, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked how E. coli bacteria keep their inner acidity steady. Cells use many tricks for that job, including chemical breakdown and ion flows across the membrane. Potassium flow is a known contributor, but how it compensates for acid stress was unclear.

The team tested osmolytes, small molecules that protect cells from water stress. They found these molecules also contribute to pH balance in E. coli. The result links two survival systems that were often studied apart.
plos-pone-0010178:
Pascal Feunou, Julie Bertout, and Camille Locht tested a new whooping cough vaccine in mice in 2010. Despite wide vaccine use, whooping cough still kills many children around the world each year. Two vaccine types exist, older whole-cell and newer acellular forms. Newer ones cause fewer reactions, yet protection can fade over time.

Their candidate was a live, weakened pertussis vaccine given to mice. It raised protection through both T cells and B cells, the two arms of immune memory. It also cross-protected against parapertussis, a related illness. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE.
plos-pone-0010278:
Ryuji Machida and Atsushi Tsuda compared plankton species by their genes in a 2010 study. Six species of Neocalanus copepods, tiny crustaceans, inhabit the world's oceans. Three species and two form variants in the North Pacific form one related group. Their PLOS ONE paper used four gene sequences, from mitochondria and the nucleus, to measure dissimilarity.

Comparing several genes guards against being misled by any single one. Their distances test whether the named species and forms are truly distinct. Copepods anchor ocean food webs, so their true diversity matters for ecology.
plos-pone-0010378:
Tamara Romanuk and colleagues tested whether stress changes how variety steadies nature, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diverse communities of species often weather change better than poor ones. Stress, though, might weaken or strengthen that link. The team used shrinking water volume as the stress in small aquatic systems. They then watched whether more diverse setups stayed more stable.

Across the stress gradient, the positive link between variety and stability held up. That is not a given; many expected stress to break the pattern. Living variety thus seems to insure communities even under strain. The finding supports protecting diversity before hard times arrive. Once a stress hits, the insurance is already either bought or lost.
plos-pone-0010478:
Sujit Dutta and Katrin Rittinger mapped how an enzyme that makes reactive oxygen is switched on and off for PLOS ONE in 2010. Reactive oxygen species fight germs but also carry signals inside cells. Too much damages tissue, so their sources are tightly governed. The enzyme component NOXO1 is one such source's organizer. The team studied its reversible partnerships with two other proteins.

NOXO1 binds one partner, p22phox, and another, NOXA1, in ways that can be undone. Those reversible contacts tune the enzyme's activity up or down. Detailed maps of such contacts help design drugs that adjust oxygen signaling. The work is basic biochemistry with wide medical echoes. It shows control by association, not just by amount.
plos-pone-0010578:
Lei Liu and colleagues explored how a drug slows moving cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug was rapamycin, already known to block a growth pathway inside cells. The signal they studied was IGF-1, which normally urges cells to crawl and spread.

Cell experiments showed rapamycin blunted the movement that IGF-1 provokes. The effect ran through a second protein, PP2A, which helps switch other proteins off. Tracing that chain explains part of how rapamycin acts. It also hints at ways to limit the spread of tumor cells, which depend on similar movement signals.
plos-pone-0010678:
Shuzhen Sim and George Dimopoulos studied how dengue virus quiets mosquito defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue spreads when Aedes aegypti mosquitoes bite people. The virus must first live and grow inside the mosquito, whose immune system fights back with its own gene responses.

In infected mosquito cells, many defense genes failed to switch on as they should. The virus seemed to damp the response rather than merely dodge it. That damping helps the virus build up numbers before the mosquito's next bite. Knowing which defenses get muted suggests ways to breed or engineer mosquitoes that resist dengue from within.
plos-pone-0010778:
Adeel Safdar and colleagues studied the energy centers of muscle in inactive older adults, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Muscle mass melts away with age, a process called sarcopenia. Faulty mitochondria, the cell's energy centers, are often blamed. What was unclear is whether a sedentary life, rather than age itself, drives much of that fault.

Muscle samples from sedentary older adults showed disordered mitochondrial upkeep. The balance between making new mitochondria and clearing worn ones had slipped. Active aging, by contrast, is known to keep that upkeep tighter. The work strengthens a practical message: much muscle decline blamed on age tracks with disuse and can likely be slowed by training.
plos-pone-0010878:
Diana Bonilla, Lan Ly, Yang-Yi Fan and co-authors published this nutrition and infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Omega-3 fats from fish oil are praised for heart and brain health, yet there were hints they might weaken defense against tuberculosis. The team tested that worry in mouse immune cells loaded with DHA, one of the main omega-3 fats.

After the fat built into cell membranes, the macrophages were switched on with an immune signal and infected with a virulent TB strain. The treated cells controlled the bacteria less well, burned less oxygen in attack mode, and matured their bacteria-trapping compartments more slowly. Bonilla and colleagues trace part of the effect to blunted signaling from the activating signal. Their results urge caution about high-dose fish oil where TB is common.
plos-pone-0010978:
Deborah Springer, Ping Ren, Ramesh Raina and co-authors published this fungal pathogen study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cryptococcus gattii is an emerging yeast that infects people and animals and lives on trees in tropical and temperate regions. Modeling its natural habitat with thale cress plants, the team watched how the yeast behaves on leaves.

Yeast cells colonized scratch-wounded leaves and spun out distinctive extracellular fibrils, hair-thin strands hundreds of times longer than wide. Only yeasts wearing their normal capsule made proper fibrils; a capsule-free mutant made none, and a sensing mutant made only disorganized strands. Springer and colleagues connect these fibrils to the yeast's niche, its virulence in mice, and its dealings with human neutrophils. A structure built for life on plants may double as a weapon in animal infection.
plos-pone-0011078:
McCormick, Velasquez, Finney and colleagues published imaging work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject was zinc in the nursing mouse breast gland. Zinc is a key mineral that mothers pass to infants through milk, yet its path inside gland cells was not clear.

Using X ray methods that map single elements, the team found separate pools of zinc inside cells. Those pools built up and were then released, presumably toward milk. The pictures give a clear view of how the gland handles a vital mineral. That view can inform work on infant feeding and early nutrition.
plos-pone-0011178:
Ozcivici, Luu, Rubin and colleagues tested gentle vibration in PLOS ONE in 2010. When limbs go unused, as in bed rest, bone weakens quickly. The team asked whether brief daily low level shaking could keep bone marrow able to make bone during recovery and renewed walking.

Vibration did preserve the marrow's bone making potential. It also improved the recovery of the spongy inner bone as animals moved again. A mechanical fix needs no drugs, which suits astronauts and bedridden patients alike. The finding offers a simple countermeasure against bone loss from disuse.
plos-pone-0011278:
Sanchez-Blazquez, Rodriguez-Munoz and Garzon traced opioid signaling in PLOS ONE in 2010. Opioid painkillers lose strength with repeated use, a problem called tolerance. The team showed that opioid receptors give a brief start to a chain of signals which then keeps pain pathway proteins active for much longer.

That sustained activation helps explain how tolerance builds in pain centers. The chain involves proteins that strengthen pain signals between nerve cells. Each step is a possible target for safer painkillers that resist tolerance. The finding connects a brief drug action to lasting circuit change, a key puzzle in addiction research.
plos-pone-0011378:
Jorge Zuniga and colleagues set out in 2010 to design blockers for the botulinum toxin, among the most potent poisons known. Once the toxin damages nerves, no drug can undo the harm, so a blocker that stops it early is badly needed. The team used the toxin's three-dimensional shape to guide their design work.

Working in repeated rounds, they built peptide-like molecules shaped to fit the toxin's active site, tested them, then refined the design. Each cycle sharpened the fit between blocker and toxin. The result is a set of refined candidates aimed at disarming the toxin before it strikes nerves. Beyond botulism itself, the study shows how structure-guided cycles can build inhibitors for other toxins where speed and precision matter.
plos-pone-0011478:
Oleg Mediannikov and co-authors described in 2010 a wholly new bacterium living inside ticks. Ticks carry many microbes beyond the famous disease agents, and their inner passengers are still being catalogued. From ixodid ticks, the team isolated a bacterium that lives only inside cells and matched no known genus, so they named it Diplorickettsia massiliensis, a new genus and species.

An obligate cell-dweller is hard to grow and easy to miss, which is why tick microbiology keeps yielding new names. Each new entry expands the map of what rides inside ticks that bite people and animals. Some such passengers later prove to cause disease themselves, so a careful first description is the foundation for medical follow-up. The paper also shows how much microscopic diversity hides in a familiar pest.
plos-pone-0011578:
Chengfu Xu and co-authors followed people over time in 2010 and found that high uric acid in the blood forecasts fatty liver disease. Uric acid is best known for gout, the painful joint disease it causes when it crystallizes. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, fat building up in the liver without drinking, is common and can progress to scarring, yet early warning signs are few.

In their prospective observational study, people with high serum uric acid went on to develop fatty liver at higher rates. A cheap, routine blood value flagging risk years ahead gives doctors a chance to intervene with weight and metabolic care while the liver is still healthy. Prospective design is what earns the claim: the marker was measured before the disease, not after. Gout clinics may turn out to be the right place to start liver prevention.
plos-pone-0011678:
Chie Sugimoto and co-authors tested a weakened-virus vaccine in monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV vaccine work is hampered by the virus's diversity and by uncertainty over what protection looks like. The team used the SIV-monkey model, where a version of the virus with sugar decorations removed from its surface had acted as a protective vaccine before.

They vaccinated macaques with widely differing immune genetics and challenged them with a mismatched virus strain. Protection held across those diverse animals. Broad protection despite genetic variety is exactly what a human AIDS vaccine would need, making the result encouraging.
plos-pone-0011778:
Tran Tinh Hien and co-authors ran a randomised trial of a one-dose oral typhoid vaccine in Vietnamese children, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drug-proof typhoid is a major public health problem, above all in Asia. A live oral vaccine taken just once, called M01ZH09, would hold big gains over multi-dose or injected options.

The trial judged the vaccine's safety and its power to raise immunity in healthy children. Its results show whether one oral dose is both well borne and able to train protection. Such data guide the candidate's path toward use in the towns that need it most.
plos-pone-0011878:
Cheng-han Yu and co-workers studied in 2010 the moving belt of actin inside the contact zone between a T cell and its target. When a T cell checks a target cell, receptors and helper proteins sort themselves into a patterned junction called the immunological synapse. Actin, the cell's scaffolding protein, flows inward through this zone in a steady stream.

The team physically restricted the space the synapse could spread into, then watched how the actin flow changed. Confining the junction altered the flow, showing that the pattern is not set by chemistry alone. Physical limits and forces, often ignored in immune studies, help shape how a T cell organizes its attack.
plos-pone-0011978:
David Hayman and colleagues reported in 2010 the long survival of a city-dwelling fruit bat that carried antibodies to two dangerous viruses. Ebola viruses cause hemorrhagic fevers with very high death rates when they spill from wildlife into people. Fruit bats are suspected reservoirs, able to carry such viruses without obvious illness.

The bat, found positive for Ebola and Lagos bat virus antibodies, survived long-term in an urban setting. A reservoir that lives for years while carrying evidence of infection can seed spillovers across many seasons. Documenting that survival in a city bat sharpens the risk picture for the many places where people and fruit bats now live close together.
plos-pone-0012078:
Ruben Hummelen and co-workers used deep sequencing in 2010 to census the bacteria living in the vagina of women with HIV. Women living with HIV who also have bacterial vaginosis face a higher risk of passing HIV to partners or newborns. Which bacterial communities count as normal or as vaginosis in this population was poorly understood.

Reading the microbes' DNA in depth showed how the vaginal community is composed and how it relates to health states in these women. A precise census replaces guesswork based on a few culturable species. That knowledge is groundwork for treatments that restore a protective community instead of merely suppressing symptoms.
plos-pone-0012178:
Heath Elrod, Songqing Fan, Susan Muller, and co-authors measured two cell-death proteins in head and neck cancers, in PLOS ONE in 2010. One is a surface receptor that can order a cancer cell to die; the other is an early executioner enzyme in that same death pathway. How their levels change as these cancers spread, and what that means for a patient's outlook, had not been reported.

The team compared cancers still at their first site with those that had spread, and checked the patterns against patient outcomes. Markers like these could flag which tumors need stronger treatment. They also matter for drugs designed to trip the death receptor, since such drugs only work when the pathway below it is intact.
plos-pone-0012278:
Yong-hui Jiang, Yanzhen Pan, Li Zhu, and co-authors studied mice modeling Angelman syndrome in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children with this condition face severe learning disability, little or no speech, seizures, and balance problems, alongside a notably happy manner. The mouse model carries a large deletion on the mother's copy of a chromosome stretch, matching the human cause.

The team documented altered ultrasonic calls in the pups and impaired learning and memory in the mice. Measurable behaviors like these give drug trials in mice something concrete to improve. A model that mirrors both the genetics and the behavior of the human condition is the platform every treatment idea must first stand on.
plos-pone-0012378:
Carine Lussier, François Brial, Sébastien Roy and co-workers removed a gene called Hnf1 alpha from mice and watched the gut, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is best known for jobs in the liver and pancreas, and faults in it cause a form of diabetes. Its role in the gut lining was thought to be minor, but direct tests were lacking.

Mice without the gene showed changed growth of gut lining cells and shifts in which cell lineages formed. The gut thus depends on this gene more than expected. Because gut lining renews fast and feeds nutrient uptake, the findings matter for understanding diabetes, gut disease, and how one gene can serve many organs at once.
plos-pone-0012478:
Chandra Deb, Reghann LaFrance-Corey, William Schmalstieg and colleagues tested whether CD8 T cells directly injure the brain in multiple sclerosis, in a 2010 PLOS ONE mouse study. MS damage is often blamed on broad inflammation, but which cells cut the nerve fibers was unclear. The team set out to test CD8 cells, the killer class of T cells, as direct culprits.

In their model, CD8 T cells caused motor disability and axon loss in the demyelinated central nervous system. Naming the direct agent matters, because protecting axons is what preserves function in MS. Therapies that calm these specific cells could slow disability rather than just quiet relapses.
plos-pone-0012678:
Li, Zhang, Li and co-authors scanned family genomes for the genes behind a jutting lower jaw. This trait, mandibular prognathism, runs in families, yet few of its gene locations had been found. Their 2010 study used pedigrees from China, tracking which DNA stretches travel with the trait.

A genome scan across these families narrowed the search to candidate regions. Knowing the genes could one day improve early advice and treatment for jaw growth problems. The work also adds to the genetics of how faces take shape. Family studies remain one of the few ways to find such genes.
plos-pone-0012778:
Liebl, McKeown, Yao and co-authors showed that changes in the Wnt2 gene reshape the sending end of fly nerve cells. Wnt proteins guide development, including how nerves grow and connect. Their 2010 study worked at the fly neuromuscular junction, a classic model synapse where a motor neuron meets muscle.

Mutant Wnt2 altered the shape of the neuron's sending tips and moved key proteins out of place there. Misplaced synapse proteins mean faulty signalling between nerve and muscle. The work adds Wnt2 to the list of signals that build working synapses.
plos-pone-0314478:
Khan and colleagues surveyed hijra people in Bangladesh about barriers to health care in a 2026 paper. Hijra, a long-recognized gender community in South Asia, face repeated stigma that keeps them from clinics. More than five hundred people across sixteen districts took part, and the analysis focused on those who had sought care while ill.

A path model measured how harassment, money trouble, and other barriers connect to blocked care. Mapping the pathways shows which barriers drive others, rather than treating each as separate. Such detail helps health planners pick first fixes, like staff conduct rules, that may loosen several barriers at once. The wide district coverage makes the findings hard to dismiss as local.
plos-pone-0326478:
Mohammad Ahmad Al-Shalalfeh and colleagues surveyed students at a large public university in Jordan about neck pain and how they study. Five hundred seven students from all twenty faculties answered face-to-face interviews covering posture, study devices, study hours, activity, and pain levels. Students with past neck injuries or known muscle disease were excluded.

Just over half the students reported neck pain within the previous week, a strikingly high share for young adults. The analysis linked pain with how students hold themselves and which devices they study on. Long hours bent over phones and books are a plausible driver. For universities, the numbers argue for teaching posture and break habits alongside study skills.
plos-pone-0330578:
Qingya Pan and colleagues tested a computer vision method for tracking tumors that move as a patient breathes. Aiming radiation at a moving lung tumor is a basic problem in cancer care. The team worked with a chest phantom. It held eight fake nodules of varied shapes and shades. They shifted the nodules in four directions. They also rotated them through several angles. Two tracking methods were then compared.

For straight shifts, the feature-based method matched the older correlation method. For rotations, it did clearly better. Direction of motion made no difference to accuracy. A tracker that handles turning as well as sliding could sharpen treatment plans. Lung tumors rarely move in straight lines, so that gain matters.
plos-pone-0335578:
Chelton Desarmes and colleagues build measuring formulas for a fast-growing acacia tree planted widely in the Republic of the Congo. Foresters need to estimate wood volume and total above-ground mass without cutting every tree, both for timber planning and for counting stored carbon. On the Batéké Plateau, the team felled and weighed several dozen trees of different sizes, separating trunks, branches, leaves, and stumps.

One simple formula based on trunk width and height fit both volume and mass well. Older trees put more of their mass into trunks and large branches and less into small branches and leaves. Applied to plantation plots, the formulas gave a wide range of yields by age. Desarmes and colleagues offer them as a local standard for carbon and harvest estimates in Congo plantations.
plos-pone-0338878:
Ali Taheri Madah and colleagues studied ninety men seen at infertility clinics whose infertility had no clear cause. Their 2026 research paper asked whether what these men ate was linked to chemical measures in their semen and blood. Each man completed a long food questionnaire, and his semen was checked against World Health Organization guidelines.

Men with abnormal semen results reported eating more advanced glycation end products, compounds formed when food is cooked at high heat. Most other diet scores, covering healthy eating, antioxidant intake, and inflammation, showed no clear link to semen chemistry. One healthy eating score did track with lower levels of those cooking compounds in semen. The authors present this as limited extra evidence that diet may play a role in male fertility.
plos-pone-0342878:
Aditya Narayan and colleagues audited every novel drug the United States Food and Drug Administration approved from 2016 through 2024. They catalogued the nearly seven thousand studies behind those approvals. Their 2026 study tracked how much evidence each approval rested on. It tracked who paid for it, and how promptly results were made public. The span covers the years before and after the 21st Century Cures Act encouraged regulatory flexibility.

The evidence base thinned. From 2017 on, a single study became the most common foundation for approval. Industry sponsorship grew while public institute support shrank. Results posting on average broke the one-year legal deadline. The authors frame the trade-off openly: faster access to new medicines, bought with less certainty about safety and benefit.
plos-pone-0343078:
Xunuo Chen leads a team of eight setting out a pilot trial of stool transplants from young donors for adults with type 1 diabetes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. A disturbed gut ecosystem is implicated in the disease, in which the immune system destroys insulin making cells. Swapping in a youthful gut community might calm that terrain. The protocol describes a randomized, double blind, placebo controlled pilot at one center, enrolling adults whose glucose stays suboptimal despite insulin.

After a run in period to tune insulin and fit glucose monitors, participants take donor or placebo capsules for six days, then are followed for twelve weeks. The headline target combines generous time in the healthy glucose range with little time spent dangerously low. Feasibility and safety come first in the authors' aims, with efficacy signals second. The design prepares a larger trial while protecting a vulnerable group from premature claims.
plos-pone-0343378:
Tanjona Ramiadantsoa and colleagues ran a large field trial in northern Madagascar on frass, the manure-like residue of farmed black soldier fly larvae, as a fertiliser for maize and soybean. Poor farmers there cannot afford much synthetic fertiliser. Plots received anywhere from none to thirty tonnes of frass per hectare, and the team measured yields and worked out the economics.

Yields kept rising with every added tonne, reaching many times the unfertilised harvests, though the gains levelled off. At the standard local recommendation, frass would need to sell at a tiny fraction of chemical fertiliser prices to pay, which the authors argue is plausible. They frame insect frass as a route to higher yields without clearing new land.
plos-pone-0343678:
Lianbin Zhou, Peiwen Zhang, and co-authors trained a hybrid deep learning model to classify airline cabin safety incidents from written reports, aiming at earlier warning of risks. Their 2026 study fed the model more than eight thousand global reports of abnormal cabin events spanning 2004 to 2024. The architecture layers pattern detectors, sequence memory, and an attention step that spotlights the words carrying the risk signal.

The model classified incidents with about ninety-five percent accuracy, beating a strong standard algorithm by over five points on both accuracy and balanced score. Beyond raw sorting, the team built a mapping from text features through risk mechanisms to hazard levels, making the output interpretable for safety managers. They present the framework as a working path toward intelligent, data-driven cabin safety management.
plos-pone-0343978:
Omkar Pai and colleagues counted the giant trees of Vanzole village in India's Western Ghats, a biodiversity hotspot where sacred groves shelter ancient forest amid farms and homes. They recorded eighty-two trees thicker than a metre around the trunk, from twenty species, spread across four groves and the surrounding settlement. The 2026 study asked what these giants do for seed dispersal by fruit-eating animals.

Groves held more species and far more saplings sprouting beneath the big trees, including fishtail palms under nearly every grove giant. A large-seeded tree species was almost missing from settlements but common in groves. The authors argue that groves plus settlement giants form a lifeline network for hornbills and other seed carriers.
plos-pone-0344378:
Charlotte Lößner and eight colleagues revisit women fifteen years after pregnancies complicated by preeclampsia, to ask whether blood pressure back then predicts cardiovascular health now, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis. Fifty-three women were examined with a full clinical and functional work-up between 2019 and 2022. Their pregnancy records were pulled, and the group split into those now hypertensive and those not.

Women now living with high blood pressure had run higher readings during pregnancy — systolic in mid-pregnancy, diastolic late in pregnancy. The samples with complete records were small, and the authors label the analysis exploratory. Still, the thread from a difficult pregnancy to midlife heart risk keeps tightening, and guidelines have since moved to stricter pregnancy targets.
plos-pone-0344678:
Xiaojuan Chen, Lufan Zhang, Xue Li, and Funan Gao built a listening system that identifies what is threatening buried fibre-optic cables under city streets. Construction digs and manual excavation near these power-grid communication cables cause frequent damage, and the vibrations they make differ subtly. Their 2026 model stacks several learning methods, reading the vibration's timing, frequency, and spread, with an improved search algorithm tuning the ensemble.

In experiments the hybrid reached about ninety-eight percent recognition accuracy, edging out six rival approaches, some by wide margins, while staying fast enough for live monitoring. The authors present it as a practical early-warning tool that helps crews protect urban power communication networks from accidental strikes.
plos-pone-0345478:
Jieyang Pan, writing in 2026, asks how local government money decisions in China steer what companies do with their assets. The study covers listed Chinese firms from 2008 to 2023. It views the question through transaction cost theory, which focuses on the hidden costs of doing business in a place.

When prefecture governments intervened more heavily in the economy, firms shifted away from operating assets. They held more financial assets instead, a clear substitution pattern. Pan argues that intervention raises local transaction costs. Higher costs then discourage long-term productive investment. The shift was strongest among private firms and firms tied closely to their local economy. The findings warn that heavy-handed local finance can push companies toward speculation rather than real production.
plos-pone-0346078:
Yang Wang and co-workers test a large language model called DeepSeek on hard diagnostic reasoning in emergency-style cases. Fast, accurate judgment matters most when minutes count, and such tools claim strong reasoning. Their 2026 study feeds the model twenty-nine standard teaching cases and has human raters score its lists of possible diagnoses, test choices, final calls, and treatment plans.

Overall accuracy landed in the low eighties in percentage terms. The model was near perfect at confirming the final diagnosis once evidence was laid out. It was weakest at the early step of listing what else could explain the case. Skill did not vary with patient age, sex, or case severity. Guided use looks more promising than solo use.
plos-pone-0347078:
Stolear and colleagues set out a review plan in 2026 on tools that measure evidence-based practice in health students. Future clinicians must learn to ask clear questions, find studies, judge them, apply findings, and check results. Many tests claim to measure those skills, but few were built for students rather than working clinicians.

Under the plan, the team will gather existing tests and judge how well each measures knowledge, skills, and attitudes. Knowing which tests are sound helps schools pick fair ways to track learning. It also exposes gaps where new student-focused tests are needed. The review follows a recognized five-step model of evidence-based practice used in teaching worldwide.
plos-pone-0347178:
Zongwei Chen and co-authors linked strength tests taken before competition to race results for professional Chinese sprint canoe and kayak athletes. Coaches want to know which gym numbers actually predict speed on the water. Their 2026 analysis used official results from the 2023 national autumn championships, covering one hundred thirty-three athletes across sprint distances, and modeled how four strength measures related to race times.

One lift stood out: the prone bench pull strongly predicted faster two-hundred-meter times, though its value faded at longer distances. The pull mattered more for men and for kayakers than for canoeists, where nothing reached clear significance. Pull-up strength mattered only among women. The authors recommend targeted upper-body pulling work in pre-competition training, tailored by sex and boat type.
plos-pone-0347678:
Lauren Scott and colleagues examine how sick the patients on virtual wards really are, in this 2026 PLOS ONE health services study. Virtual wards treat people at home with remote monitoring as an alternative to hospital beds, a British National Health Service priority. The team reviewed more than twenty-five hundred monitored admissions in the Bristol area from late 2023 to early 2025.

Patients spanned respiratory, frailty, home antibiotic, heart failure, and general pathways. Standard early-warning scores, calculated from bedside observations sent remotely, were tested for how well they predicted readmission to hospital. Understanding real acuity at home matters: it decides staffing, visit schedules, and whether virtual wards genuinely substitute for wards or quietly skim the least ill.
plos-pone-0347878:
Alex Thabane and colleagues gathered every study they could find on whether walking boosts creativity, then pooled the results mathematically. Twenty-three studies covering just over a thousand people, mostly university students, measured two kinds of thinking: divergent thinking, generating many novel ideas, and convergent thinking, narrowing to the single best answer. Study quality and evidence certainty were graded with formal tools.

Walking showed a large positive effect on divergent thinking with moderate certainty, holding up when only the strictest trials were counted. For convergent thinking the pooled effect was near zero and the evidence shaky. The authors suggest a walk is a cheap, plausible intervention when the task is brainstorming, while warning against expecting it to sharpen the final narrowing-down stage of problem solving.
plos-pone-0348078:
Muhammad Ali designs and simulates a microbial fuel cell that cleans wastewater while generating electricity. Bacteria on one electrode eat organic waste and release electrons, which flow through a circuit before completing reactions at the other side. The 2026 study models the full system across four software platforms, covering microbe growth, heat and mass balance, and inner concentration maps.

Electrode material dominated the voltage results in the statistical screening, with platinum on top by a wide margin. The platforms agreed on a workable design built around a membrane dividing the two chambers. Platinum is costly, so the workflow's real gift is a repeatable way to screen cheaper materials and shapes before building hardware that might disappoint.
plos-pone-0348178:
Heba A. S. El-Nashar and co-workers compare two preparations from frankincense resin, a steam-drawn essential oil and a solvent extract. Frankincense has a long history in traditional remedies, and its chemistry varies with how it is processed. Their 2026 study profiles both preparations by chemical fingerprinting and runs a battery of lab tests on cell protection and enzyme blocking.

The essential oil held dozens of identified parts and beat the extract on most protection tests. It also blocked enzymes tied to memory loss, blood sugar, and skin darkening more strongly. The extract won on one sugar enzyme and one protection test. The oil looks the richer candidate for work on aging-related conditions, at least in the dish.
plos-pone-0348278:
Jan Willem de Gee and colleagues used pupil size to measure misophonia, the condition where everyday sounds like chewing trigger intense anger or panic. Diagnosis today rests on self-reports, which vary between studies and leave mild cases in doubt. The team played trigger sounds, generally unpleasant sounds, and neutral sounds while tracking how listeners' pupils widened, an involuntary sign of arousal.

Pupil responses cleanly separated misophonic reactions from ordinary dislike of nasty sounds. Even people with mild or moderate symptoms showed the arousal signature, suggesting their symptoms belong to the same condition rather than mere sensitivity. An objective body measure like this could anchor diagnosis and let treatments be tested against something more solid than questionnaires alone.
plos-pone-0348378:
Juan Manuel Rosero Ñañez and his team built a vest of sensors to grade stiff muscles by number. Stiff limbs, called spasticity, often follow stroke or cerebral palsy. Doctors now grade stiffness by feel, which shifts from hand to hand. The vest reads muscle signals, joint turns, and push-back force as a limb is bent. Nine people with stiff arms took part.

Six readouts merged into one score. That score split mild from bad stiffness well. Muscle signals in a slow stretch weighed most. The team calls the vest sound and easy to wear. They ask for trials in much larger groups next.
plos-pone-0348578:
Nasif Morshed and co-authors ranked what it would take for blockchain record-keeping to spread through Bangladesh's healthcare supply chains. Working in two stages, they first gathered candidate factors from the literature and experts. They trimmed the list with a fuzzy voting method. Then they weighted the survivors with a structured ranking technique and stress-tested the order.

Leadership came out on top: support from top management, overall organisational readiness, and trust among stakeholders outweighed every technical factor. Flashier items, such as smart contract automation, ranked near the bottom. The authors argue that in emerging economies, blockchain succeeds or fails on basic groundwork rather than advanced features. They offer hospital executives a ranked roadmap for spending limited money where it unlocks the most progress.
plos-pone-0348678:
Chengshu Liang and Kai Wang mined a large American intensive care database to test a simple blood-based score called EASIX in patients with acute kidney injury. The score combines three routine lab values linked to damage in blood vessel linings. Their 2026 study covered more than seventeen thousand critically ill patients and tracked deaths in intensive care and over the following year.

Patients with higher scores died at clearly higher rates, and the link held after careful statistical adjustment. The score predicted best in patients who were younger, less severely ill, or free of sepsis and chronic kidney disease. One caution emerged: steroid treatment looked riskier at low scores. The authors propose the score as a cheap aid for sorting patients by risk.
plos-pone-0348878:
Tae Yoon Lee and colleagues built LEAP, a computer model that simulates asthma across entire Canadian lifetimes to help governments plan ahead. The model follows a shifting open population person by person through five linked parts. They cover births and deaths, risk factors, developing asthma, living with it, and the costs and quality of life that follow. Early versions focus on age, sex, family history, and antibiotic exposure in the first year of life.

Calibrated against national databases and a long-running birth cohort, the model reproduced real population projections and asthma rates closely. It is released openly as free software for other researchers to extend. The authors aim it at testing early-life interventions on paper, such as changing infant antibiotic use, before any province spends real money on them.
plos-pone-0348978:
Negesso Gebre and colleagues hunted for the infections hiding behind negative tuberculosis tests in Harar, eastern Ethiopia. Adults suspected of having TB who tested negative on the standard gene test are often treated on guesswork there, yet other bacteria cause look-alike chest illness. The team cultured sputum from three hundred and seventy-one such patients, named the bacteria found, and tested which antibiotics still worked against them.

About a third of patients carried a disease-causing bacterium in the lower airways, with Gram-negative types prominent. The results give clinicians a local map of what these missed infections are and which drugs remain reliable against them. The authors argue that routine culture for test-negative patients would replace guesswork with targeted treatment and slow the misuse of antibiotics.
plos-pone-0349178:
RETRACTION NOTICE: The PLOS One Editors issued this 2026 notice withdrawing an earlier study on heart protection linked to lowering a protein called CD151. Readers should not rely on the original findings. The notice explains that concerns arose after publication about figures in the paper.

Several figure panels appeared to overlap even though they were said to show different test conditions. The lead author said one figure was wrong and sent replacements plus original images. Editors then found further problems in the underlying data that raised doubts about the results as a whole. With the authors unable to settle which images were correct, the journal retracted the article to protect the record.
plos-pone-0349278:
Sweden grants home care to people living with dementia, but someone must turn the granted hours into real daily help. Annika Taghizadeh Larsson and colleagues describe a study plan, in PLOS One in 2026, following that chain from decision to doorstep.

The project will record which services older people actually receive, whether a formal diagnosis unlocks extras, and how towns differ. It will watch how providers organize visits and bend routines to each person's wishes, and ask recipients, including partners, how the help feels. Comparing towns and providers should reveal where the system adapts well and where it stays rigid.
plos-pone-0349378:
Ylva-Li Lindahl and colleagues interviewed thirty women who were pregnant in Sweden during the COVID-19 pandemic. Sweden avoided a full lockdown, but maternity services barred partners from many appointments and scans, breaking a strong national tradition of shared pregnancy care. The women described what that period felt like from the inside.

Four themes ran through the accounts: living in the pandemic's shadow, missing out on a shared journey, worry fed by unpredictability, and finally adaptation and growth. Many women felt alone and anxious, yet also found new strength and coping strategies. A clear request emerged for steadier communication and rules that keep partners included. The authors say future crisis planning for maternity care must protect family support, not treat it as optional.
plos-pone-0349578:
Zhipeng Pan and colleagues present the protocol for a trial testing a two-step brain stimulation method to help stroke patients walk again. Magnetic stimulation can nudge the brain's motor areas, and a calming pattern given first may prime the brain so a later exciting pattern works better, an idea called metaplasticity. The method is established for arms in healthy people but barely tested for legs after stroke.

Sixty patients in early recovery will be split into three groups: true priming, partial sham, or full sham stimulation, all paired with robotic exoskeleton leg training. The trial will measure walking recovery and brain changes. This protocol reports the design in advance, so the eventual results can be judged against a fixed plan.
plos-pone-0349678:
Nouf Sahal Alharbi and colleagues translated a health decision scale into Arabic and checked that it still measures what it should. The scale asks how much say patients want in choices about death risk, illness risk, and quality of life. Five hundred five adults in Saudi Arabia completed the Arabic version.

The translation followed World Health Organization steps for adapting such tools. Statistical checks found a clear four-factor structure, steady internal consistency, and scores that worked the same for men and women. A tested Arabic scale lets clinics and researchers in the region measure patient preferences properly instead of guessing from an English tool.
plos-pone-0349778:
Keita Umejima, Yuki Sunada, and Kuniyoshi L Sakai scanned readers of Japanese manga in 2026 to test whether paper beats screens in the brain. Stories were told in two halves, each from a different hero's view, a format that demands joining both parts.

Volunteers read the first half on paper or on a tablet, then read the second half during scanning while rating empathy. Tablet readers were slower on questions needing both halves, and brain activity differed for the paper group in a left frontal area tied to joining ideas. The results back the idea that paper leaves a stronger memory trace for later parts of a story.
plos-pone-0349878:
Gilvan Vilarinho da Silva Filho, Augusto Paranhos Jr, and co-authors checked whether two commercial artificial intelligence programs can spot glaucoma from simple eye photographs, alone and together. Glaucoma quietly steals sight, and the advanced scanners used to confirm it are missing in many clinics. Their 2026 study ran both programs on photographs from three hundred seventy eyes, comparing their calls against full structural scans and visual field tests.

Each program performed strongly on its own. Combined, their accuracy rose further and matched a standard visual field measure, with no meaningful difference between them. The authors present the pairing as a practical screening route for places lacking expensive eye scanners, where a photograph plus software could flag who needs referral.
plos-pone-0349978:
Philip Osung published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It aims to predict household food insecurity in Nigeria before it strikes. The inputs join two data sources: experience-scale surveys, where households report their own food hardship, and open geospatial data, map-based information available to anyone.

The result is a reproducible machine-learning pipeline, a step-by-step workflow other teams can rerun and check. If map data can flag at-risk areas between surveys, aid can move earlier and cheaper. Humanitarian agencies and Nigerian food policy planners are the readers who need early warning that does not wait for the next survey round.
plos-pone-0350278:
Montse Mesalles and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One validation study of an automated blood analyzer for gilthead seabream, a cornerstone fish of Mediterranean aquaculture. Fish blood differs from mammal blood because the red cells keep their nuclei, so machines need species-specific checking. The team ran the analyzer on its bird settings and tested precision, accuracy across dilutions, contamination between samples, and how long samples stay usable.

Red cell counts and related measures proved precise and matched manual counts well, and refrigerated samples held up for a day. White cell breakdowns were less reliable, especially when tracking inflammation triggered by a bacterial compound, and one blood thinner clearly outperformed the other. The authors approve the machine for routine farm health checks, with microscope review when white cell details matter.
plos-pone-0351078:
Construction work produces mountains of wet waste slurry. Hauling it away costs money and land. Ping Gao and colleagues found a way to harden it into a useful material. They foamed the slurry with carbon dioxide gas. They bound it with magnesium oxide, slag, and carbide residue. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

The team squeezed samples under different pressures. A binder share near one tenth gave the best strength. A foam share just above one third held its shape best. Too much foam linked the pores and weakened the material. Pressure helped samples keep carrying load after cracking. The results guide recycling of slurry into light building fill.
plos-pone-0351878:
Nicolas Kjerulf and colleagues review in 2026 whether massage can harm people who have cancer or are in treatment for it. Their search gathered dozens of controlled studies and a few follow up studies, checking how well harms were reported and whether massage raised harmful events compared with usual care or attention controls.

Over half of trials never reported harms at all, and reporting quality was poor. Pooled results showed no added risk from light to moderate massage. Two weaker studies linked massage over a bone tumour site to worse survival, so direct pressure on tumours is discouraged for now. Overall certainty was rated very low.
plos-pone-0352178:
Shamsuddeen Adamu and seven colleagues present a 2026 machine learning study on storing carbon dioxide underground. Injecting CO2 into rock gets harder over time as the rock clogs. Predicting that decline is vital for safe, lasting storage sites. Most prediction tools give a single number with no sense of how sure they are.

The team built a Gaussian process model with physical laws baked into it. Two rules were added: one about particle behaviour, one about how permeability falls as pores block. Tested on forty-four laboratory cases, the plain model predicted accurately. Its uncertainty estimates were also well calibrated. The physics-guided version broke the built-in physical rules far less often. Operators gain forecasts they can trust, complete with honest margins of error.
plos-pone-0352578:
Bingbin Tian, Yunyuan Deng, and Mingcheng Jiang present this 2026 PLOS One study measuring fairness in the public spaces of Chinese villages where old and new housing stand side by side. The authors propose a three-part lens on justice: whether villagers feel recognized, whether resources are shared fairly, and whether people can take part in decisions. They surveyed more than three hundred residents in two villages and modeled the results.

The three parts proved tightly connected, together explaining a large share of how fair villagers judged their spaces. Fair distribution of infrastructure mattered most, while participation lagged badly in both villages. One village's home-grown governance seemed to support recognition, while outside capital in the other appeared to squeeze participation. The authors offer their measure as a starting tool for similar aging villages.
plos-pone-0352678:
Tadele Zeleke and four colleagues explore depression as lived by women with HIV in Gondar City, Ethiopia. Their 2026 study is phenomenological, built on deep face-to-face interviews. Sixteen women attending local health facilities shared their experiences. Depression is common among women living with HIV worldwide. It drags down overall wellbeing and treatment success. Yet Ethiopian women's own accounts of it were largely missing from the record.

The interviews mapped several themes. Women described their symptoms and what depression means to them. They named what they believed caused it, and what made it worse or lighter. Their views on treatment, and the coping strategies they rely on, also emerged. Practical challenges in getting help threaded through the accounts. For health services, such testimony is design material. Mental health support fitted to women's real explanations of their suffering stands a better chance of being used.
plos-pone-0352778:
Rahel Marti, Karin Hediger, Elena Pauli, and Jan Hattendorf published this 2026 survey study of pet ownership and human health in Switzerland. More than two thousand adults answered a representative survey covering health, social support, loneliness, satisfaction, and well-being. The team compared owners, people with regular animal contact, and others, weighing attachment, species, and time spent.

Simple owner-versus-nonowner gaps explained little. What mattered was the bond with the animal, the support people felt from it, and how much contact they had. Marti argues pet ownership must be treated as a bundle of factors, not one switch.
plos-pone-0352878:
Hasimah Ismail and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One report from the 2022 Orang Asli Health Survey, the first nationwide diabetes assessment among Malaysia's Indigenous Orang Asli adults. More than nine thousand adults across nine states answered questions and gave fasting blood samples, with sampling designed to represent urban, fringe, and remote communities and the major tribal groups.

About one in six adults had diabetes, a rate that climbed with age and was highest among urban residents and certain tribes. Diabetes tracked with obesity, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, and, notably, with higher household income and city living, reflecting lifestyle change. The authors say targeted prevention is urgent for a population long underrepresented in national health statistics.
plos-pone-0352978:
Rilwan Yahaya and four colleagues set out this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a review of reviews on how climate change harms the health of children and teenagers. Heatwaves, floods, drought, and spreading desert threaten the young disproportionately, yet the evidence sits scattered across many existing reviews. The team will search six major databases plus web sources, following established scoping review guidance.

As a protocol, the paper describes the plan: gather prior reviews, extract their findings, and synthesize them thematically into a map of known harms and gaps. The authors register the protocol publicly and aim to give policymakers in hard-hit regions, especially Sub-Saharan Africa, a single organized account of what climate change is doing to young people's health.
plos-pone-0353178:
Ahamed Khalyfa and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of liver failure stays across the United States. They ask whether rural hospitals and weekend arrivals worsen outcomes in decompensated cirrhosis. Earlier studies disagreed. The team used a national inpatient database from 2016 to 2020. They compared death rates, use of key procedures, and timing. They adjusted for patient mix and illness severity.

Rural stays actually showed lower death rates than urban ones. Rural hospitals did fewer procedures. They also transferred the sickest patients onward far more often. Weekend arrival carried only a tiny mortality gap, which the authors call clinically trivial. The two factors did not interact. Delays to procedures were mostly alike, except rural patients got dialysis sooner. The authors say the feared weekend and rural penalties look small in current data.
plos-pone-0353378:
Ezgi Aytürk and five colleagues rebuild a well-known questionnaire. It measures holistic thinking: seeing wholes and context over parts. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The old scale had reliability problems. It was also validated in few cultures. The team worked with Turkish samples. Together they totalled nearly a thousand people. Sharper items were written. Two muddled dimensions were split apart. One is compromise-seeking. The other is tolerance of contradiction. Modern statistical methods tested the result.

A general holistic factor stood behind four dimensions. Collapsing the answers from seven points to four helped. That change improved measurement.
