Higher holistic scores tracked with stronger preventive health behaviour. That link appeared during the pandemic. The revised scale gives cross-cultural psychology a sturdier tool.
plos-pone-0353478:
Wu Li and five colleagues published this 2026 PLOS One survey study on flu shots for young children in Shenzhen, China. Flu is a serious threat to children under five, yet yearly vaccination rates among Chinese preschoolers stay low. The team asked parents across six districts of the city what they knew about flu vaccines, how hesitant they felt, and whether their children had actually been vaccinated.

Nearly eighteen thousand parents answered, and only about one in five said their child had received the shot in the past year. Roughly one in five parents counted as hesitant, most often fearing serious side effects or doubting that yearly shots are safe and effective. Parents who knew more about flu and vaccination were notably less hesitant, pointing to parent education as a practical lever.
plos-pone-0353778:
Ahmed and colleagues measured what pregnant women in Hargeisa knew about warning signs in pregnancy in a 2026 study. Knowing when bleeding, swelling, or fits mean danger can speed up care and save lives. The team interviewed more than two hundred women attending pregnancy clinics at eight health centers in the Somaliland city.

Overall knowledge was low, the study found. Bleeding was the sign women knew best, while fits and blurred sight were named far less often. Women with more schooling, media access, or a past birth in a facility knew more signs. The authors call for stronger teaching in clinics, wider use of radio and other media, and more births in facilities.
plos-pone-0353878:
Natalie Pandher and seven colleagues compare body clocks in older men and women. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. One hundred and twenty-six healthy adults took part. They were aged sixty-five to ninety. All answered questionnaires on morningness and daily rhythm traits. About half also wore wrist monitors for a week. The monitors recorded their real rest and activity.

Older adults leaned toward morning habits. They kept firm routines and reported vigour. Men's rhythms were less stable than women's. They were also more broken up. In men only, a fragmented rhythm went with slower verbal processing. Stated preferences predicted real rhythm timing in men only. Sex, the authors argue, should not be averaged away in sleep research.
plos-pone-0354278:
Dong and colleagues, in a 2026 engineering study, shake model foundations to see how single piles and pile groups behave in strong earthquakes. Piles are the deep posts that carry bridges and buildings, and groups of piles do not simply act like several single ones. Their tests used a shaking table, a platform that replays recorded earthquake motion.

Single, four-pile, and six-pile foundations faced four different earthquake records at a design-level shaking strength. One famous record, from Kobe, pushed pile heads furthest and bent piles hardest, while an older California record amplified shaking most. The six-pile group resisted movement and bending best. The single pile amplified shaking least. After the tests, scans and close looks found no visible damage in any foundation; all had flexed and sprung back. The authors turn their measurements into design suggestions for bridge piles in earthquake country.
plos-pone-0354378:
Jia and colleagues, in a 2026 field study, compare three oat varieties for salty, high-altitude farmland in China's Qaidam Basin. Salty soils cover vast areas worldwide and shrink the land fit for crops. Forage oats can grow there, but farmers must choose between yield, feed quality, and steadiness across years. Three local varieties were grown over two seasons.

Each variety played a different strategy. One gave the most fresh yield, thanks to thick stems and strong photosynthesis, but swung with the weather. A second gave the best feed quality, with the most protein, and stayed steady. A third was the most reliable all round and used water most efficiently. Traits pulled against each other: chasing bulk tended to cost quality. The authors frame the choice plainly for farmers: maximum bulk, best feed, or safest bet, depending on what the farm needs most.
plos-pone-0354478:
Okano and colleagues, in a 2026 study, check the knees of young rugby players for an early warning sign of arthritis. The medial meniscus is a cartilage pad in the knee; when it bulges outward, joint wear often follows. The team used ultrasound to measure that bulge in college rugby players with no history of knee injury, and in students who did not play rugby.

Ninety-four players and forty-two controls were scanned in three knee positions, including standing on one leg. In every position, the players' meniscus bulged out significantly more than the controls'. No one had symptoms or past injury, so the change looks like an early effect of the sport's hard loading. Because the study is a snapshot, it cannot prove rugby caused the difference. The authors say a cheap ultrasound check could flag players early, while training and load changes might still protect their joints.
plos-pone-0354678:
Susan J Melhorn and colleagues present the protocol for ADAPT, a study designed to catch the moment weight loss stalls while it is happening, in real life. Their 2026 protocol enrolls adults with obesity in a standard diet and activity program. It weighs them remotely every day. New analytics spot each person's phases and spontaneous plateau as they unfold, rather than imposing an artificial endpoint.

At those personal turning points, the team layers deep measurements. They cover metabolism, appetite signals, and brain responses. Activity wearables and blood, fat, and muscle samples are included. Past work showed appetite rises and energy use falls during weight loss. But the sequence was never mapped in free-living people. ADAPT's dataset aims to reveal which mechanism fires first, a clue for keeping weight off.
plos-pone-0354878:
An-Le Van and co-authors optimised hot-press bonding for aluminium sheets and for a three-layer aluminium-steel-aluminium sandwich. Diffusion bonding of plain aluminium pairs is less studied than mixed-metal joints, and the layered structure, steel core wrapped in protective aluminium, is scarcer still. Their 2026 study varied pressing conditions within one shared experimental frame.

Bond strength answers to several processing settings at once, so the team searched for the combination that maximises tensile performance in both structures together. Treating the two systems side by side exposes where one recipe serves both and where it must compromise. Van and colleagues aim the results at makers of lightweight laminated panels for transport and construction.
plos-pone-0354978:
Lisa Langsetmo and colleagues checked whether published models that predict older adults' healthcare costs still work in new people and later years. The original models mixed billing-derived measures with direct assessments of function and frailty. Their 2026 validation study applied the models to a national ageing survey cohort followed for three years.

Predicted costs lined up acceptably with real costs in both a fresh sample and a later slice of the original group. The full model, using both data types, sorted future high spenders slightly better than billing data alone. Results were similar for women and men. Langsetmo and colleagues say bedside checks of function and frailty earn their place in cost forecasting.
plos-pone-0355278:
Catherine El Zerbi and colleagues explore in 2026 why some children in northeast England reach intensive care or children's surgery late, with worse results. Interviews covered young patients, caregivers, health staff, and charity workers in community settings. Analysis used quality standards for children's critical care as a starting frame, while letting new themes emerge.

Barriers grouped into communication problems, system problems, and money related problems in family life. The first two match existing standards, but money pressures sit outside them while shaping access strongly. The authors urge standards and policy to name social and economic barriers plainly, and call for wider voices in later work.
plos-pone-0355478:
HeeJun Lee, Hyeontaek Oh, and Yoonkyung Jeong run an online experiment on whether people conform to opinions from AI as they do to opinions from humans. Several hundred participants judged a series of tasks. Some tasks had clear right answers. Some were matters of taste. Each judgment followed a stated opinion sourced either from an AI or from people. The team also measured how socially excluded each participant felt.

Feeling excluded reduced conformity to the AI's opinions but left conformity to human opinions untouched. Task type, objective versus subjective, did not change the source effect. Lee and colleagues read the split as a sign about motives. Following AI rests more on judging its usefulness as information. Following people rests more on social pull. The gap widens when people feel disconnected.
plos-pone-0355678:
Garen J Wintemute led a team of eight authors surveying Americans on political violence, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The nationally representative survey asked about party ties, ideology, and views on democracy and society. It then measured how those beliefs connect with backing for violence used to make a political point in America.

Wintemute's group mapped which beliefs predict a willingness to endorse force for political ends. That map matters for prevention: leaders who want to lower the temperature need to know which attitudes carry the risk. The survey approach also shows how widespread such support is, and among whom. Firm numbers help public debate move past guesses about a deeply serious topic.
plos-pone-0355778:
Shamilah Namusisi and coauthors published a 2026 ethnographic study in PLOS ONE returning to Bundibugyo, western Uganda, ten years after its 2007 Ebola outbreak. That outbreak, killing dozens, also revealed a new Ebola species named for the district. The team reviewed archives, observed community life, and interviewed nineteen survivors and affected family members about the outbreak's aftershocks, reading the story through an eco-health lens with stigma at the center.

Widows bore the heaviest load: exclusion, economic strain, and grief for their orphaned children's lost chances. Fear of another outbreak curdled into ethnic tension over who was blamed for the first. Survivors reported lasting effects such as weakened bodies and damaged vision. Not everything darkened: people described better care-seeking habits, and health workers stayed sharply alert to early Ebola signs, a genuine gain for detection. Outbreak planning, they argue, must fund the decade after, not just the emergency.
plos-pone-0355978:
Fuyuan Zeng and colleagues exposed Pacific white shrimp to the broken cells of a toxic red tide alga. Pacific white shrimp is the world's most farmed shrimp. The team read the genetic response in the animals' main digestive and immune organ. Their 2026 study sequenced the organ's active genes three days after exposure. It compared them with unexposed shrimp, identifying which genes switched up or down.

A few hundred genes moved. Defense and cleanup pathways woke up. They included the cell's recycling system, a lectin-based immune circuit, and peroxide handling. Energy production and protein building shifted too. The profile sketches how shrimp mount their defense against algal toxins. Hatcheries could use that knowledge to breed or feed for resilience as red tides intensify.
plos-pone-0356078: Xu and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on parenting styles and child behavior. Data came from the ECHO program, a large United States research effort on child health. The team grouped parents into profiles and linked them with children's inward troubles, like anxiety, and outward ones, like acting out. Grouping styles, rather than single habits, may guide support that fits each family.
plos-pone-0356178:
Brooke A Hawkes and colleagues compare, in children and adults, the COVID antibody levels left by vaccination and by natural infection. Their data come from a large Arizona worker and family cohort. Age clearly shaped illness risk during the pandemic, but its effect on lasting antibody response was murkier. The team split records into a vaccinated group with no prior infection and an infected group with no vaccine, then modeled antibody strength against age bands.

Finer age splits, from young children to older adults, let the authors test whether response climbs or falls across life rather than splitting at eighteen alone. Models adjusted for health conditions, medicines, timing, and virus strain where relevant. Hawkes and colleagues aim the comparison at vaccine planning, where knowing which ages hold antibodies longest helps set booster timing.
plos-pone-0356378:
Jessica Veenstra and seven colleagues compare four ways of measuring iron inside mouse brain tumors, in this 2026 methods study. Iron oxide nanoparticles are being explored as combined diagnostic and treatment agents for brain cancer, but researchers need to know how much iron actually reaches a tumor. The team tested MRI scanning and X-ray fluorescence in living animals, plus two laboratory assays on removed tissue. They used a standard iron particle preparation and treated the most exacting lab method as the reference.

Both living-animal methods tracked the injected dose and agreed with the reference assay, but X-ray fluorescence correlated far more strongly; MRI's unique advantage is showing where in the tumor the iron sits. A cheap color-based assay worked in cell cultures yet failed in real tumor tissue. The authors lay out a practical framework for choosing a method by concentration, equipment, budget, and sample type.
plos-pone-0356478:
Tilakezi Tuersun and colleagues ask whether a simple cholesterol ratio predicts the re-narrowing of heart stents in patients with coronary disease. Re-narrowing inside a drug-coated stent remains a stubborn problem, and blood fat balance is a prime suspect. Records covered several hundred patients treated at a hospital in Kashgar over about six years. All were followed after their procedure. They were grouped by thirds of the ratio. The ratio balances harmful cholesterol against the protective kind.

The study compares event rates across those thirds. It probes the shape of the relationship with flexible curves. Then it tests whether the ratio predicts re-narrowing on its own, using regression models. Tuersun and colleagues aim to give cardiologists a cheap blood-based flag, drawn from routine panels, for patients who merit closer watch after stenting.
plos-pone-0356778:
Sumaiya Nusrat and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on family planning in Bangladesh. It focuses on adolescent girls who have never married, a group often left out of family planning programs that target wives. The subject is what these girls know and understand about family planning.

Awareness gaps among unmarried teenagers matter because knowledge gained early shapes later health choices. Surveying this group directly shows whether information reaches girls before marriage, when schools and clinics can still reach them easily. Health educators and youth program planners in Bangladesh are the audience for evidence about where awareness is weakest.
plos-pone-0356878:
Shailendra Mishra, Reem Alshenaifi, and Ruba Ahmed Alfahidah published a 2026 computer security paper in PLOS ONE on detecting intrusions into networks. Older detectors miss new attacks and cry wolf too often. Their hybrid system mixes two families of machine learning: supervised models trained on known attacks, and unsupervised models that flag anything unusual, combined by weighted voting. A blockchain-style chained log records every detection so records cannot be quietly altered.

Tested on two widely used benchmark datasets, the combined system reached accuracy close to ninety-nine percent, dipping only slightly when the audit ledger was switched on. The ledger runs on a single private node, so it adds tamper evidence without the cost of a full blockchain network, and logging overhead stayed small. The authors also report fewer false positives in limited repeat testing. The design aims at intrusion detection that security teams can trust and audit afterward.
plos-pone-0357278:
Karim Abbasi and three colleagues present a drug discovery model that adapts itself to each new question, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Predicting how tightly a candidate molecule binds its protein target is central to computer aided drug design, but one fixed global model treats every query alike. Their framework first retrieves the hardest comparison cases, past protein and molecule pairs whose near neighbors point in conflicting directions, and builds a small graph around the query.

A graph convolutional network then learns from that tailored neighborhood, and the model is fine tuned for the individual query before answering. Across four standard benchmarks the method beat the leading published approaches, sometimes by wide margins, and it held up on protein families it had never seen. The lesson for screening pipelines is that a model willing to study before it answers can outperform one that only memorizes.
plos-pone-0357378:
Kokab Farooq and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on breast cancer. It combines methylome analysis, the pattern of chemical tags on DNA, with transcriptome analysis, which genes are switched on. Together these point to LHX3, a gene the authors identify as an epigenetically downregulated marker.

Downregulated here means the gene is quieted by chemical tags rather than damaged. The authors also report tumor suppressive properties for LHX3, suggesting that losing its activity helps cancers grow. Cancer biologists can use such a marker to understand tumor behavior, and it may in time inform tests that read a tumor's likely course.
plos-pone-0357478:
Simone Ispa-Landa and colleagues published a 2026 survey study in PLOS ONE on how Jewish students at American colleges are faring. After protests over the Israel-Hamas conflict spread across campuses from late 2023, leaders often justified interventions by citing Jewish students' welfare, yet direct evidence was thin. The team surveyed several thousand students in early 2025 about mood, loneliness, flourishing, belonging, and how they saw their campus climate.

Nearly half of Jewish students said they were concerned about campus antisemitism. Still, their scores for depression, anxiety, and loneliness, and for flourishing, looked similar to peers of other religions and better than students with no religious identity. Feeling a stronger sense of belonging, and seeing the campus as less hostile, went along with better well-being for Jewish students. The authors say policy debates should rest on this kind of direct measurement rather than assumption.
plos-pone-0357578:
Naokazu Chiba and coauthors published a 2026 surgical study in PLOS ONE on bile duct cancer outside the liver. Knowing before surgery whether cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes shapes the whole treatment plan. Existing scans judge nodes poorly. Looking back at patients who had curative surgery, the team measured three imaging quantities across each patient's nodes and tested how well each predicted spread found afterward.

The winner was a simple statistic from ordinary CT scans: how much the brightness values of the nodes varied, relative to their average. It beat both an MRI water-motion measure and a PET scan uptake measure, and it stood alone as an independent predictor in their modeling. Its accuracy was moderate, correctly classifying roughly seven patients in ten. The authors suggest this cheap, already-available number could help select patients for chemotherapy before surgery and refine operative planning, rather than adding new scans.
plos-pone-0357778:
Adem Nega Yimer and Bewketu Takele published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on protecting stored sorghum from the maize weevil, a beetle that eats grain after harvest. Working in Ethiopia, where sorghum is a staple food, they tested powders made from three local plants as possible alternatives to chemical insecticide. They mixed each powder into grain at several doses and tracked weevil deaths, new offspring, and grain damage over fifteen days.

One plant, Phytolacca dodecandra, killed nearly all adult weevils at the tested doses, clearly ahead of tobacco powder, while a third plant powder worked least well. All three powders cut grain damage and weight loss compared with untreated grain. Because the plants are locally available, the authors see them as promising low-cost options for small farmers, though they say farm-level storage trials still need to confirm the lab results.
plos-pone-0358078:
Ela Cohen Nissan led a team of five authors studying knee replacement in dialysis patients, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. People on chronic dialysis who need a new knee face compounded surgical risks, from infection to poor healing. The team ran a nationwide analysis, matching patients so the comparison with other patients was fair.

Nissan's results quantify the added danger of primary total knee replacement in this group during the hospital stay. Hard numbers help patients and surgeons face a hard go or no-go choice with open eyes. They also help hospitals prepare dialysis support around surgery. For some patients the pain relief will be worth the risk; this study helps identify where that balance tips.
plos-pone-0358178:
Gong Cheng, Jinhui Qiu, and Shengtao Li published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a Bayesian network meta-analysis of exercise and the brain. The authors examine effects on BDNF, a protein that supports brain cells, and on depression, in adults in midlife and old age whose memory and thinking have mildly declined.

The analysis separates effects by dose and modality, meaning how much exercise and which kind, such as aerobic or resistance training. Combining many trials in a network lets the authors rank options never compared directly. Clinicians advising patients with early memory problems can use the ranking to suggest exercise types with the best support.
plos-pone-0358578: Liang and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on HIV testing among men who have sex with men in Southern China. They examined how often these men test and how testing links to sexual behavior. They also looked at use of preventive medication against HIV. Regular testing and prevention work best together, so knowing how they pair up helps clinics design outreach.
plos-pone-0358778:
Retna Sheeja Pushpa Raj and Prakash Babu Kodali measure what caesarean births cost mothers in Tamil Nadu, India, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Just over half of the four hundred seventy-five recently delivered mothers they surveyed, in mid 2023, had given birth by caesarean, a strikingly high share. The study linked how a woman delivered to her out of pocket spending and her physical and mental quality of life in the weeks after birth.

High risk pregnancies and private facilities were the strongest predictors of a caesarean. Mothers who delivered surgically faced roughly double the odds of heavy out of pocket costs, and markedly worse physical quality of life scores, while the mental side differed less. The authors say the pattern, surgical birth concentrated in private care and paid for by families, deserves policy attention in a state where one in two births now arrives by operation.
plos-pone-0359278: Kinsman and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on psychiatric prescribing in Botswana. At the country's only referral institute for mental illness, they counted how many adult patients receive many psychiatric drugs at once, a practice called polypharmacy. The snapshot design covered patients at one point in time. Many drugs at once can help, yet raise risks, so a clear count guides safer care.
plos-pone-0359778:
Yi-Chao Zhou, Yi-Chang Chou, Yin-Ling Hung, and Yen-Jung Chang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on ageing in Taiwan. It is a longitudinal cohort study running from 2005 to 2016. The authors link marital status to incident screen-positive cognitive impairment, new cases flagged by screening tests for thinking decline.

The title itself warns that the links vary with the cognitive screening instrument chosen, meaning the answer depends on which test defines impairment. That caution matters for every study that sorts people by a single screen. Researchers of marriage, widowhood, and dementia risk are the readers, and they gain a lesson in measurement as well as a result.
plos-pone-0359878:
Jingmei Liang, Yuyun Hu, and Bing Liao traced in 2026 a chain of signals that injures kidney filter cells in acute kidney injury. The cells are podocytes, which wrap the kidney's tiny blood vessels and keep protein out of the urine. The authors show that signaling between cells through a pair of proteins, GAS6 and its receptor AXL, can trigger a form of cell death called cuproptosis in these podocytes.

Above that pair sits a regulator named CEBPD, which the team places upstream of the signal. Acute kidney injury strikes suddenly, often during severe illness, and has few targeted treatments. Mapping a death pathway step by step gives drug researchers named points where the chain might be cut.
plos-pone-0360478:
Wen Li and colleagues piloted in 2026 a blend of music therapy and artificial intelligence for university students. Their exploratory randomized study added verbal suggestions, generated by a large language model and adapted to the students' culture, into music therapy sessions. The spoken guidance was designed to deepen the therapy's calming and focusing effects.

As a pilot, the study's job is to test whether the approach is workable and promising enough to justify a larger trial, rather than to settle its value. Culturally adapted wording matters because therapeutic language lands differently across backgrounds. The work sits at a new crossing point, where universities search for scalable mental health support and AI tools are eager to supply it, with evidence still catching up.
pmc-13178578:
Dmitrii Aleshin is first author on a 2026 study of odd spectral effects in hyperpolarized NMR experiments. NMR, nuclear magnetic resonance, reads molecular structure from atomic nuclei, but its signals are weak. A technique called dissolution dynamic nuclear polarization boosts water's signal hugely, and that boosted water can sensitize co-dissolved small molecules.

The authors analyze what the strongly magnetized water does to its own peak and to solute peaks nearby. A feedback effect called radiation damping broadens the water line and shifts the size and phase of solute signals within that width. Cross-relaxation and chemical exchange add further effects. Derivations and demonstrations are given, with consequences for measuring solutes this way.
pmc-13196978:
Corine Oldhoff-Nuijsink and colleagues published a 2026 interview study on digital health research panels. People in vulnerable positions often miss out on digital health tools and on the research behind them. A standing panel could give them a voice, so the team explored what draws people in.

They held 23 in-depth interviews, mostly with people in vulnerable positions. Most were keen to join a panel. They wanted to make digital health easier to use for themselves and their peers. Outreach at community centers and clear flyers seemed the best way to recruit. Clear updates and prompt sharing of results kept people engaged. Dutch setting limits how far the lessons travel.
pmc-13197078:
Toshiko Furukawa and Takuya Iimura present a 2026 model of trade between legumes and root bacteria. Legume plants house Rhizobium bacteria in root lumps, trading plant carbon for bacterial nitrogen. The model adds energy budgets, since each side spends ATP, the cell's energy unit, to take in its share.

Trade balance is kept by shifts in bacterial mass when one side gives more. The model makes three forecasts, and the authors show each fits past data. Conditions for the partnership to form match measured energy costs. At balance, plants give modest carbon while bacteria give rich nitrogen. The plant's carbon share falls as its own carbon-to-nitrogen ratio rises.
pmc-13197278:
Catarina Leitão and colleagues describe expert review of a new prostate cancer questionnaire in 2026. Prostate cancer is among the most common cancers in men. Habits such as diet and activity may sway its course, so the team built a form that joins lifestyle and clinical data.

The form grew from literature reviews and talks with clinic staff. It spans four parts: personal background, diet, lifestyle, and clinical data. Twenty-five experts in urology, family medicine, and public health rated it, with input from language and mind-health experts too. Scores were high for fit and accuracy. The lifestyle part scored a bit lower on completeness. Small fixes followed, and the form is now ready for larger studies.
pmc-13197478: Silvia Pietrobono and colleagues issued a 2026 author correction to a study on pancreatic cancer response. A reader flagged errors in the work, which links the signal CCL3 to strong response to a TGF-beta blocking therapy. Source data for three figure panels were wrong. One figure legend lacked a needed citation. Staining panels in another figure were pasted in error, and two supplement scratch assay panels were also wrong. The original article has been corrected.
pmc-13202678:
Tiny membrane parcels shuttle signals between cells in the mouth, and a 2026 review headed by Abdelhabib Semlali surveys their roles in oral health and disease. The article reviews what is known about extracellular vesicles in saliva and gum fluid, including exosomes, microvesicles, and apoptotic bodies.

Vesicles from host cells and oral microbes help regulate inflammation, biofilm behavior, tissue repair, and microbe colonization, the review finds. When that traffic goes wrong, it contributes to gum disease, oral thrush, and oral cancer progression in the evidence surveyed. Salivary vesicles also look hopeful as test markers, though isolation and testing methods still lack shared standards.
pmc-13202978:
Somalia's health system leans on community health workers, and a 2026 article authored by Liibaan Abdulahi Sudi argues they are central to its resilience. Written as a letter drawing on Somali and global evidence, the piece examines how these workers support care amid conflict, outbreaks, displacement, and severe staff shortages.

During the COVID-19 response, community workers identified about a third of suspected cases and found higher positivity than facility surveillance, the authors note. They also raised use of maternal health services in underserved areas. Weak integration, uneven supervision, and fragmented donor funding limit the programs, so the authors urge formal recognition, stable financing, and standardized training.
pmc-13207878:
Early liver cancer can hide aggressive traits, and a 2026 study authored by Huiying Li builds an MRI score to flag them before surgery. The multicenter retrospective study covers 994 patients with very early or early hepatocellular carcinoma who had contrast MRI and then curative resection at three institutions.

The score combines irregular tumor shape, a washout pattern, blood products inside the tumor, and a blood marker threshold. It predicted vessel invasion or high tumor grade with fair accuracy in training and validation groups in the authors' testing. Patients scoring positive relapsed sooner, and extra therapy after surgery appeared to help only that high-risk group.
pmc-13210178:
Engineering students support blood donation in principle yet rarely roll up a sleeve, and a 2026 survey led by Bhola Teli documents that gap in Nepal. The cross-sectional study questioned 191 first-year students at Pulchowk Engineering Campus between April and June 2022 about what they know, feel, and do regarding donation.

Attitudes were strongly favorable across the group, but fewer than one in five students had actually donated blood at the time of the survey. Women scored higher on knowledge while men were considerably more likely to have donated in practice. The commonest barriers were having no particular reason and lacking the opportunity, prompting calls for campus drives.
pmc-13210378:
Mothers who use substances face stacked risks, and a 2026 cohort profile by Lindsay A Wilson describes the British Columbia resource built to study them. The article introduces a population cohort linking health records for mothers with substance use indications around pregnancy and for their children, drawn from ten provincial databases.

The cohort holds 38,670 mothers and 45,823 children from deliveries between 2000 and 2022, with a median of nine years of follow-up available. Records span care use, prescriptions, housing and income support, incarceration, and deaths for both generations in the linked files. Three planned studies will judge specialized pregnancy care, compare opioid treatment regimens, and trace child outcomes.
pmc-13240878:
Qu and co-authors in Yantai blended physics with machine learning to design concrete mixes that reliably hit strength targets. Their surrogate starts from a physical baseline built on the effective water-to-binder ratio and curing age. A small neural network then learns only the leftover nonlinear patterns. Calibrated uncertainty estimates accompany every prediction.

On a public set of one thousand thirty mixtures, the hybrid reached a test R² above 0.92 on held-out mixes. Accuracy held even when training shrank to forty percent of the data. Prediction intervals landed close to their nominal ninety-five percent coverage. The team turned the model into reliability maps that recommend mixes for a forty-megapascal target.
pmc-13240978:
Authier and colleagues at Aarhus University built a mouse model of OGT congenital disorder, an intellectual disability syndrome. Faulty O-GlcNAc transferase unbalances a sugar tag placed on brain proteins. Their male mice showed small heads and motor problems mirroring patients. Blood and brain both carried the biochemical imbalance.

The team crossed the model with mice whose tag-removing enzyme was disabled. That genetic rescue partly restored balance in brain and blood alike. A simple messenger RNA ratio tracked the correction in both tissues. The result supports blocking the remover enzyme as a treatment strategy.
pmc-13241378:
Néill and colleagues at Trinity College Dublin compared two cell sources for repairing degenerated spinal discs with microRNA therapy. Their treatment pairs a microRNA mimic with an inhibitor to calm matrix breakdown. Goat cells and whole disc organ cultures modeled the human condition. Native disc cells faced off against bone marrow stem cells.

Both cell types quieted the matrix-chewing enzymes and inflammatory signals. Only native disc cells, though, ramped up fresh matrix markers inside cultured discs. Marrow stem cells delivered to the same organs showed no such response. Néill backs the disc's own cells as the delivery vehicle.
pmc-13242478:
Marco Rendine and colleagues tested whether breakdown products of blueberry polyphenols can protect telomeres under metabolic stress. Their paper appeared in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2026. Telomeres are the caps on chromosome ends that shorten with age and strain. The team exposed human monocyte cells to fatty acids and an inflammatory signal to mimic metabolic syndrome, then treated them with four compounds from blueberries, alone and mixed.

The metabolic insult shortened telomeres, but pretreatment with ferulic acid or vanillic acid largely prevented that loss. The four-compound mixture also protected telomeres at a combined dose. Two other compounds showed little effect at the doses tried. The benefit did not come from simply lowering reactive oxygen inside the cells. The authors suggest these food-derived molecules may help guard these caps when the body is under strain.
pmc-13243878:
Zahra Vasegh and co-authors asked what drives the streaky artifacts that metal leaves in dental cone beam scans. Their laboratory study appeared in Radiology Research and Practice in 2026. Four scanner models were compared, two with detectors aligned to the beam and two with offset detectors. A dry human skull was scanned holding a titanium implant, a crowned tooth with a metal post, and an amalgam-filled tooth, in varying positions and numbers.

Every factor mattered. Detector design, the metal's composition, how many objects sat in the field, and whether they sat near or far from the region of interest all shifted artifact severity significantly. Image slices were scored by gray value spread, where cleaner images read brighter and steadier. The authors distill the physics into practical guidance: scan planning that minds metal position and count can rescue diagnostic quality. Scanner choice itself, they show, is part of the prescription.
pmc-13244078:
Shani Upadhyay, Rakesh Verma, and Shikha Gupta reviewed the case for Indian borage as a functional food. Their review appeared in Food Science and Nutrition in 2026. The herb, Coleus amboinicus, also called Mexican mint, is native across Southeast Asia and Africa and long used in folk cooking and medicine. It carries vitamins, minerals, and a crew of active compounds led by thymol, carvacrol, and rosmarinic acid.

Those compounds underwrite laboratory findings of antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, germ-killing, and gut-friendly prebiotic action. Traditional uses map onto modern chronic disease targets including heart problems, diabetes, and breathing conditions. Its antimicrobial punch also makes it a candidate preservative to replace synthetic ones in packaged food. Blocking wider adoption are uneven active content from batch to batch, a thin record of human trials, and missing regulatory approvals. The authors chart the research needed to move the herb from tradition into dietary systems.
pmc-13245078:
Blayne Oliver, Michael Sun, and Young Seo Lee review the case that tiny parcels shed by gut bacteria are hidden couriers in cardiometabolic disease. Their article appeared in Gut Microbes in 2026. Bacterial extracellular vesicles are nanoscale spheres budded from bacterial membranes, packed with proteins, fats, genetic material, and immune-triggering fragments. The authors call them microbial dark matter: described in 1966, then overlooked for decades.

The vesicles can cross the gut wall, travel the bloodstream, and lodge in metabolic organs, where their cargo nudges inflammation and insulin sensitivity through the body's pattern-recognition alarms. That reach makes them double agents: plausible drivers of disease and attractive tools. The review weighs their promise as blood biomarkers read from a stool-linked signal, and as engineered delivery vehicles. Their closing ask is standardization, so a field built on invisible couriers can compare results.
pmc-13245278:
Ndoci, Bhattacharya, Agrawal, and co-authors study how cells ration a vital molecule in this 2026 Journal of Cell Biology paper. The molecule is coenzyme Q, which mitochondria need to make energy and which also protects other cell parts from oxidative damage. When cholesterol production is stressed, cells must choose where their limited supply goes.

Using a genome-wide CRISPR screen in human cells, the team found that mitochondria hold onto their coenzyme Q instead of exporting it, keeping their own energy production running. The cost falls elsewhere: defenses outside the mitochondria run dry, leaving the cell open to ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. The trade-off may matter for diseases tied to cholesterol and cell stress.
pmc-13246478:
Rebellato and colleagues tested a new plant-based burger ingredient in this 2026 Food Science and Nutrition study. Defatted baru flour is a protein- and fiber-rich by-product of the baru nut, native to Brazil's Cerrado savanna. The team blended it at several levels into burgers made from soy protein concentrate and wheat gluten.

Burgers with modest baru flour additions carried more protein and fat than the plain control and looked darker. In taste tests with eighty-seven people, those versions scored better on appearance, texture, and overall impression, and the products stayed microbiologically stable through sixty days frozen. The results support valuing a native by-product as a functional food ingredient.
pmc-13246578:
Lee, Chung, Cha, and co-authors analyzed a rare set of hand fractures in this 2026 Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery paper. The hamate is a small wrist bone, and fractures splitting its body often come with instability of the joints where the fourth and fifth fingers meet the wrist. The team reviewed fifty-eight male patients, classifying fracture patterns from CT scans and recording how each injury happened.

Two patterns appeared: a dorsal oblique type, usually from punching, and a splitting type, more often from falls. Most patients also had other fractures, commonly at the base of the fourth finger bone. Surgery with several small screws healed nearly all cases, with grip strength and function scores near normal, provided repair came within about three weeks.
pmc-13246878:
Nogueira Coelho and colleagues tested a kidney transporter's role in surviving potassium shortage, in this 2026 Pflügers Archiv study. NHE3 moves sodium and hydrogen ions in the kidney tubules, and its levels rise when dietary potassium falls, but the reason was unclear. The team fed mice lacking NHE3 only in the kidney a nearly potassium-free diet for ten days.

The knockout mice developed worse low blood potassium and more severe metabolic acidosis than normal mice, even though their kidneys had nearly stopped excreting potassium. They also drank far more water, showed reduced machinery for making ammonium to carry acid out, and some showed early kidney damage from potassium deficiency. The authors conclude NHE3 blunts the acid and potassium crises of a low-potassium diet.
pmc-13248078:
Sotiriadis and co-authors set out the plan for a Cochrane network meta-analysis in this 2026 protocol in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Preeclampsia, dangerous high blood pressure in pregnancy, threatens mothers and babies, and several preventive treatments exist for women at increased risk, from aspirin to calcium. Head-to-head trials between all options do not exist, so a network approach can rank them by combining direct and indirect evidence.

The protocol specifies the question precisely: interventions started by just before seventeen weeks of pregnancy in women at increased risk, compared for benefits and harms to mother and baby. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet; it commits the reviewers' methods in advance, so readers can later judge the finished review against its promises. The value lies in that pre-commitment to transparent, unbiased synthesis.
pmc-13249178:
Camargo and a Brazilian team describe patients receiving an implanted stimulator for bowel leakage, in a 2026 multicenter study. Eighty-seven patients at several centers had sacral neuromodulation, a device that gently stimulates the nerves controlling the bowel, after ordinary measures failed. Most were women around sixty years old, and nerve-related causes were the commonest reason for their incontinence.

Standard severity scores fell dramatically after implantation, with the median score dropping from the mid teens to near two. Episodes of urgent rushing to the toilet also became less frequent. The authors report the improvement as clinically meaningful, with safety matching earlier literature, supporting the device for patients whom conservative care leaves behind.
pmc-13249678:
Miegel and co-authors reviewed what helps or hinders prehabilitation before cancer surgery, in a 2026 review. Prehabilitation builds fitness, nutrition, and strength in the weeks before an operation, and it improves outcomes, yet uptake is patchy. The team combined twenty-five interview-based studies reporting the views of patients and staff who had lived through such programs.

Patients joined in when programs felt personal, when staff ties were strong, and when they believed the effort would pay off. Services struggled with staff capacity, weak backing, and the short window before surgery. The authors advise making prehabilitation a standard part of care, shaped to each patient's life rather than offered as one fixed package.
pmc-13249778:
Föttinger and an Austrian team added eye scans to the scorecard for multiple sclerosis treatment success, in a 2026 Journal of Neurology study. The standard score, NEDA-3, counts relapses, disability worsening, and MRI activity. One hundred twenty-four patients starting a disease-modifying drug had eye layer scans and MRI at the start and after one year, then were followed for years.

By the standard score alone, quiet disease at one year did not clearly predict later disability. Adding retinal thinning changed the picture: patients failing the combined test faced a far higher risk and progressed sooner. The authors argue the eye reveals ongoing nerve loss that inflammation-focused scoring misses, and they propose the combined measure for judging treatment response.
pmc-13249878:
Tscherne, Halwe, and Krammer survey the medical toolbox against Andes hantavirus in this 2026 brief report. The immediate prompt was an outbreak aboard a cruise ship, which drew attention because this hantavirus, alone among its family, can pass from person to person. Infections with hantaviruses have been climbing worldwide in recent years.

The authors judge a hantavirus pandemic unlikely, while treating person-to-person spread as a genuine concern worth preparing for. Their report weighs the state of vaccine candidates and treatments for Andes virus, a pathogen with no licensed countermeasure. It is a stock-taking piece, meant to show where development stands before the next outbreak tests it.
pmc-13250278:
Jackman, Burrow-Sánchez, and Cohen ask how social media habits and beliefs about harm combine in teen vaping. Their 2026 Tobacco Use Insights study reanalyzes the 2023 National Youth Tobacco Survey, a representative sample of more than twenty-two thousand United States adolescents. The team separated passive viewing of content from active posting and engagement.

How harmful teens believed vaping to be changed the link between social media use and recent vaping. The gap between high and low harm beliefs was widest among teens with heavy active engagement with vaping content. Passive use showed a smaller contrast between the belief groups. The authors suggest that prevention messages should address vaping content on social media alongside direct teaching about health effects.
pmc-13251078:
Aziz and co-authors compare three ways of fixing mesh in keyhole groin hernia repair: glue, stitches, and metal tacks. Their 2026 BMC Surgery trial randomized seventy-five adults having laparoscopic TAPP repair at one center, twenty-five to each method. Pain and hernia-specific quality of life were tracked for six months.

Tack patients hurt substantially more on the first day and at one month than the other groups. By three and six months, pain was low and similar everywhere after surgery. Glue patients felt the mesh least and scored best on comfort at every check, and they returned to work fastest. Glue caused no extra early complications, leading the authors to favor it for early recovery.
pmc-13251678:
Carolin Oetzmann and a large team sort depression by wrist data in this 2026 study. Depression looks very different from person to person, and self-reports capture only part of it, so the team turned to wearable trackers for an objective view.

Fitbit records from 623 people with repeat depression were grouped by a learning method that was given no diagnoses in advance. Three activity types emerged, from high to low, and four sleep types, including early, late, disrupted, and variable sleepers. People mostly stayed in their type over time, suggesting steady personal patterns rather than passing moods. The authors propose these types for cleaner research groups and tailored monitoring.
pmc-13253778:
Camille Wynn and colleagues built a new survey tool in a 2026 study on how people judge talks. No well-tested tool existed to rate whether a single conversation felt worthwhile and satisfying. The team drafted the Person-Reported Outcome of Conversational Success, called PROCS, from past research and expert input.

Interviews with 39 people refined the wording and format. Then 50 people used it after live talks, and 817 people rated talks they recalled. The final tool can score one conversation, and the authors say careful input from varied users supports its clarity and use in research and clinics.
pmc-13253978:
Muhammad Hamza and a large team report a rare shunt complication in a 2026 case report. A seven-year-old boy had a shunt placed after injury caused hydrocephalus, a build-up of brain fluid. He grew drowsy and unsteady, and a CT scan first suggested a tumor at the back of the brain.

An MRI instead showed a trapped fourth ventricle, where one fluid space swells shut and presses on the brainstem. Surgeons opened the blocked area and freed scarred tissue, restoring fluid flow. His symptoms fully cleared within one month, and the paper reviews past cases to stress fast imaging and surgery.
pmc-13254178:
Shuo Zhang and colleagues create a bacteria-killing wound material in a 2026 study. Burn wounds infect easily, and silver dressings, the usual first-line option, can be costly and toxic. Their Ag-CuO nanozyme, a tiny particle with enzyme-like action, combines silver with copper oxide flowers made in fluid.

The particles flood bacteria with reactive oxygen, starve them by cutting sugar uptake genes, and build up copper inside cells to trigger a copper-driven death. In animal tests, it beat commercial silver dressings with the same silver content and helped new blood vessels grow, aiding healing.
pmc-13254278:
Leah Grebner and Angela Campbell rethink health information jobs in a 2026 article. The field still sorts roles into traditional and nontraditional, labels born when most work sat in hospitals. The authors combined federal workforce data, published literature, and surveys of practitioners and educators.

They found health information work is now cross-sector, tech-driven, and tightly linked, with much of it outside hospitals and outside federal job classes. They propose the Health Information Continuum, a framework that sorts work by shared skills and the life cycle of health data. They offer it as a fairer model for training and identity.
pmc-13255378:
Nicholas P Howard and colleagues trace the wild roots of the cultivated apple in a 2026 genetics study. The domestic apple is thought to descend mainly from three wild species, with possible input from tiny-fruited ones. Using a 20K marker array, the team built a library of species-specific DNA markers from wild trees, then read ancestry in 436 wild accessions and in cultivars.

All cultivars proved to be mixtures of the three main progenitors, and some carried tiny-fruited input too. Older cultivars and those from eastern Europe or western Asia held less M. sylvestris ancestry than modern western ones. The work also flagged taxonomy problems in wild collections.
pmc-13255678:
Soumya Bhattacharyya, Jose Wojnacki, Nathalie Brouwers, and Vivek Malhotra report a new view of collagen handling in cells in a 2026 paper. Procollagen 1 is a bulky molecule built inside the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding compartment, before export. Its rigid, long shape poses a puzzle, since standard shipping vesicles are far too small to hold it.

Against the prevailing view, the team reports that procollagen 1 gathers into a liquid condensate inside cells. This droplet-like assembly could explain how cells store and export large amounts of the molecule. The finding reframes a long-standing problem in collagen biology.
pmc-13257978:
Solomon Mohammed Salia and colleagues wrote a 2026 observational study of newborn care quality in Ghana. Observers watched 158 health workers in six facilities and scored their work against World Health Organization standards and Ghana Health Service standards for newborn care. Group talks with the workers afterwards helped explain the scores. Newborn deaths in Ghana remain above the world average, and deaths inside facilities are rising.

Only twenty percent of workers showed good practice on infection prevention and control, while forty-six percent did poorly there. Scores were middling for essential care for every newborn, at fifty-three percent, and for respectful care of mothers and newborns, at fifty-one percent. Workers blamed badly placed handwashing supplies, parent preference for methylated spirit for cord care, and missing rules for checking pain.
pmc-13258078:
Tiantian Chu, Aijun Xu, and Feng Gao wrote a 2026 reply letter about their trial of esketamine given to prevent postpartum depression in first-time mothers. Postpartum depression is depression after childbirth, and esketamine is a fast-acting anesthetic-related drug. Commentators Du and Liu had raised questions about breastfeeding safety, recovery after surgery, and whether the trial's effects matter in practice. The authors answer each point in turn.

They agree that measuring drug levels in breast milk would be the strongest safety proof, which their trial did not do. They cite low milk levels in earlier ketamine work and note their dose was limited to twenty-four hours of infusion. Brain-related side effects within one hour, at 31.7 percent, faded before surgery ended. Dizziness at twenty-four hours was mostly mild, and they admit recovery milestones were not systematically assessed.
pmc-13259578:
Emmanuel Stip wrote a 2026 commentary on preparing Canada's health system for conflict. He responds to work by Grushka and co-authors calling for stronger civilian and military medical readiness, with better coordination and surge capacity. Stip argues that this planning rests on an unspoken psychological model: resilience, the idea that people adapt and recover after hardship. He questions whether recovery is a fair expectation when adversity is long-lasting and unresolved.

As a complement, Stip offers sumud, an Arabic word conveying steadfastness, deep roots, and collective endurance under ongoing adversity. Sumud aims at continuity, dignity, and meaning rather than bouncing back. He notes that Canadian clinicians already care for refugees and diaspora patients whose distress persists because conflicts abroad continue. Planning, he argues, must ask whether systems restore health or sustain dignity where restoration is impossible.
pmc-13259878:
Sarah Bekaert wrote a 2026 commentary on a paper by Byrne and Mulvogue about using metaphor in nursing research degrees. A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another, and the original paper argues it helps researchers shape understanding, organize ideas, and communicate complex concepts. It offers an eight-step framework for using metaphor on purpose, from clarifying why to use one, to finding the right one, to using it as a signpost and a closing thread.

Bekaert stresses that metaphor is already woven through nursing language, as when illness is called a journey or treatment a battle. Used deliberately, she argues, it can reveal emotional and systemic sides of care that plain technical analysis may miss. Examples include a study using metaphor analysis to uncover nurses' perceptions of missed care. She links the approach to deeper thinking for both researcher and reader.
pmc-13260178:
Eduardo Henrique Amorim Silva leads a 2026 case report of heavy parasitism in a common marmoset in northeastern Brazil. Marmosets often live near towns, which raises their exposure to parasites. A weakened female marmoset was rescued near Garanhuns, Pernambuco, and taken to a university veterinary hospital. Her condition was so severe that she was euthanized, and a post-mortem exam was done, including a stool sample taken from the rectum.

The exam found widespread skin lesions on her left limbs, an intense tick infestation, and nematode worms in her intestine. The ticks were named as Rhipicephalus sanguineus sensu lato, and the worms and eggs as the species Primasubulura jacchi. The authors say this is the first record of that tick species parasitizing this marmoset in northeastern Brazil. They urge health monitoring of primates living near people.
pmc-13260278:
Esra Zeybek, Asım Kart, and Özlem Özmen present a 2026 animal study of whether chrysin, a natural plant compound, protects rats against aflatoxin B1. Aflatoxin B1 is a fungal poison that damages the liver and kidneys. Forty male rats were split into control, chrysin, aflatoxin, and combined groups. Chrysin was given by mouth for eleven days and the toxin for seven days, after which tissues and molecular markers were examined.

The toxin caused clear liver and kidney injury, draining protective glutathione and raising markers of fat and DNA oxidation damage. Inflammation signals rose, cell-death proteins increased, and tissue structure was disturbed. Giving chrysin alongside the toxin lessened these changes, restored antioxidant defenses, and preserved liver and kidney structure. The authors propose chrysin as a candidate protective agent against this mycotoxin, pending further study.
pmc-13260478:
Saskia Karenina Latif and colleagues present a 2026 pilot lab study comparing chicken eggshell paste with a commercial mineral product for repairing early tooth enamel damage. Tooth decay in baby teeth affects over eighty percent of children in many developing countries. Eggshell is rich in calcium carbonate and is a cheap waste product. Nine baby incisor teeth with artificially induced white spot lesions were split among eggshell paste, the commercial product CPP-ACP, and a control group.

Micro-CT scans measured lesion depth and mineral density before and after treatment, with three teeth per group. Both treatments improved significantly from baseline, while controls worsened. Eggshell paste reduced lesion depth more than CPP-ACP, by a mean difference of 28.09 units, while mineral density gains were comparable between the two. The authors call eggshell paste a promising sustainable alternative for early decay care.
pmc-13261078:
Fatemeh Afra and colleagues present a 2026 case report and literature review on methotrexate toxicity. Methotrexate blocks folate use in the body and treats rheumatoid arthritis and some cancers. It has a narrow safety range, so harm can occur even at normal doses in high-risk patients.

Their patient was a 58-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis and chronic kidney disease. He developed gut symptoms, brain impairment, and a pus-filled rash, with pancytopenia and acute kidney injury added to his chronic disease. His blood methotrexate level was normal despite strong signs of toxicity. He received urgent dialysis, leucovorin rescue, blood support, and intensive care. His course was complicated by acute pancreatitis, and he died. The authors stress that blood levels may not predict toxicity, so clinicians should act on clinical signs, stop the drug, and start leucovorin promptly.
pmc-13262578:
Zhiyuan Luo and colleagues turn a plant compound's chemistry into a weapon against ulcerative colitis in mice. Beta-elemene, an oily anti-inflammatory from old folk medicine, bristles with carbon double bonds that react with oxygen radicals. Their 2026 nanoemulsion delivers it straight to inflamed colon tissue.

Inside angry macrophages, the radicals flooding the tissue trigger the droplets to clump exactly at mitochondria. The clumps jam the energy chain, slashing the oxidative burn that fuels the attack. Treated colitis mice showed calmer tissue and fewer attack-mode macrophages. A partner glowing probe tracked the inflammation and the healing, a first for how this compound works.
pmc-13262678:
Hoang Anh T Phan and colleagues design a longer-lasting imaging probe for certain brain and nerve cancers in a 2026 journal article. The probe targets a receptor called Y2R, found at high levels on neuroblastoma and glioblastoma cells. Peptide probes, made of short amino acid chains, normally break down in under 30 minutes, too fast for imaging.

Swapping one oxygen atom for sulfur in the peptide backbone, and closing the chain into a ring, changed that. The lead probe kept moderate strength and high selectivity for Y2R cells, the team reports. Its half-life rose from about 30 minutes to over 8 hours in mouse serum tests. The stabilized probe could selectively image neuroblastoma cells that carry the receptor.
pmc-13263278:
Michael Guger and colleagues use an Austrian registry to study how age affects multiple sclerosis treatment in a 2026 journal article. Disease-modifying therapies calm the immune attack in multiple sclerosis, but ageing changes immunity and adds other illnesses. The registry analysis covered patients on such therapy for at least a year by March 2025, split at age 50.

Of 2,117 patients, about a third were 50 or older. Yearly relapse rates were slightly lower in the older group, and their risk of a first relapse was lower too in time-based models. Yet disability worsening was more likely in older patients at both the 12-week and 24-week confirmations. The authors say both disease activity and age itself shape treatment outcomes.
pmc-13264278:
Yahui Nie, Nuannuan Deng, and Dandan Huang wrote a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of balance training for children with developmental disorders. These children often have weak motor skills. The authors pooled trials to see whether balance work lifts balance and wider movement.

They searched seven databases and kept 22 trials that used random assignment. Balance training gave moderate gains in still balance, moving balance, and daily-use balance. Gross motor function, meaning large movements like running and jumping, also improved by a moderate amount. A few studies found gains in strength and coordination too. The authors warn that methods varied a lot, and clear dose guidance is still missing.
pmc-13264978:
Dian Tjahyadi and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a giant growth of womb-lining tissue inside a cesarean scar. Endometriosis is tissue like the womb lining growing outside the womb, and in scars it is rare; giant forms over eight centimetres are rarer still. Their patient was a 35-year-old mother of two.

For three years she had cyclic pain and bleeding from her old cesarean scar during periods, with pain rated seven to eight out of ten, plus a growing lump at the scar. Her cesarean with sterilization was in 2020, and symptoms began two years later. A scan showed a fluid-dark lesion under the skin. Surgeons cut out the whole mass, about eight centimetres across and stuck to deep tissue. Lab tests confirmed scar endometriosis. The authors urge doctors to suspect it when scar pain follows the monthly cycle.
pmc-13266578:
Deyan Y Yosifov and a large team report 2026 results from the CLL12 trial in early-stage leukemia. The trial tested the drug ibrutinib against placebo in untreated patients at middle to high risk of worsening. The team checked a gene variant called IGLV3-21R110, which lets cancer cells signal on their own.

Samples came from 515 patients, and four testing methods gave matching results. About 7 percent carried the gene setup, and most of those had the variant. Carriers did worse in every trial arm, with shorter time free of disease events. Lab tests confirmed that the variant blunted how well ibrutinib worked on the cancer cells.
pmc-13267978:
Christopher Seifen and colleagues present a 2026 step-by-step case report on robot surgery for throat cancer. The da Vinci SP system, a single-port robot, won European approval for mouth-route surgery in January 2024. European experience is still thin. Their patient was a 51-year-old man with virus-linked cancer of the right tonsil.

Through the mouth, the single-arm robot removed the cancerous tonsil. The team also removed the other tonsil and lymph nodes on both sides of the neck. The report walks through the setup and steps in detail. The authors say this is among the earliest cancer uses of the system in Germany since approval. They frame it as part of standard combined treatment and call for multi-center studies to define its place.
pmc-13269178:
Manami Utsunomiya and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a small white globe seen during stomach camera exams. They asked whether that mark predicts a new stomach cancer at a different site a year or more later. All patients had first had early stomach cancer removed through the camera.

The study included 160 patients whose cancer showed the white globe and 284 whose did not. New separate cancers appeared more often in the globe group. When other factors were weighed together, only the globe stayed a clear risk factor. Germ infection and longer follow-up mattered in simpler checks. The authors urge closer camera follow-up when the globe is present.
pmc-13269378:
Muhammad Junaid Iqbal and co-authors published a review in 2026 on vitamin D shortage in ataxia-telangiectasia, a rare disorder that affects movement, immunity, and other body systems. Short reports had flagged low vitamin D in these patients, but no pooled figure existed. The team combined the published studies that measured blood vitamin D.

Only four studies were found. Pooling them, 50.8 percent of patients fell below the shortage cut point, and 26.8 percent were severely low. Another 21.9 percent had levels in the borderline range, while 38.1 percent had enough. The average level was 19.65 units on the scale used. The authors urge routine checks of vitamin D in these patients and better planned studies.
pmc-13269678:
Andre M N Renzaho and co-authors published a review in 2026 on food value chain programs and household food security in sub-Saharan Africa. These programs act on farming, storage, transport, or selling to raise food access. Seven databases were searched, with no date limits, for studies with hard numbers.

Of 739 studies screened, 31 qualified, giving 37 study units across many countries. Households in the programs had food insecurity 16 percentage points lower than non-participants. Diet quality, daily energy intake, and food spending all rose, by 506 calories and about 42 dollars per person yearly. Children weighed more for their age, farm income rose, and harvest losses fell by 4 percent.
pmc-13270678:
Frederick Kremser led a 2026 laboratory comparison of two replacement lenses used after cataract surgery. One, Hanita's Extend, is an enhanced single-focus lens built on the Bessel principle and meant to improve middle-distance sight. The other, Johnson and Johnson Vision's Eyhance, served as the established comparison.

Testing followed international standards on an optical bench with a model cornea, at two opening sizes. Measures covered image sharpness, light spread, and standard test charts. Both lenses performed much alike, with nearly identical far-focus scores and only tiny gaps at stronger defocus, below what normal vision testing can resolve. The authors conclude the Extend matched the Eyhance under laboratory conditions.
pmc-13270878:
Fatma Mohamed Magdy Badr El Dine is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional survey of health workers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices on snakebite poisoning across sub-Saharan Africa. Snakebite remains a major health problem in the region, and front-line care quality varies widely.

In total, 3,544 health workers from nine countries took a validated questionnaire, about half of them general practitioners. Knowledge and attitude scores varied by country; Uganda scored highest on both, yet showed weak practice scores. Some workers still reported harmful habits, such as tying a tight band above the bite, sucking out venom, or cutting the wound. Training, antivenom access, and schooling in toxicology linked to better knowledge.
pmc-13271278:
Byeonggyu Kim is lead author of a 2026 journal article on a gene called AtGATA5 in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The article covers its role in how the plant hormone abscisic acid, shortened to ABA, controls seed germination. ABA also governs leaf pore closure and stress responses. Two key ABA genes are NCED3, which helps make the hormone, and ABI4, which passes its signal on.

Plants with extra AtGATA5 germinated less under added ABA, and plants with the gene knocked out also reacted strongly, a puzzle the authors note. Levels of NCED3 and ABI4 rose in the overexpressing plants, and cell tests confirmed AtGATA5 switches both genes on. They propose AtGATA5 as a new regulator of ABA balance.
pmc-13272278:
Nicholas Pischke and Thomas Powell present a 2026 mathematics paper on how fast a noisy step-by-step method settles down. Their method mixes two older schemes for finding fixed points, which are points that a map leaves unchanged. Noise is treated in a fully general way, with no fixed sampling rule assumed.

The authors prove rates at which the method becomes steady, called rates of asymptotic regularity. For special cases the rates are linear, matching or beating the best known results. In inner product spaces, which are spaces with a way to measure angles, the general rate is quadratic. They also discuss minibatch sampling, cost bounds, and use in Q-learning.
pmc-13272878:
Jessica Foley leads a 2026 study of how long life evolved in Heliconius, a genus of tropical butterflies. Lifespans in animals range from days to centuries, and these butterflies are known for living unusually long for insects. The team gathered data from butterfly houses, field mark-and-recapture work, and captive colonies.

They found a three-fold lifespan extension in Heliconius over close relatives, with some species living nearly a year at most. Captive tests showed the longer life came with slower ageing in both survival and body function. The authors present Heliconius as a strong new model for studying how long life evolves and what drives healthy ageing.
pmc-13272978:
Hiroyuki Kodama leads a 2026 case report of a 61-year-old man with esophageal cancer who responded again to an immune therapy he had received before. His cancer, a squamous cell type of the food pipe, had returned in neck lymph nodes after surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and maintenance immune therapy. Later chemotherapy lines failed.

Gene profiling showed extra copies of the PD-L1 gene, with a copy gain of 8, and tissue tests showed high PD-L1 levels. Doctors restarted nivolumab 8.8 months after the first immune therapy ended. The tumor shrank partly after 3.1 months, though it grew again after 5 months. The authors suggest PD-L1 gene gain may help predict rechallenge benefit.
pmc-13273278: Correction notice for a 2025 paper on upper mantle temperatures, the Iceland hotspot track, and ice-Earth interactions in Greenland. One methods sentence is corrected: the wave curves came from a global shear wave model, not a North Atlantic one. The acknowledgments add thanks to Pascal Audet for input on the joint inversion work. Two scientists, Chiara Civiero and Sergei Lebedev, are added as co-authors in eighth and ninth place. The author list and contributions have been updated.
pmc-13273878:
Wu and colleagues test diet education for older adults in China in a 2026 cluster-randomized trial. The intervention taught a dietary pattern designed to cut cardiometabolic risk. Participants were community residents aged 61 to 80 in Tianjin.

The trial enrolled 694 older adults in four clusters. The intervention group had 349 people and the control group 345. Education ran for twelve months. The main outcome was a clustered cardiometabolic risk score. That score fell more in the intervention group. The beta value was minus 0.25. Artery wall thickness also fell, by a beta of minus 0.05. Cholesterol, blood sugar, blood pressure, and body weight all improved. The authors conclude the education lowered disease risk.
pmc-13274678:
Jin Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article uncovering an extra way the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine fights ovarian cancer. Beyond its known DNA damage, the drug's full mechanism was unclear. The team traced a chain involving HIF1A, a low-oxygen sensor, and UBR5, a protein that tags other proteins for disposal.

In ovarian cancer, HIF1A switches UBR5 on, and UBR5 destroys LATS2, a brake protein in the Hippo growth-control pathway. Gemcitabine lowered HIF1A and UBR5, sparing LATS2 and switching the Hippo brake back on, which quieted two growth signals, YAP1 and FGFR1. Treated cancer cells grew, moved, and invaded less, and tumors shrank in an orthotopic mouse model.
pmc-13275578:
Yael Dann and Noa Gueron-Sela present a 2026 daily diary study of how war news exposure affects Israeli families with young children during active regional conflict. For seven days, 193 Jewish-Israeli parents of children averaging four and a half years old reported each day on media use, direct war exposure, mood, and friction with their child.

On days when children saw more war media, they showed more negative mood and more parent-child strain, and the same held between families. Parents' own news engagement reached children indirectly: heavier parental viewing raised the parent's negative mood and relationship strain, which in turn predicted the child's worse mood. Direct exposure and media exposure also combined to shape well-being. The authors highlight media habits as a lever for protecting family emotional climate.
pmc-13276278:
Ying Lu and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on the horse genome and what it reveals about horse history and traits. Horses have served humans for thousands of years in transport, farming, war, and sport. Their DNA also records how domestication reshaped an animal.

The review tracks better reference genomes, capped by a complete Y chromosome sequence, the male sex chromosome. DNA from ancient and modern horses points to a domestication heartland in the Volga-Don region. Later Bronze Age herds replaced earlier lines almost entirely. Maternal lines stayed diverse while paternal lines narrowed sharply under human breeding. The authors link specific genes to racing performance, high-altitude living, coat color, and inherited muscle diseases. They look ahead to complete genome assemblies and population-wide references for breeding and conservation.
pmc-13277078:
Augustus Osborne and Morie Vandi wrote a 2026 viewpoint arguing that women's leadership in health systems needs direct support. Women form most of the health workforce yet hold few top posts in ministries, hospitals, universities, and aid bodies. The gap is sharpest in fragile and conflict-hit settings, where schooling and civic life are disrupted.

Looking through gender plus class, disability, place, and other factors, the authors trace how authority and chances are shared out. They propose four steps: online mentoring and training, local leadership incubators, reform fellowships, and shared research and advocacy networks. Without changes to workplace culture and promotion, they warn, training alone will change little.
pmc-13277278:
Citing Guo leads a 2026 review of a cancer protein called PD-L1 when it appears inside the cell nucleus. PD-L1 is best known on the cell surface, where it helps tumors hide from the immune system. Inside the nucleus, it seems to act on the cancer cell itself, without that immune route.

Nuclear PD-L1 has been linked to aggressive disease, resistance to treatment, and poor outcomes in several cancers. It may aid DNA repair, shift cell fuel use, and reshape nearby tissue. Measuring it well is still hard, and firm proof in patients is limited. The authors outline drugs that could block its move into the nucleus or its actions there, as a future treatment path.
pmc-13279378:
Alena Vollmannova and colleagues report a 2026 study of quince fruit peels as a food resource. Quince is a hard yellow fruit, and its peels are a main waste from food plants. Turning waste in new foods cuts strain on land and water. The team checked nine quince types from an organic farm in the Czech Republic over three years.

Peels proved rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, with low salt metal sodium. Trace metals like iron and zinc sat in safe, useful ranges, while lead and cadmium stayed below test limits in most lots. Peel extracts held strong plant phenols, health linked plant compounds, and good defence against cell harm in lab tests. A key phenol was chlorogenic acid. Waste peels could add worth to new foods.
pmc-13279478:
Sonia M. McCallum and colleagues report a 2026 study that builds a web resource for parents of youth with mental health strain. Parents often act as gatekeepers who spot trouble and seek help, yet few digital tools serve them. The team used a three phase design that put parent views at the centre. Work ran with Australian parents.

A survey of six hundred thirty one parents proved strong demand for such a web tool. Top topics were anxiety, low mood, self harm and suicide in children and teens. Fourteen parent interviews then shaped the draft content. A test version went back to parents for feedback and polish. Step by step parent input aims to make a tool families will trust and use when worry first strikes.
pmc-13280978:
Jake Sypniewski and colleagues reported a new chemistry route to imaging tracers in a 2026 study. Doctors scan the body with tracers that carry a short-lived form of fluorine. The tracers must be made fast and pure, since the fluorine fades in about two hours. The team made a family of salts based on selenium, a chemical cousin of sulfur. They tested how well each salt handed its fluorine slot to the tracer form.

Many salts gave high yields of the wanted tracers, above seven in ten tries. Some weaker salts still gave useful yields. Helper groups on the salt pushed some yields close to full. In direct tests the selenium salts matched or beat the sulfur salts used now. The team also built two known tracers this way. They say the route widens the menu of scans doctors can order.
pmc-13281478:
Yingying Huang and colleagues built a smart grading tool for knee arthritis in a 2026 study. Doctors grade knee wear on X-rays with a five-step scale, but grades vary by reader. The team gathered more than two thousand seven hundred knee X-rays from three hospitals, spanning 2018 to 2024. Their tool reads the image and also uses facts like age and weight. A new fusion step blends the two streams and weighs how sure it is.

On a fresh hospital's images, set aside for testing, the tool matched expert grades at a very high level. It beat eight rival designs, including image-only and facts-only tools. It caught most severe cases while rarely flagging healthy knees. A chart version of its logic also sorted risk cleanly. The authors say such tools could make knee grading faster and more even across clinics.
pmc-13281578:
Zhihang Zhang and colleagues hunted gut fungi for signs of colon cancer in a 2026 study. Most gut work in this cancer has centered on bacteria and viruses. Fungi are scarce in the gut and their gene records are patchy, so they were skipped. The team pooled gene data from nine public groups, with more than fourteen hundred stool samples.
