They charted how fungal mixes shift in cancer and how fungi pair with bacteria.

Fifteen fungal species changed again and again across the groups. Two were richer in healthy people, and two others in cancer patients. Fungal signs alone sorted patients weakly. But added to bacterial signs, they sorted cancer a bit better in fresh test groups. Sorting rose in five of six outside groups. The authors call fungi a helpful extra signal, not a test on its own. They urge better fungal gene records to sharpen the signal.
pmc-13281878:
Shiyang Li and colleagues linked a copper gene to sun damage in skin in a 2026 study. Strong sun rays scar skin over time, a process called photodamage. A cell death path tied to copper has been floated as part of the story. The team mined public gene data from sun-exposed human skin. They crossed changed genes with copper-death genes and a network module tied to damage. One gene survived all three cuts. It moves copper across cell membranes.

Single-cell data showed the gene fell sharply in skin cells after sun exposure. Cells rich in the gene linked tightly with support tissue through glue-like signals. Cells poor in it answered weakly to their surroundings. Lab tests in cells and mice confirmed the gene's drop after damage. The authors say the gene may guard skin's ties to its base. They propose it as a care lead.
pmc-13282478:
Alexander O Everhart and co-authors present a 2026 study tracking two decades of digital components in medical devices authorised in the United States. Regulators at the Food and Drug Administration lack a systematic way to flag which authorised devices contain software. That gap limits safety monitoring and understanding of digitisation by specialty. The team pioneered text analysis of tens of thousands of regulatory documents for newly authorised devices.

Their method reads device records to detect digital features, building the first broad map of the trend. Devices with digital components grew substantially over the two decades. Growth varied meaningfully across clinical specialties and product categories, digitising some fields far faster than others. The authors argue such tracking is a prerequisite for software-aware oversight after devices reach the market.
pmc-13282978:
Allergy shots against dust mites can trigger whole-body reactions in children, the risk profiled in Qin Wang's 2026 hospital study. The treatment can ease asthma and hay fever but may trigger reactions. The team looked for child traits that raise that risk.

Records covered 250 children treated from July 2022 to July 2025 at one hospital. Just under half had a body-wide reaction across more than nine thousand shots. Most reactions were mild and fast, with only two severe cases and no deaths. Risk rose when asthma and hay fever occurred together. Risk also rose with high total and mite-specific antibody levels in blood tests.
pmc-13283178:
Deer fed mixed plant toxins barely change intake, while a urine marker tracks dose faithfully, in Katie L Anderson's 2026 feeding trials. Wild deer eat plants rich in defense chemicals that need detox work. A key idea is that mixing toxin types spreads the load across body pathways.

Two captive deer species ate five mixes of four pure plant chemicals. Intake, urine markers of detox work, and gut bacteria in dung were tracked. Mix type had little effect on how much deer chose to eat. A urine acid marker rose steadily with toxin intake in all mixes. Plant phenols shaped gut microbes more than scent oils did. Results only partly fit the mixing idea for large ruminants.
pmc-13283378:
Difficult preschool behavior erodes mothers' flexibility through stress, unless partner teamwork is strong, Tianqi Qiao's waves of surveys show in 2026. Most past work asked how parents shape children, not the reverse. Parenting stress and partner teamwork are the focus paths here.

Families with preschool children were surveyed three times, six months apart. More than one thousand mothers and children stayed in the final sample. Early child problems predicted lower maternal flexibility later through higher parenting stress. Good perceived teamwork between parents softened that harm in the second path. When teamwork felt weak, stress cut flexibility more sharply. Support for parents may protect maternal mental health.
pmc-13284878:
Jiangjiao Qin and co-authors build a prediction tool, published in 2026, for airway over-response in toddlers with suspected asthma. The standard methacholine challenge is risky and hard in children aged zero to three years. The team used records of children who had breathing tests, nitric oxide breath measures, and the challenge on the same day.

Seven factors predicted the challenge result, led by family asthma history, wheeze, and breath nitric oxide levels in the model checks. The tool sorted cases well in training data and fairly in a held-out group. The authors offer the chart as a non-invasive aid for early asthma judgment, while noting it still needs outside testing before wide use.
pmc-13285278:
Sumra Irum and co-authors present a 2026 case report of bowel telescoping backward after weight-loss bypass surgery. Backward jejunal intussusception is a rare late problem after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and its vague signs overlap with other post-surgery ills. Contrast CT plays the central role in spotting its shape, level, and threat to bowel health.

The patient developed a high-grade small bowel blockage several years after bypass. Imaging showed the backward slide at the bowel join, a known weak point where gut motion changes after surgery. Scan findings shaped the surgical plan. The authors urge early CT when bypass patients show blockage signs, since delays risk bowel damage.
pmc-13285378:
Tiny lab-grown liver tissues help untangle how two signal paths steer early liver cell fate in a 2026 study by Brock Grenci and co-authors. Liver growth needs tight timing of chemical and physical cues, yet few models let researchers vary the setting cleanly. The team built flat microarrays and 3D microwells to test Wnt and YAP signals in liver precursor cells.

Cutting a Wnt brake gene boosted bile duct markers and switched on Notch targets, but scrambled the spatial layout. Blocking YAP mainly shifted liver cell fate on flat arrays, yet blocked bile fate hard in 3D tissues. Paired tweaks showed Wnt and Notch team up on bile fate, while YAP acts through shape-linked routes.
pmc-13285678:
Jean-Pierre Chaboureau built a giant fake sky to train a coming storm-watching satellite, detailed in a 2026 dataset paper. The C2OMODO mission will read up-and-down air speeds inside storm cores from microwave glints taken moments apart, yet real core speeds are almost never measured. A twenty-five day run of a storm-resolving model at fixed warm sea heat fills the gap.

The set holds nine hundred twenty million air columns across thousands of half-hour steps, each with paired snaps one and two minutes apart. Layers include full 3D air fields, surface facts, radar echoes, and fake satellite views in heat and microwave bands. Teams can now test how well space signals betray hidden storm motion.
pmc-13286078:
Darian Lawrence-Sidebottom and colleagues review family digital care for children's oppositional behavior in a 2026 retrospective analysis. Angry, defiant moods in youth strain the whole household, wearing down parents' sleep and calm along the way. A family-centered online program paired coaching and therapy for children with support for their caregivers, and the team checked both sides of that bargain.

Records held 3,781 child-caregiver pairs for children aged 6 to 17 in real-world care. About one in five children began with clinical-level symptoms, and those children carried more co-occurring problems and more strained caregivers. By the end of care, most children with marked symptoms had improved, with the fastest gains in the first months. Caregiver stress, burnout, and sleep also eased fastest where the child improved fastest, which shows the family-wide reach of the program.
pmc-13286878:
Frantisek Nehaj and colleagues probe a hidden flow problem behind a young man's cardiac arrest in a 2026 clinical case report. The 31-year-old collapsed in his sleep with ventricular fibrillation and was revived by a single shock. Angiography revealed his right coronary artery was completely absent, leaving a single coronary system to feed the whole heart. Heart scans looked normal in structure, and he received a defibrillator implant.

Stress testing and nuclear imaging both came back clean, which might have closed the case as unexplained. A CT flow scan told another story: a sharp flow drop through the middle and far reaches of his remaining arteries. The authors argue this flow-based scan can unmask dangerous flow limits in coronary anomalies that ordinary tests bless as safe, sharpening risk judgments for survivors.
pmc-13287178:
Gargi Yonatan and colleagues looked for repeatable patterns in 2026 in how the blood pressure drug noradrenaline is dosed over ten days during septic shock. Records covered 1,111 adults treated in Israel and 9,343 adults in a large United States database, used to test whether patterns held elsewhere.

Clustering hourly doses found five pattern groups in one cohort and six in the other, yet the same broad families appeared in both. Death rates by ninety days rose steeply across groups. Total dose and timing during days two to four mattered most. Using only the first day of data, models could already predict the final group with good accuracy.
pmc-13288478:
Rana Hameed Jabr and Omar Husham Ali compared spit stress markers in 2026 among 400 adults classed as gum-healthy, having gum inflammation, or having deep gum disease. Saliva from ninety of them was lab-tested for cortisol, chromogranin A, and an enzyme tied to stress response, beside a standard stress questionnaire.

All three markers ran higher in both disease groups than in healthy controls. One marker climbed in a clean staircase from health to deep disease. Self-rated stress also scored higher in patients. Exact group means are reported in the study. The authors suggest spit markers could support gum assessment, while stress itself may feed the disease.
pmc-13288678:
Rebecca M Smith and colleagues report mixed-methods results from a 2026 UK feasibility trial on treating positional vertigo after head injury. Hospital patients with post-traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo at three major trauma centers were assigned by chance to repositioning maneuvers, Brandt-Daroff exercises, or advice alone, while interviews explored how the trial ran.

Recruitment pace and screening success differed between sites for local reasons. Being assigned to advice alone landed differently with staff and patients, hinting that a later full trial should rethink that arm, while assessment and hands-on treatment were acceptable to participants. Blending counts with interview material exposed strengths and flaws that will shape the design of a definitive effectiveness trial.
pmc-13288978:
David Dasa and Philip Davies test a camera-based blood pressure app in Nigeria. Their 2026 field study ran at three hospitals. All adults had dark skin types V or VI. The app reads blood flow from face video. Cuff readings served as the true standard.

Of 306 adults, 249 gave usable readings. Errors ran large for top and bottom numbers. The app missed most true high readings. It flagged few false highs, though. Slow internet links tied to failed readings. Most patients and staff liked the tool. Darker skin raised the odds of failure. The authors warn of unfair care without fixes.
pmc-13289078:
Cecilia Bolling and colleagues present a 2026 trial plan on sleep and cannabis in the US. The trial deals with adults who use cannabis often. Poor sleep and heavy use feed each other. Sleep therapy may cut both at once. The host is the University of Michigan.

The trial will enroll 200 adults aged 21 and up. All will have chronic insomnia and frequent use. Half will get six online sleep therapy sessions. Half will get sleep hygiene lessons. Checks run before, after, and months later. Brain wave sleep tests will run twice. Sleep depth is the key body measure. Data will be shared in a national archive.
pmc-13289178:
Muhammad Homayoon Manochehr and colleagues map sex health access for teens with HIV in 2026. Their scoping review covers sub-Saharan Africa. Such teens face blocks to sex and birth care. Stigma and fear of disclosure loom large. Three databases plus grey sources were searched.

The search screened 6,835 records in all. Just 14 studies met the entry rules. Programs ranged from broad to narrow fixes. Schools, clinics, and phones hosted them. Most stressed that services feel welcoming. Peer support helped teens engage. Outreach and digital tools also helped. Fit to local culture stood out most. Cost and distance got less focus.
pmc-13289978:
Omar Asdrúbal Vilca Mejia and colleagues argue a 2026 editorial case for recognizing coronary bypass surgery as a formal superspecialty in Brazil. Bypass grafting remains the gold standard for complex coronary disease, yet state death rates for isolated bypass ranged from 2.6 percent to 13.1 percent between 2008 and 2017 in national data. Such spread signals a policy crisis, not just surgical variation, the authors contend.

Focused training can raise graft use, speed operations, cut harm, and improve survival and patient experience, they argue. The plea is framed as democratizing excellence, not excluding generalists from practice. Small-cut methods and enhanced recovery plans should anchor the new specialty, backed by multi-site registry proof from Brazil. State gaps make that case hard to ignore.
pmc-13290078: A short 2026 correction in Gut Microbes adds a conflict of interest addendum to an article on a bile acid network and probiotics in colitis by Biagioli and coauthors. Three senior authors clarify co-founder roles in a university spin-off, Precision BioTherapeutics, founded in 2019. The notice states neither that company nor a partner firm played any role in the study at any stage. Disclosure was omitted at submission because the authors saw no competing interest. The journal confirms handling was unaffected. No research content changes.
pmc-13290678:
Posting ultrasound pictures online is remaking what it means to become a parent, Ilenia Picardi and Maria Carmela Agodi argue in a 2026 article. Three- and four-dimensional scans have moved from clinics into commercial studios and social platforms, and the authors ask what that does to expectant parents.

Using multimodal critical discourse analysis on two UK parenting forums, they studied how parents describe and emotionally handle their scan encounters. The images cut both ways: they promise reassurance and bonding, yet spark anxiety when the pictures fall short of idealized images of the foetus and of good parenthood. Forums act as emotional infrastructure where members trade stories, humor, and support. The authors name the result a digital foetus, socially recognized before birth, and call the process digital birth.
pmc-13290778:
Combining every weapon at once lengthens survival when glioblastoma returns, Jean-Baptiste Barbe-Richaud and colleagues report from the FROST study in 2026. Three of four patients see this brain tumor recur within a year, and no standard playbook exists for that moment.

The multicenter real-world study followed 271 patients treated at first recurrence. Most (70%) received systemic therapy alone, 21% got a multimodal mix of drugs, radiation, and surgery, and 9% had local treatment only. Median survival from recurrence was 9.9 months overall, but the multimodal group reached 16.2 months against 9.3 for local therapy alone and 7.9 for systemic therapy. Adjusted analyses kept the ordering. The authors argue for planning recurrence care as a package rather than a sequence of single moves.
pmc-13290978:
Austrian guidance for opening the chest to restart the heart after severe injury is set out in a 2026 consensus study led by Martin W Dünser. Resuscitative thoracotomy is advised only for selected cases of traumatic cardiac arrest, and most prior evidence comes from busy centers with many penetrating injuries, unlike the setting studied here.

Twenty-four specialists from 10 Austrian medical societies and two emergency services worked through a modified Delphi process over four rounds. A literature review fed 22 open questions, which became 28 agreed statements: a single strong recommendation, fifteen weaker ones, and a dozen best-practice statements. The guidance gives lower-volume settings a shared, structured way to prepare for a rare and urgent procedure.
pmc-13291078:
Blocking tiny abnormal blood vessels through an artery to ease long-lasting shoulder pain is reviewed in a 2026 narrative article led by Nicolò Ubaldi. Conditions from frozen shoulder to tendon pain and muscle pain share inflammation and new vessel growth that can feed pain signals, and many patients stay sore after standard care.

Transarterial embolization aims to shut those vessels down while sparing the joint itself, using materials that range from antibiotic particles to calibrated microspheres. Reports in frozen shoulder describe strong pain relief and better movement with few side effects, and tendon and muscle cases show similar gains in the papers surveyed. Safety looks favorable overall, though the authors flag antibiotic resistance worries and call for firmer trial evidence before wide use.
pmc-13292578:
Jay Prakash and co-authors write a 2026 letter building on a review of tracheal intubation in critically ill patients, which framed the procedure as a hemodynamic event, not just an airway task. Induction, apnea, and positive-pressure ventilation each batter circulation in sequence, and the review named the physiologically difficult airway. The letter writers propose sharpening that framework at the bedside.

They suggest classifying patients by their dominant physiological vulnerability rather than by anatomy alone. Vasoplegia calls for pre-emptive pressor support, preload dependence warns that ventilation will slash venous return, and a failing right ventricle can collapse under rising airway pressures. Severe metabolic acidosis needs its own handling. Because several problems often coexist, the point is spotting the main actionable derangement first. Individualized preparation, they argue, beats one-size intubation routines.
pmc-13292678:
Bende Zou, Xinmin Xie, and Ludmila Gerashchenko present a 2026 methods shortcut for recording brain waves in mice without drilling the skull. Standard EEG implants demand stereotaxic drilling and screws, eating time and stressing animals. Their approach presses thin needle electrodes into set skull positions, hooks extra needles along the skull's sides for grip, and cements a connector in place with dental composite.

The whole surgery finishes in under fifteen minutes, with no drilling or screw placement at all. Recordings from the needle setup proved no worse than those from conventional screw electrodes in the team's comparisons, across the sleep and brain-activity measures they examined. The authors pitch the method as faster, gentler, and accurate enough for epilepsy, sleep, and drug-response studies. Animal welfare and lab throughput both gain, they argue.
pmc-13293278:
Daniel J. Ahn and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, a new transplant policy meant to help stable heart patients on long-term pump support. A 2018 rule change had lowered their priority, so a time-based status rise was approved.

Using national transplant data, the team tracked 4967 listed adults who got a durable left ventricular assist device after the 2018 change. By six years, most had a device problem, a status upgrade, or had left the list, and only 47 of those fully followed remained waiting, a count the authors give. Applying the new rule at once would shift status for just 4.7% of the waitlist.
pmc-13293378:
Richard Kronick and co-authors weigh, in a 2026 study, the money effects when sicker members leave Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare. Prior work shows high-need members leave more often, but the cost to plans had not been counted.

For people who left in 2019, traditional Medicare spent 30% more in the first year after leaving than plans would have been paid to keep them, based on figures the authors report. Leaving was rare, though, at 1.7% of members that year and lower later. Spread across all members, the added cost to plans was only about 0.6% overall. A measured policy reply still seems apt.
pmc-13293478:
Mirijana Irnich and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a classification system for video-based artificial intelligence that watches for epileptic seizures. Tools vary widely in cameras, methods, and aims, and no shared scheme existed to compare them.

Five rounds of work blended a literature review, a market scan, and checks with ready products, drawing on studies from 2013 onward found in three databases. A total of 40 original studies shaped 16 starting dimensions, and nine experts added more through a Delphi process. The final scheme holds 23 dimensions with 102 traits. Gaps in the evidence base were also mapped for future work.
pmc-13293978:
Sachith Gallolu Kankanamalage and colleagues detail a 2026 protocol for finding transgene RNA and protein in the same mouse spleen cells. The PrimeFlow method mixes flow cytometry with branched DNA probes, so single cells reveal both messages and products. Mice had received luciferase messenger RNA in lipid nanoparticles, a model for RNA drug delivery.

Steps cover spleen breakup, fixing, staining for luciferase protein inside cells, and marking T cells, B cells, monocytes, and other groups with CD antibodies. Probes target luciferase and a control gene. Reading both signals by cell type shows which cells took up the drug and how RNA timing compares with protein timing.
pmc-13294178:
Michal Trnka and colleagues observe polarized light therapy added to standard care for chronic skin wounds in a 2026 single-arm study. Fifty patients, mostly women with mean age 69.4 years, got light at 626 nm for 10–20 minutes per field several times daily alongside normal conservative and surgical care. No sham group was used, a limit the authors state plainly.

Healing moved in a good direction for 92% of patients, and 52% closed fully. In the chronic pain subgroup of 17 people, pain eased for 12 and vanished for 5. Only two mild short-lived skin reactions appeared. Gains tied to wound type and treatment length, but proof needs a controlled trial.
pmc-13295378:
Maksuel Gatto de Vitt and a large team add a protein-cutting enzyme to Jersey cow diets in a 2026 study. Better protein use could cut feed costs, the biggest expense in dairy diets. Free enzyme and a coated, rumen-protected form were compared in milking cows.

Feed intake and total milk volume stayed unchanged with either form of the additive. Milk from enzyme-fed cows, especially the free form, carried more fat and protein and held production longer into lactation. Protein digestion and rumen fermentation markers improved, and blood signs pointed to better protein handling. The coated form sat between the free form and no enzyme on most measures.
pmc-13295778:
Karlijn de Joode and colleagues test blood enzyme patterns as immunotherapy predictors in lung cancer in a 2026 study. The standard tissue score for PD-L1 misses many patients who could benefit from checkpoint drugs. Activity of signalling enzymes in blood immune cells offered a possible extra signal.

Altogether 210 patients with advanced disease gave blood before treatment across several centres. A model mixing enzyme patterns with the tissue score sorted patients by later progression in a validation group. Predicted-benefit patients stayed progression-free longer, and the combined model beat the tissue score alone. The blood test may sharpen selection for costly immune treatment.
pmc-13297878:
Cutting one gene weakens the seals in lymph vessel walls, Nada S Ahmed and her team report in a 2026 cell study. The gene, ZEB1, is known for guiding cell change in other tissues. Its role in the lymph system was not mapped.

The team read both protein and gene data from lymph vessel cells. Cells that lost ZEB1 showed less of a key mark on VE-cadherin, the glue protein at cell seams. The cell sheet leaked more, and white blood cells crossed it more freely. Loss of ZEB1 also cut the kinase YES and shifted YAP1, and muting YAP1 alone copied much of the leak. The work ties ZEB1 to the upkeep of lymph vessel walls.
pmc-13298978:
Aging eyes lose teamwork at reading distance more than at arm's length, shows a 2026 vision study by Bingqing Sun and co-authors. Using a rotating ring test viewed through red-blue glasses, they measured dynamic vision at four distances in 54 presbyopic and 77 non-presbyopic participants.

Sharpness discrimination and dynamic depth perception showed no group differences. Binocular integration, how well the two eyes' images merge, told another story: presbyopic participants passed less often at 0.4, 0.7, and 1 metre, though not at 3 metres. Those needing stronger reading additions, at least 1.5 diopters, lagged at every distance. The authors say the test exposes addition-dependent deficits that static charts miss.
pmc-13303878: Wenqi Chen and colleagues issue a 2026 author correction to a study on epigenetic control of thymus homing and T cell development in embryos. Control graphs, source data entries, and images in several main and supplementary figures were copied or swapped by mistake. Two supplementary figure titles were mislabeled, and an extra data file was included. All listed items have been corrected in the article and its source data file. The notice gives a figure-by-figure account of each fix so readers can check the updated record for themselves.
pmc-13305278:
James Alex Sumawe reports a 2026 radiology case of parotid gland cancer spreading widely through the body. Cancers of this saliva gland are rare, and spread to lung, brain, and liver at once is rarer still.

A 60-year-old man first had face nerve weakness and bulky local disease treated with surgery plus chemo and radiation. Scans later showed many lung nodules with a large mass near the airway, ring-shaped brain deposits with heavy swelling, chest lining spread, and liver spots. A thyroid lump proved harmless on needle testing. Gentle chemo and support care followed.
pmc-13305578:
Huisen Yu, Bin Gao, and Yuanyuan Li review monitors that gauge anesthesia depth during surgery in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Brain-wave tools such as the bispectral index promise steadier dosing than clinical signs alone.

Keeping depth in the right band lowers chances of waking mid-surgery, blood pressure drops from overly deep dosing, and confusion or thinking problems afterward. Brain-guided care looks most helpful for older patients and those with heart disease. Tool limits remain, including varied algorithms and uneven drug sensitivity. Mixing several signals plus smart computing may sharpen personal dosing next.
pmc-13306378:
Wentao Cheng mapped where glacier-fed debris flows are likely in China's Gaizi River Basin in a 2026 hazard study. The alpine basin, crossed by the Karakoram Highway, faces complex terrain, active faults and shifting ice that make forecasting hard.

Hybrid models joined statistics with one-class anomaly detection trained on past disaster records, since labelled safe and unsafe sites are scarce. Land shape factors such as slope, roughness and wetness carried most signal, while distance to ice and rainfall added little in this dataset. One generative model gave the most balanced maps, avoiding the over-warning seen in rivals.
pmc-13307578:
Balcha Girma Masresha and co-authors review in 2026 a quarter century of measles and measles rubella campaigns across the WHO African Region, from 2001 to 2025. They drew on campaign reports and post campaign surveys sent to the regional office, as the region aims to end both diseases in most countries by 2030.

In all, 326 campaigns in 44 countries gave more than 1.5 billion doses to children in the years covered here. Most campaigns hit the national cover goal on paper, yet district goals were rarely met in full. Survey based cover lagged the paper figures, which hints at weak counts. Better tools to find unvaccinated children are now urgent.
pmc-13308578:
Ivana Bureš Valentić and Krešimir Reiner report in 2026 anaesthetic care for a first time mother with Klippel-Feil syndrome who needed a planned caesarean birth. The syndrome fuses neck bones from birth and often brings spine curve and other body quirks that make airway and spinal care hard.

The woman, aged 32 years, had fusion from the third neck bone to the first chest bone, plus raised shoulder blades and right side deafness. Spinal anaesthesia worked for the birth, yet the team stood ready to switch to general anaesthesia if the block failed. No single method suits all such patients, so each plan must fit the body at hand and put safety first.
pmc-13308778:
Jiadong Yu and co-authors probe in 2026 why people follow health guidance when rival claims flood formal and informal channels, using survey data from 742 adults in the United States. They modelled how trust in each channel shaped risk views, plot beliefs, and plans to mask and vaccinate during COVID-19.

Trust in formal sources tracked with graver risk views, weaker plot beliefs, and stronger plans to act for safety. Trust in informal sources pulled each of those the other way in the model runs. Felt severity sat at the hub, lifting mask use at once and vaccine plans through lower plot belief. Crisis teams must work both channels, not just the formal one.
pmc-13309478:
Oskar W. Persson and co-authors track swelling signals in blood and spinal fluid after severe head injury in a 2026 study. Swelling drives much of the damage after such injury, yet its first-week pattern in both fluids was poorly mapped. Two lab platforms for measuring these signals had also rarely been compared head to head.

Twenty-one adults with severe injury gave samples in the first days and again later in the first week, with orthopedic patients as a comparison group. Many signals rose in both fluids, and three key signals rose in both places. Agreement between the two lab platforms varied by signal. The authors offer the paired fluid data as a guide for timing future anti-swelling care.
pmc-13309578:
Mhamed Benaissa models heat and mass flow of a special nanofluid over a stretching round cylinder in a 2026 study. Such flows appear in heat exchangers, pipelines, and vehicle bodies. The fluid here is a second-grade nanofluid, meaning it carries tiny particles and resists flow in a memory-like way, under a magnetic field.

Governing equations were reshaped into simpler forms and solved on a computer with a finite-difference method. The study varies magnet strength, fluid grade, chemical reaction rate, and slip at the surface to see how heat and particle spread respond. Density that shifts with heat is also included. The author reports trends meant to guide design of cooling and coating systems.
pmc-13310378:
Maryam Hekmat and co-authors present a face rash that mimicked a common pigment disorder in a 2026 case report. The true disease was lichen planopilaris, a rare immune condition that scars hair follicles and causes permanent hair loss. On the face rather than the scalp, it is exceedingly rare and easy to misread.

A 38-year-old man showed a flat dark patch across cheek and forehead that looked like melasma, the common pigment condition. Tissue study proved the scarring follicle disease instead. Standard melasma care would have missed it, costing time while damage advanced. The authors urge tissue checks when facial pigment patches resist usual treatment, and call for more published skin-scope images of this presentation.
pmc-13310778:
Zhang Yanxin and colleagues test a body signal called phase angle as a survival marker in throat cancer care in a 2026 cohort study. Patients with nasopharyngeal cancer get combined drug and radiation care, and poor nutrition worsens outcomes. Standard nutrition scores have limits, so the team checked a cell health signal from a body scan device.

Care followed 380 newly diagnosed patients for a median of 60 months of checks, during which 27 deaths occurred. Higher phase angle linked to better body weight, blood protein, and nutrition scores. After accounting for age and cancer stage, higher angle still linked to longer survival. The signal may aid early risk sorting, pending larger proof.
pmc-13310878:
Karthika Bahuleyan Arun and co-editors open a 2026 collection on bacterial products as tools against drug resistance. Resistance killed over a million people in 2019 by direct count, and forecasts warn of far more deaths by 2050 if trends hold. New antibiotics are scarce, yet bacterial products gave most past drug classes and remain rich ground.

Thirteen studies in the set span desert germs, genome guided hunts, and products that alter germ behavior rather than kill outright. One desert germ made a sulfur drug active against resistant Staphylococcus aureus and farm fungi. Work reframes products as modulators of resistance and therapy response.
pmc-13310978:
Qiqi Sun and co-authors build a deep learning tool to read hormone status from brain scans in breast cancer in a 2026 study. Cancer spread to the brain needs hormone data to guide care, yet biopsy is risky and may miss varied lesions. Scan based reading could fill the gap if it joins image, texture, and place data.

Training used 268 scans from 165 patients in a public archive with expert tumor outlines. The model fused deep image traits, measured texture traits, and tumor place codes, and learned three receptor tasks at once. Scores for each receptor passed strong marks in tests. Lesion wise sampling guarded against data leaks.
pmc-13311078:
Mariko Sugiyama and colleagues track immune cell clones in a rare pituitary cancer during checkpoint therapy in a 2026 case study. A woman aged 34 years with Lynch syndrome had a hormone secreting pituitary carcinoma that spread to the liver. A PD-1 blocking drug held disease steady for over a year, and predictors of response were unknown.

Untreated tumor tissue held both helper and killer T cells. Gene codes for T cell receptors showed top tumor clones also ruled the blood during good response, topping both cell groups. A later ovary spread held fewer helper cells in tissue. Blood tracking of tumor clones may mirror response.
pmc-13311278:
Zhihao Shi, Genyuan Li, and Zhehua Zhou present a 2026 survey of Chinese factory workers on the joint effect of xylene fumes and noise on hearing. Both exposures sat within national limits, yet harm was suspected.

Hearing tests were given to 899 workers, of whom 295 faced both noise and xylene and 604 faced noise alone. High-tone hearing loss showed in 5.76 percent of the joint group and 2.48 percent of the noise-only group in this survey. The joint group carried about fivefold higher odds after adjustment. The results argue for tighter guard rules when solvents and noise mix.
pmc-13311378:
A. Aziz Ould Ismail and co-authors evaluate AI-written exam questions for pathology trainees in a 2026 study. GPT-4 wrote multiple-choice items across six clinical pathology fields during the 2024 to 2025 school year.

Faculty experts scored 260 items for clarity and accuracy and chose to keep them as-is, keep with edits, or discard them. About 41.5 percent were kept untouched and 25.4 percent were discarded in this review. Molecular pathology items fared best, while microbiology items were discarded most. Higher clarity strongly predicted a keep decision. Reviewers faulted poor difficulty fit and weak ties to real lab work.
pmc-13311678:
Shaima Wasim Khan and co-authors give a 2026 cohort study on immune reactions against anti-TNF drugs in Middle Eastern patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Such reactions are a top reason these drugs stop working.

The study covered 314 treatment courses in 248 patients at a tertiary center in the United Arab Emirates. Antibodies against the drugs arose in 28.3 percent of courses over a median of two years in this cohort. Reaction-driven failure was the leading cause of stopping treatment. Drug level cutoffs that flag coming reactions were derived for both main drugs. Prior surgery was the strongest predictor of a reaction.
pmc-13312278:
Lisa Cynthia Niwenahisemo and co-authors compare, in a 2026 network analysis, how depression and body symptoms hang together in adolescents from China and Rwanda. Distress is often voiced through physical complaints outside Western settings, and Western-made diagnostic tools can miss culture-specific patterns, so the team mapped symptoms as networks rather than single scores.

The cross-sectional sample held 3,830 adolescents, 2,017 in China and 1,813 in Rwanda, who completed adapted questionnaires on somatic and depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms were more common in Rwanda, reported by 54.6 percent against 29.2 percent in China, while somatic complaints ran higher in China, at 71.0 percent against 64.0 percent. Low energy and sleep problems sat near the center of the networks. The authors aim to guide screening that fits each culture's way of showing distress.
pmc-13312478:
Kang Zhu and colleagues explore, in a 2026 qualitative study, what draws Chinese adolescents into school recess activities or keeps them away, in both urban and rural schools. Recess is a built-in chance to raise daily movement, yet participation varies widely, and the reasons span far more than personal preference.

The team interviewed 49 people, 33 students and 16 teachers, in focus groups and one-on-one sessions, and coded the material with grounded theory methods. Fifteen shared factors sorted neatly into the social ecological model's levels: personal motivation and academic pressure, peers and teachers, facilities, weather and safety, and school rules and recess length. Urban schools added a space-size concern, while rural schools added motor skills and policy factors. The authors offer the map as a guide for targeted recess design.
pmc-13313178:
Makoto T. Fujiwara and Ryuuichi D. Itoh present a 2026 study of how chloroplasts divide inside living leaf cells of the plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Their focus is MinE, a protein gained from bacteria that helps place the ring of parts that splits a chloroplast in two.

The pair tagged MinE with a yellow glowing protein and watched it under a microscope in mutant plants whose own MinE had been restored. They saw a ring at the middle of the chloroplast, built from dots and thin threads, which held its shape while the chloroplast pinched shut. They also found a twin dot form and one-sided spread of MinE, patterns that differ from how MinE acts in bacteria and hint that plant division works in its own way.
pmc-13313278:
Ignacio Salamanca de la Cueva leads a 2026 trial of a six-in-one infant vaccine in preterm babies in Spain. Babies born early face higher risk of death, disability, and infection, yet proof for these combined vaccines in very early births is thin.

The open-label phase IV trial tested a schedule of 2 plus 1 doses of the DTaP-IPV-HB-Hib vaccine, which guards against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, hepatitis B, polio, and Hib disease. Babies were grouped by birth timing, from 24 to 27 weeks up to 34 to 36 weeks. In all, 143 infants got at least one dose, with 22 born at 24 to 27 weeks and 29 at 28 to 30 weeks per the counts in the report. The team described protection rates and both sought and unsought side effects, giving clinics rare data for the frailest babies.
pmc-13314778:
Ibrahim M. Deyab, Khaled A. Alshdokhi, and Ahmed M. A. Abdelbaqy run a trial of a mixed health-sports program for Saudi students in a paper from 2026. Volunteering and exercise each lift body and mind, but their joint effect in a planned program was little tested in Saudi Arabia.

The trial enrolled 70 healthy university students, 35 men and 35 women with a mean age near 19.3 years as stated in the report, split evenly into program and control groups. The 8-week program wove functional training with short teaching and behavior pieces. The team then scored movement quality, fitness, and the drive to volunteer. A program that lifts fitness and civic drive at once could be a cheap win for campus health policy.
pmc-13315878:
Mengge Zhang and co-authors mapped hepatitis B across China in 2026 over eighteen years, hunting for clusters and high-risk areas. Using province-level surveillance data, they tracked new cases and deaths and tested spatial patterns with Moran statistics and scan methods in GeoDa and SaTScan.

Reported cases rose slightly from 916,426 in 2004 to 976,233 in 2021, a change that was not statistically clear. Death rates fell steadily, by an average of 4.03 percent per year. High-high case clusters gathered in the southeast in later years, while high-low death clusters centered on Beijing and Shanghai, and high-risk zones sat in the northwest and southeast coast.
pmc-13316078:
Takuya Yamada and co-authors checked in 2026 how well an Interest in Health Scale works for older adults living in the community in Japan, where no validated tool for this trait existed. A mail survey in 2024 reached 7,203 independent older adults in Tsuru City.

Factor checks supported the original three-factor shape of the 12-item scale, with a comparative fit index of 0.965 and internal consistency of 0.80 by Cronbach's alpha. Short 6-item and 4-item forms tracked the full scale closely, with correlations at or above 0.85. Lower interest scores linked with worse health behaviors and outcomes.
pmc-13316178:
Yibo Ma and a large team built a multi-control nanomedicine in 2026 for osteoarthritis, a joint disease where oxidative stress, inflammation, cell death, and matrix breakdown together destroy cartilage balance. Advanced joint injections improve local delivery, yet packing a multi-part active core into a smart carrier remained hard.

Their K@BMT@HM system joins a built-up core of peptide, bisdemethoxycurcumin, and MnTBAP inside treated hydrogel microspheres. In cartilage cell tests the core boosted antioxidant defense, restored autophagy flow, and tuned TGF-beta signals, easing stress, inflammation, and cell death while favoring matrix building. Such local delivery keeps the active core concentrated inside the affected joint.
pmc-13316278:
Jie-Yu Huang and co-authors review in 2026 how galectins, sugar-binding proteins, shape Epstein-Barr virus infection and its linked diseases. The virus infects over 95 percent of adults worldwide and then hides for life in memory B cells. It is linked to cancers such as Hodgkin lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, yet no licensed antiviral therapy exists.

Galectin-1, galectin-3, and galectin-9 stand out as major modulators, steering viral latency, immune escape, and tumor growth. Their dual roles in T-cell exhaustion and antiviral defense cut both ways. Targeting the galectin and glycan axis offers a possible treatment path.
pmc-13316878:
Juliana do Espírito Santo Russo and colleagues ran a 2026 smile perception study. They edited photos to vary how much upper and lower front tooth shows and how tall the lower lip's red part appears. Smile looks guide orthodontic planning, yet tooth display rules were fuzzy.

A panel of 162 raters, spanning orthodontists, dentists, and laypeople, scored appeal and guessed ages. Full and near-full upper tooth display won the highest appeal across all groups, while lower lip changes moved nothing. More lower tooth showing made faces look older, and older lay raters minded it less. Orthodontists scored harshest overall. Planning, the authors say, should weigh personal taste alongside these shared patterns.
pmc-13317478:
Sooyoung Oh and colleagues present a 2026 veterinary case of a spinal blood vessel malformation in a 2-year-old spayed female cat. She could not walk on her back legs and struggled to pass urine and feces. Two rare conditions, a spinal arteriovenous fistula and vertebral angiomatosis, were both in play.

CT and MRI scans showed a growing bone lesion at the eleventh chest vertebra squeezing the spinal cord, without the swollen veins these cases usually show. Surgery relieved the pressure, and two tissue reviews returned the two different diagnoses. The authors read them as two views of one vessel-growth spectrum rather than rivals. Imaging, they argue, best guides which mechanism to treat in such tangled cases.
pmc-13317778:
Jian Xiao and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, pairing exosomes with engineered materials to treat diabetic skin infections, above all foot ulcers. There, infection, biofilms, low oxygen, and stalled repair gang up against healing. Plain exosome drops wash away too fast to work.

Gels, microneedle patches, membranes, and smart scaffolds can shelter the parcels, hold them in the wound, and release them on cue, while also fighting biofilm and oxygen shortage. Animal evidence shows gains in closure, vessel growth, and infection control. The review is frank about blockers: source choice, dose standards, potency tests, shelf life, and unclear regulatory boxes. Solving manufacturing consistency is the gate to real trials.
pmc-13318878:
Yonglong Yan and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional survey of gout patients in Xiamen, China. Questionnaires ran from November 2023 to January 2024 through an online platform. They measured knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices about gout care. Valid answers came from 462 of 622 questionnaires collected.

Median knowledge score was 16 points, with attitudes at 34 and practices at 40 in the reported results. All three domains correlated positively with each other. Knowledge linked most strongly to practice, at r = 0.539 in their analysis. Modelling showed knowledge directly shaped practice, with an effect of 0.644 in the fitted model. The attitude route was not significant. The authors describe knowledge as limited and attitudes moderately negative, yet self-management as fairly proactive.
pmc-13318978:
Konstantin Semash and colleagues describe a 2026 case of closing a large liver shunt in a three-month-old boy through a vein. The rare birth defect let portal blood bypass the liver. He showed lasting jaundice and poor growth. His bilirubin reached 316 µmol/L, and liver enzymes were very high.

Scans found a shunt up to 25 mm wide inside the liver, with an underdeveloped right lobe. A specialist team chose coil closure through the jugular vein. One coil migrated to the lung artery but was retrieved by catheter. Afterwards his liver tests normalised quickly and portal flow returned. Growth caught up during follow-up. The authors present catheter closure as feasible and effective even in very young infants.
pmc-13319078:
Nana Guo and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two anaesthetics for older patients having abdominal surgery. Propofol infusion was weighed against inhaled sevoflurane. The question was which leaves less cognitive dysfunction afterwards. Seven randomised trials with 802 patients met the inclusion rules.

No outcome differed significantly between the two drugs. Operating time, anaesthesia time, and low blood pressure rates were similar. Rates of postoperative cognitive dysfunction matched as well. Severity scores on days one, three, and seven after surgery also showed no gap. The authors conclude neither agent is proven better for elderly patients. Larger trials are needed before any recommendation, they note. The review was registered prospectively on PROSPERO.
pmc-13319178:
Mateja Virovec, Roberto Barumerli, and Paola Cesari present a 2026 brain stimulation study of body perception in girls with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Participants judged images of spinal curvature to find their detection thresholds. Magnetic pulses over the motor cortex then probed readiness while they viewed distorted spines. Hand muscle responses served as the readout.

Patients detected smaller curvatures than healthy controls. Their sensitivity matched their own trunk appearance ratings, not their measured Cobb angles. Motor excitability in patients peaked right at their low personal threshold. Controls peaked only for curvatures beyond what they could detect. The authors read this as a heightened motor gain tuned to lived body experience. Scoliosis, they argue, reshapes the sensorimotor system, not just the spine.
pmc-13319378:
Yaxin Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of tiny plastic bits in sewers and how they change sewer microbes. Sewer water is low in oxygen and rich in sulfur gases, a mix that ages plastics and feeds key chemical cycles. Two common plastics were tracked as they broke down and as microbes reacted to them.

Attack by harsh oxygen forms cut key bonds in both plastics, roughened their surfaces, and split their chains. At higher doses the plastics hurt microbe health, cut sulfur gas output, and thinned microbe links. Gas making microbes that release methane grew more common, which hints that plastic loads could shift sewer gases toward more methane over time.
pmc-13319878:
Mohammed Turky and Paul MH Dummer wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 warning about chatty software that agrees too easily in dentistry. Smart tools now help with diagnosis, care plans, and study, and much debate has centered on accuracy, bias, and clear rules. A newer risk is flattery by design, where a tool echoes what the user seems to want rather than weighing the proof.

Such agreeable answers can feel helpful at first, yet in care work they may affirm a wrong call and dull sharp judgment. Unlike bias from skewed training data, this habit grows from tuning tools to please users in live chats. The letter urges makers and clinics to guard against praise that comes without proof.
pmc-13320278:
Yuya Okuzaki and co-authors study a retrovirus like gene in chicken germ cells in a 2026 article on breed saving. Germ cells are the sole seed of eggs and sperm, and growing them in dishes offers a way to bank rare chicken breeds since eggs cannot be frozen like mammal eggs. Some breeds and female lines resist dish growth, for reasons tied here to one gene and its control strip.

Lines that grew well showed higher voice of the gene, while damping its control strip lowered calm keeping genes in the cells. Damped cells stalled their growth cycle, coped poorly with DNA harm, and settled poorly into young embryo ridges after transfer. The gene pair seems to help germ cells adapt to dish life.
pmc-13320378:
Abdirahman Said Deheye and co-authors study sugar control in type 2 diabetes in Borama, Somaliland in a 2026 hospital survey. Data on long term illness care in the region is thin, and daily habits plus money strain may drive poor control more than drug access alone. Adults at one regional hospital were asked about activity, food, and work, and their long term sugar marks were read from records.

Among 152 patients seen from March to September 2023, near two thirds showed poor sugar control in the counts reported. Low activity and poor diet each stood as solo drivers of poor control after full checks, as did jobless or casual work status and low schooling. Age and sex did not hold as solo drivers. Local plans should lift movement, food quality, and work support together.
pmc-13321378:
Selim Mert and colleagues test two feed additives in broiler chickens in a 2026 feeding trial. Humate and Yucca schidigera extract were fed alone and together to 240 Ross 308 birds over 42 days, with a plain feed control group for comparison. Outcomes covered growth, carcass traits, gut shape, nutrient uptake, and antioxidant defences.

Birds on the combined diet reached the highest slaughter weight and the best carcass, breast, and thigh yields. Gut villi grew taller and wider in all supplemented groups, with the combined group strongest, and protein uptake peaked there too at day 21. Antioxidant enzymes rose in yucca fed groups. The pairing looks useful for meat bird production.
pmc-13323678:
Jan Domaradzki leads a four-country survey of nursing students on patient blood management, published in 2026, testing whether global policy reaches the classroom. Replies came from 645 master's students in Poland, Germany, Kazakhstan and Iran between October 2023 and April 2024.

Self-rated awareness sat at moderate levels, while tested knowledge ran consistently low across all countries and topics. Gaps covered alternatives to transfusion, drug-based strategies and risks of blood management itself, with some variation by country. Regression checks linked scores to background and work factors. The authors call the awareness-knowledge gap a curriculum failure and press for structured teaching of blood management in nursing degrees.
pmc-13324578:
Ekaterina Varkentin and colleagues test how sudden stress affects picture story understanding in younger and older adults, in a 2026 study. Modern life leans on images and visual stories, yet the role of stress in reading them was little explored.

Two online experiments covered 203 younger adults and 212 older adults. Timed math and logic tasks with social pressure created stress before a three-panel story task with the middle panel missing. Stress hurt younger adults, who judged the missing event worse and felt less sure of their answers. Older adults scored the same with or without stress. The authors suggest richer life-built story schemas may shield older readers.
pmc-13326778:
Darlene Heinen-Stach and co-authors systematically review randomised trials of nature-based interventions for mental health, from gardening therapy to green exercise and nature walks. Their 2026 review follows standard reporting guidance and requires a non-nature comparison group and at least one mental health outcome.

Of more than ten thousand records, forty-seven trials qualified. Seventeen reported significantly greater improvements with nature interventions than controls, particularly for depression, anxiety, and stress. No trial found nature interventions worse than established treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy or art therapy. Studies, however, varied widely in design, duration, and outcomes, and many carried moderate to high risk of bias. The authors call the early evidence supportive but ask for longer, higher-quality studies, subgroup analyses to find who benefits most, and tests of combining nature interventions with standard treatments.
pmc-13328378:
Ridha Horchani critically reviews modern active learning for trustworthy AI in a 2026 article. Active learning fights the labeling bottleneck by asking humans to tag only the most useful examples. But the field has splintered across strategies, supervision levels, and test setups, making gains hard to compare. Horchani covers uses from medical imaging to recommender systems.

A four-axis sorting scheme organizes the field by query logic, supervision grain, operating regime, and how realistic the evaluation is. Families from uncertainty sampling to cost-aware and shift-aware methods are weighed for hidden assumptions and failure modes. The core challenge has moved, Horchani argues, from finding informative samples to building labeling pipelines that stay fair and robust in real work.
pmc-13329478:
William Wanzor and Aakriti Bhargava present a 2026 case of fast-spreading skin death in a toddler from West Texas. The boy was 15 months old and had been healthy. Carers found a dusky patch on his buttock that grew within two days, blistered, and turned black in the centre. No bite or injury had been seen.

Doctors cut away dead tissue, placed a temporary skin matrix, and later applied a skin graft. At 60 days a small open area remained and was treated with silver nitrate. The team judged the cause to be presumed brown recluse spider bite damage, based on the look of the wound and the region. Care rests on wound support, with surgery for severe cases.
pmc-13329578:
Henrietta Bánfai-Csonka and colleagues describe a university first aid responder scheme in a 2026 letter. The University of Pécs holds about 25,000 students plus several thousand staff, yet readiness for cardiac arrest varies across workplaces. A campus-wide programme began in 2022 to train staff as first responders.

Since launch, 266 employees finished the first 10-hour course, and yearly refreshers drew 390 attendances in total, as reported in the letter. Training stresses hands-on resuscitation and defibrillator use, taught by paramedics, with yearly 4-hour scenario refreshers. An online group shares updates and case talk between courses. Defibrillator coverage also grew, reaching 15 devices across the university in the account given.
pmc-13330978:
Hui Wang and colleagues scan United States harm reports for dual-target antibodies in blood cancer care in a 2026 study. Reports tied to CD3 by CD20 bispecific drugs were drawn from the FDA system from late 2022 to early 2025. In total, 2,237 reports covered three drugs: epcoritamab, glofitamab, and mosunetuzumab.

Signal counts came to 93 for the first drug, 65 for the second, and 41 for the third in the reported analysis, with methods agreeing closely. Some signals are absent from current labels, including a brain white matter disease and a severe immune overreaction for one drug. Fatal outcome and timing patterns were also charted. The authors urge closer watch and further study of fresh signals.
pmc-13332478:
Myles N. Arrington and co-authors linked brain responses to faces with teenagers' social lives in a 2026 analysis of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Social health means having enough good relationships, and early adolescence is when peer bonds take center stage, yet brain studies usually examine single social measures at a time.

They paired brain scans at ages 8 to 11 with social data at ages 10 to 13. The data covered 5,832 adolescents, grouping peer measures such as friend counts, bullying experiences, and peer support into profiles. Three profiles emerged: concerning at 12.96 percent, robust at 33.95 percent, and selective at 53.09 percent. Amygdala reactivity to emotional faces interacted with sex in predicting profile membership, while other regions mattered only for single outcomes. The authors read this as evidence of divergent paths between brain function and social health.
pmc-13332978:
Satoshi Kikuchi and co-authors present early family-tree results for Japan's willows in a 2026 phylogenetics study, with special care for species found nowhere else. Willows are notoriously hard to classify because they hybridize freely and vary widely in form.

The team used multi-locus data from low-copy nuclear genes plus chloroplast sequences for all available native species. They found three major lineages inside the Japanese subgenus Vetrix and showed that subgenus Chamaetia is not a single natural group. Two species, S. hukaoana and S. futura, look like survivors of ancient lines splitting in the mid to late Miocene, while the Hastatae section species appear to be fresh offshoots of S. vulpina. Signs of past hybridization turned up in S. miyabeana and S. nakamurana. The authors note tangled gene trees and old cross-breeding mean genome-scale work is still needed.
pmc-13333378:
Stephan Neidhart and colleagues charted the brain-wave fingerprint of epilepsy that follows autoimmune encephalitis in a 2026 study, comparing it with ordinary temporal lobe epilepsy. After the immune attack settles, doctors often struggle to tell whether ongoing seizures stem from that earlier inflammation or from a separate cause.

The team studied 72-hour EEG recordings, scans, and spinal fluid results from 25 patients with post-encephalitis epilepsy and 30 with temporal lobe epilepsy. The autoimmune group showed far more slowing and epileptic discharges arising independently on both sides of the brain, the two patterns often appearing together. It also showed a wider spread in the EEG spectrum across wake and sleep, most over the temporal regions. A combined score built from EEG, imaging, fluid, and clinical features separated the groups sharply. The authors propose the patterns and score as biomarkers to guide immune testing, seizure drug choices, and surgery decisions.
pmc-13336378:
Lingzhi Chen and co-authors built a sensing facemask that screens for tuberculosis from breath droplets or sputum in a 2026 diagnostics study. Conventional TB testing is invasive and slow, which delays control of a disease that spreads through the air.

The mask carries an array of silver-gold nanoflowers. A second sensor uses urchin-shaped gold-silver particles in a covalent organic framework. Together they detect the TB antigen pair ESAT-6/CFP-10 by surface-enhanced Raman scattering. On clinical samples the assay sorted 12 negative and 17 positive patients with 100 percent specificity and 76.5 percent sensitivity in the study, and sputum testing caught two cases droplets missed. It also flagged two of six close contacts with suspiciously high antigen, hinting at hidden infection.
pmc-13336878:
Yan Zu and colleagues identify a protein-tagging enzyme that drives harmful heart enlargement in a 2026 study. RNF115 was high in failing human hearts, in mouse hearts squeezed by a narrowed aorta, and in heart cells dosed with angiotensin II. Quieting it eased cell enlargement in the lab, and removing it only in heart cells protected mice from pressure-induced damage.

RNF115 tags a scaffold protein, SPTBN1, for destruction, which unravels actin fibers, switches off the Hippo-YAP pathway, and turns on growth genes. A compound called DTD blocks RNF115, spares SPTBN1, and protects the heart in models. Blocking this enzyme could become a therapy for heart failure.
pmc-13337078:
Shijie Qian and colleagues unmask a non-enzyme trick behind kidney cancer drug resistance in a 2026 study. Sunitinib blocks tumor blood supply and growth, yet resistance always emerges. Using patient-derived grafts sorted into resistant and sensitive models, protein profiling fingered DHODH, a metabolic enzyme, as a key driver.

DHODH shields the protein TRIM28 from tagging and destruction by competing for its binding partner. Stable TRIM28 switches on VEGFA, restoring the growth signal the drug tries to cut. A small molecule, lisaftoclax, breaks the DHODH-TRIM28 grip and restored sunitinib's power with a synergistic effect in models. Targeting a protein's side job, not its enzyme work, opens a fresh resistance strategy.
pmc-13337878:
Can Cui and co-authors study allergy to hair products in scalp seborrheic dermatitis in a 2026 clinic study. The scaly, inflamed scalp condition weakens the skin barrier and makes topical products hard to tolerate. Links between product allergy and scalp microbes were unclear.

Sixty-three people had patch tests with 62 allergens and were grouped by scalp involvement. Severity, water loss, and moisture were measured, and 36 patients with scalp disease gave samples for bacterial and fungal sequencing. Cobalt, nickel, and several product ingredients were common triggers. Certain allergens tracked with water loss and with microbes such as Malassezia and Candida in the reported links.
pmc-13338678:
Sarah Vollam and a large team review wearable monitoring of hospital patients with COVID-19 in a 2026 data study. Wrist or patch systems track heart rate, breathing rate, and oxygen nonstop. Evidence on real ward use and on how often nurses still take manual readings was thin.

Three isolation wards in a large United Kingdom hospital displayed live readings on a central dashboard. Records were reviewed to describe vital sign patterns outside intensive care. A later exploratory check asked whether showing the data changed manual measurement frequency. Findings help wards judge what continuous monitoring adds beyond standard spot checks.
pmc-13340678:
Breast inflammation in pregnancy caused by an unusual germ is reported by Hassan Alyami's team in a 2026 case report. The 42-year-old woman, early in pregnancy, got pain, swelling, and redness in her left breast that kept returning despite several rounds of antibiotics and repeated drainage work.

Tissue showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, and culture in the third trimester grew Mycobacterium avium complex, never before seen in an immunocompetent pregnant patient. Steroids and anti-mycobacterial drugs were held back until after delivery. Eighteen months of rifampin, ethambutol, and azithromycin after delivery then cleared the disease fully, on examination and imaging alike.
pmc-13341078:
Predicting where microRNAs bind their targets is the job of miRNAProtPred, a 2026 software paper by Somenath Dutta and colleagues. The Python package merges seed matching with thermodynamic stability checks from ViennaRNA into one workflow needing little manual setup.

It draws on 2,656 curated human miRNAs and accepts DNA, RNA, or protein inputs, scoring candidates by seed fit, free energy, flanking AU content, and match type. A strict mode demands exact seed pairing, while a relaxed mode allows G:U wobble. Tests recovered all 16 known antiviral miRNAs for SARS-CoV-2, with 75% rated high confidence, and benchmarking used 62,215 miRNA-target pairs from miRAW.
pmc-13341178:
Heart safety questions around the osteoporosis drug romosozumab are weighed by Beom-Jun Kim in a 2026 review. The antibody blocks sclerostin, building bone while slowing its breakdown, and produces fast density gains and fewer fractures in severe postmenopausal osteoporosis.

Trial results conflict: FRAME against placebo looked reassuring, while ARCH against alendronate showed more major cardiovascular events in the first year, prompting boxed warnings. Kim asks whether the signal reflects true heart toxicity or a protective effect of the comparator drug. Lab and tissue studies have not found a convincing mechanism for harm, leaving real-world evidence to help settle the question.
pmc-13342978:
Xiaoman Wang and colleagues present a 2026 genomic dataset for Aristida triseta, a protected wild grass in China. The team sequenced its full chloroplast genome from dried leaf material and then built richer DNA barcode sets for the whole Aristida genus by merging new reads with public sequences.

The circular chloroplast genome runs 138,428 base pairs with the typical four-part layout and 133 annotated genes. Six core barcode regions were pulled from the data and combined with database sequences for relatives. Matching and tree analyses showed each barcode tied the species to its genus while carrying differing signals. The sets support species identification, breeding work, and diversity studies for this protected plant.
pmc-13347078:
Asma Ali and co-authors set out a protocol for a qualitative study. The protocol was issued in 2026. It covers metabolic syndrome care in two countries. One site sits in Memphis, in the United States. The other sits at a health sciences university in Saudi Arabia. Each site will recruit 20 to 30 adults. Clinic partners will help with recruiting. Sampling will vary on purpose.

Each person will join a one-hour guided interview. Daily self-care is one topic. Barriers and supports are others. Views on digital health tools will be asked too. Themes will be drawn out with mixed coding. Enrolment was set to begin in August 2026. The value lies in the comparison plan, not in findings.
pmc-13347778:
Dineo Monaheng and colleagues check lasting hepatitis B protection in South African health students, in a study from 2026. Infant vaccination entered the national program in 1995, so 122 students born after that start gave blood at entry and after booster doses at set months. Antibody levels marked whether protection still held.

At entry only 43 percent held antibody levels counted as protective, a gap that matters for ward work where exposure risk is real. One booster lifted the protected share to 92 percent, and three doses brought it to 100 percent in the reported counts. No split appeared by race or sex. Immune memory survives even when blood levels fade.
pmc-13348378:
Kiersten R. Fullem and colleagues present draft genomes for two peanut fungi. Their announcement came out in 2026. The fungi cause early and late leaf spots. Spores came from spotted leaves in Florida. A trial field supplied the leaves in 2016. Treated agar cleaned the spores. Long-read sequencing then read their DNA. Few public genomes exist for either culprit. Yet both diseases rank among the widest peanut threats.

Assemblies differed in size and piece count. The early spot fungus reached about 37.75 million bases. Its draft holds 194 pieces. The late spot fungus reached about 49.04 million bases. Its draft holds 571 pieces. Open genomes should speed several lines of work. Fungal variation is one line. Spray resistance is another. Tougher peanut lines are the goal.
pmc-13349778:
Xiaoou Wang and co-authors published a review in 2026 comparing psoriasis and Crohn's disease, two long-term immune-driven illnesses of the skin and gut. They ask how far the two conditions truly overlap and where their biology parts ways.

Shared upstream signals, chiefly TNF and IL-23 driven type 17 immunity, sit at the centre of the argument, while later IL-17 responses behave differently in skin and bowel. Gut-skin links through barrier damage, microbes, and moving immune cells are weighed with care, since direct proof in people is still thin. Treatments that can suit both diseases are set against those that help one organ and harm the other, guiding patient grouping by signs, markers, and past therapy.
pmc-13349978:
Hua Zhong and co-authors used an image-generating AI in 2026 to map lung blood vessels from scans taken without dye. Planning partial lung removal needs a clear three-dimensional picture of arteries and veins near a nodule, but some patients cannot receive contrast dye.

Their generative model learned from paired spectral scans in 130 patients to fake contrast-style images from plain ones, using attention and a mixed slice approach to handle breathing shifts. It was then tested on 82 patients scanned on machines from two makers. Vessel rebuilding within a zone around each nodule was checked. Success could widen safe surgical planning to dye-free patients.
pmc-13350178:
Cassandra A. Omane and Sarah Forberger reviewed in 2026 how young adults judge online nutrition information. Young people search the internet daily for diet advice, while traditional health gatekeepers matter less and misinformation spreads fast.

Screening five databases and grey literature through late 2024 yielded 48 papers and 82 separate factors shaping trust. Clear writing was named most often, followed by the reader's own prior knowledge and education. Far fewer studies covered the channel, setting, or design of the information. Knowing what earns trust helps health communicators present sound diet advice in forms young adults will actually believe and use.
pmc-13351378:
