Robert Waterhouse, Mathieu Seppey, Felipe Simão, and coauthors described wider uses of BUSCO in 2017. New genome projects pour out data, but judging whether an assembly is complete is hard. Simple technical scores miss whether the expected genes are really there.

BUSCO checks a genome against a set of genes that nearly all species in a group should carry. Missing or broken genes signal gaps in the assembly. The same idea can guide gene prediction and compare whole branches of the tree of life. Genome teams now report BUSCO scores as a routine quality stamp.
pmc-6007078:
Kelly Street, Davide Risso, Russell Fletcher, and coauthors introduced Slingshot for single-cell data in 2018. Single-cell studies can catch stem cells partway toward mature types. Ordering cells along that path reveals how development proceeds.

Slingshot first groups cells, then fits smooth paths through the groups to order cells by progress. It can handle branching paths where one start leads to several end types. The output gives each cell a pseudotime value along each branch. Biologists use those orderings to find genes that switch on or off as cells mature. Worked examples in the paper use both simulated and real developmental data sets.
pmc-6269478:
Chirag Jain, Luis Rodriguez-R, Adam Phillippy, and coauthors tested species boundaries across many prokaryote genomes in 2018. A basic question in microbiology is whether bacterial diversity is smooth or falls into clear species. Whole-genome similarity measures can answer that at scale.

Using a fast method, the team compared tens of thousands of genomes by average nucleotide identity. Genomes cluster into groups with a clear gap between clusters, which supports real species boundaries. The result calms fears that sequence data would dissolve bacterial species into a blur. It also validates fast identity checks for sorting new genomes.
pmc-6650278:
Jason Lloyd-Price, Cesar Arze, Ashoka Ananthakrishnan, and a large team profiled the gut ecosystem in bowel disease in 2019. Inflammatory bowel diseases affect millions of people worldwide. They are tangled disorders, mixed at clinical, immune, genetic, and microbial levels.

The study follows patients over time with many omics layers at once, from microbes to blood chemistry. Disease flare-ups line up with shifts in microbes and their products. Some changes look like causes, others like fallout. The deep data set is now a shared resource for testing ideas about what drives Crohn disease and colitis.
pmc-6964678:
Nikos Koundouros and George Poulogiannis reviewed fatty acid metabolism in cancer in 2019. Cancer cells rewire their chemistry to supply energy and building blocks for growth. Renewed interest has fallen on how they handle fats.

Tumors boost fat making, storage, and burning in patterns that differ by cancer type. These shifts help them survive low oxygen and resist some drugs. Enzymes in the fat pathways are now drug targets in trials. The review gives a clear map of which steps matter and where the therapeutic openings look real. The review closes by weighing which fat-pathway drugs look nearest to clinical use.
pmc-7044178:
Ioannis Manisalidis, Elisavet Stavropoulou, Agathangelos Stavropoulos, and coauthors reviewed air pollution and health in 2020. Air pollution ranks among the great health scourges of the era. It harms both the climate and the bodies of people who breathe it.

The review covers the main pollutants, from fine particles to ozone and nitrogen gases. It links them to lung and heart disease, stroke, and early death. Children and older adults bear extra risk. By gathering the evidence in one place, the authors make the case for cleaner air as basic preventive medicine.
price-free-discussion-materialism-1778:
Price and Joseph Priestley argued the nature of the soul in print. Their exchange appeared in 1778 as A Free Discussion of the Doctrines of Materialism and Philosophical Necessity. Both men were dissenting ministers and friends, which made the fight livelier: the dissenter against the dissenter, mind against matter. Priestley held that mind is a power of organized matter; Price defended an immaterial soul.

The letters also take up necessity, the claim that every act is fixed by prior causes, which Price feared would dissolve moral responsibility. The two friends argue hard and stay friends, a model of public controversy. The book preserves the liveliest theological debate of its age in open letters. It shows Enlightenment religion arguing with itself, in public, at full strength.
resume-d-une-histoire-de-la-matiere-depu: Résumé d'une histoire de la matière, 1878. The history of matter. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
the-life-of-george-combe-author-of-the-c: The Life of George Combe, 1878. The constitution's author. This book preserves that biography. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Book twenty-eight: the old rover looks back across it all. The very long tale is nearing its close at last. A great and checkered life’s last bright pages. A great and checkered life’s last bright pages.
tob-10078:
Rufus M. Jones, a Quaker historian, profiled men and women of the 1500s and 1600s who sought a living, inward faith outside the established churches. These spiritual reformers differed from the famous leaders of the Reformation. Many were dissenters, seekers, and small-group leaders rather than founders of large churches.

Drawing on their letters and writings, Jones shows how each tried to renew religion from the inside, through direct experience of God. V1 evidence calls the result a sympathetic gallery. Readers meet reform as a personal, risky practice, carried on by people willing to be punished or ignored for following conscience over custom.
tob-4178:
Saadi of Shiraz finished the Gulistan, the Rose Garden, in 1258, and Persia has treasured it since. Anecdotes in prose break into short poems throughout: kings and dervishes, misers and lovers, all caught in tales that end with a pointed moral. The text here follows the 1865 Boston edition.

Saadi traveled for thirty years before he wrote, and the book smells of roads, courts, and caravanserais. Its wit is dry, its mercy wide, and its sentences became proverbs across half of Asia. Verified from the 1919 edition record, this Gulistan carries the most beloved book in Persian after Hafiz, in a plain old American dress.
turgenev-dream-tales-1878:
Dream Tales and Prose Poems gathers Turgenev's late, strange writings in Constance Garnett's English. The dream tales let ghosts, visions, and doubles walk through his usual clear prose. A realist by trade, Turgenev here explores the fears and wonders that reason leaves unexplained.

The prose poems, written near the end of his life, are brief meditations in lyrical form. They treat age, death, Russia, language, and the small mercies of daily life. One famous piece praises the Russian language itself as a stay in dark times. The volume shows the visionary underside of a writer famed for balance. It closes Garnett's Turgenev with his most personal pages.
un-ga-res-a-69-78:
Nuclear arms in the Middle East would pose a grave threat, warns Resolution A/69/78, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text takes note of the latest vote of the world atomic body's main meeting, in September 2014. It presses the urgent need to place all atomic plants in the region under the full checks of that body, the International Atomic Energy Agency.

The vote recalls the 1995 world meeting on the pact against the spread of nuclear arms. There, states urged all lands to join the pact at the soonest date. The call falls hardest on the states of the region that run atomic plants no world check has seen. That hint, at Israel's plant at Dimona, is plain to all who read it.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/78 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, addresses the risk of nuclear proliferation in the Middle East. It states that Israel remains the only state in the region not party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. It calls on Israel to join without delay, give up nuclear weapons, and place all its nuclear facilities under full-scope IAEA safeguards. It regrets that the planned 2012 conference on a Middle East zone free of weapons of mass destruction was never held.
un-sc-res-1278: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1278, adopted on 30 November 1999, is a brief procedural text about the International Court of Justice. One of the court's judges had resigned, with the move taking effect on 29 February 2000. His seat would fall open partway through his term. Under the court's statute, the Council must fix the date to fill such a vacancy. The text sets the election for 2 March 2000, at meetings of both the Security Council and the General Assembly.
un-sc-res-1378: Entered in the record as Resolution 1378, this Security Council text is catalogued at 2001. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1478: Formal decisions of the Security Council carry numbers, and 1478 is this one's place in the sequence. The text is preserved as an English Wikisource transcription of the United Nations record. Within it, the fifteen members set out the facts they acted on, then vote the orders and requests that follow from those findings into effect.
un-sc-res-1578:
UNDOF's term on the Golan Heights ran to December 2004. On 15 December 2004 the Security Council renewed the force until 30 June 2005. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission a week earlier. The Council also restated its standards for peacekeeper health. The terms of the mission stayed unchanged. Its soldiers kept the separation zone between Israel and Syria under watch.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. A report was due at the end of the new term. It would cover events and steps toward applying 338. The renewal fell in the mission's thirtieth year. Few peace operations have run so long on six-month cycles.
un-sc-res-1678: Security Council Resolution 1678 is preserved in this collection in the official wording transcribed by English Wikisource. A resolution's life begins in negotiation and ends in the record; only the record version binds. The text kept here is that version, opening findings through closing instructions, with nothing summarized away or paraphrased.
un-sc-res-1778:
War in Sudan's Darfur region spilled into Chad, and Resolution 1778 sent a UN mission to guard the border camps. Hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced Chadians lived there in harsh conditions. The Council acted in 2007 to protect them.

The new mission, MINURCAT, was mostly police and support staff rather than combat troops, working beside Chadian officers and a European force. Its duties covered camp security, aid routes, and the rule of law in the east. The text shows how one country's war can pull peacekeepers into its neighbor's territory.
un-sc-res-178:
An incident at Bouniak, on Senegal's border, brought Portugal before the Council in 1963. On 24 April 1963 the Council heard both governments. Portuguese forces had crossed into Senegalese territory. Senegal bordered Portuguese Guinea, where a liberation war had begun. The Council deplored the incidents near the frontier. It worried that such clashes could feed wider tension in the area.

Portugal had to act to prevent any violation of Senegal's sovereignty. The Council noted Lisbon's stated intent to respect that sovereignty. It asked Portugal to match its words with deeds. The Secretary-General had to keep the situation under review. The text is an early sign of the Council's colonial-era border disputes.
un-sc-res-1878: In 2009 the Council passed Resolution 1878, preserved in this collection as an official-record text via Wikisource. The genre demands economy: a few pages must carry findings, law, and instructions at once. This entry shows the economy at work and preserves it whole, so the act can be read as its addressees read it.
un-sc-res-2078:
The question of the Democratic Republic of the Congo came to a vote in Resolution 2078, adopted on 28 November 2012. The M23 rebels had seized Goma days earlier. Experts kept tracing outside support and stolen gold to the armed groups. Serious abuse of civilians, including child soldier use, went on across the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the sanctions regime until 1 February 2014. The arms embargo, transport checks, travel bans, and asset freezes all continue. Attacking peacekeepers now counts as grounds for listing. The Group of Experts serves the same new term. M23 and the other named groups must stop all attacks, free child soldiers, and lay down their arms for good.
un-sc-res-278:
Bahrain's future was settled by a fact-finding report the Security Council endorsed on 11 May 1970. Iran and Britain had each written to the Secretary-General in March 1970 about the island's status. His personal representative visited Bahrain and reported on 30 April. The question was whether Bahrainis wanted union with Iran, continued British protection, or independence.

The Council endorsed the report and welcomed its central finding. The overwhelming majority of the people of Bahrain wished to gain recognition of their identity in a fully independent and sovereign state. Bahrain would be free to decide its own relations with other states. The finding cleared the way for Bahrain's independence the following year. It also ended Iran's claim through a United Nations test of the people's wishes rather than through force or a imposed settlement.
un-sc-res-378:
The Sinai emergency force won its longest renewal yet in October 1975. On 23 October 1975 the Security Council extended the force for a full year. The term ran until 24 October 1976. The Secretary-General had reported on the force's work. He warned that easing the search for a full settlement could be dangerous. The months ahead, in his view, called for urgent effort by all sides.

The parties had to carry out resolution 338 without delay. The Council voiced confidence the force would run with care and economy. A new Sinai disengagement deal had been signed that September. The force's buffer role grew more settled under it. Yearly renewals replaced the tense three-month terms of the summer.
un-sc-res-478:
Jerusalem's status brought censure of Israel from the Security Council on 20 August 1980. The Israeli Knesset had passed a basic law changing the Holy City's character and status. Israel had not complied with resolution 476 (1980), which had warned against the move. The Council restated that taking territory by force is inadmissible.

The Council censured the basic law in the strongest terms and held it a breach of international law. All Israeli measures that had altered or aimed to alter Jerusalem's character and status were declared null and void. They had to be rescinded at once. The Council decided not to recognize the law or any acts flowing from it. Member states were called to accept that decision. States with diplomatic missions in Jerusalem were told to withdraw them from the Holy City. The Secretary-General had to report on the outcome before 15 November 1980.
un-sc-res-678:
Iraq still held Kuwait as a January deadline took shape in late 1990. On 29 November 1990 the Security Council gave Iraq one final chance to comply. Baghdad had defied the demand to withdraw and a chain of later resolutions. The Council acted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The vote was twelve to two, with one abstention.

If Iraq did not fully comply by 15 January 1991, member states could act. States working with Kuwait's government could use all necessary means. That phrase authorized the coalition war that freed Kuwait. States were asked to support the effort and to keep the Council informed. It remains the classic modern case of the Council licensing war.
un-sc-res-78: Plans for controlling conventional arms moved between United Nations bodies in 1949. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had adopted proposals that August. They concerned the use of a General Assembly resolution from 1948 on armaments data. On 18 October 1949 the Security Council asked the Secretary-General to transmit the proposals to the Assembly. The records of debate in both the Council and the commission went with them. The one-sentence act kept the work in the open.
un-sc-res-978:
Men accused of Rwanda's genocide had fled across its borders by 1995, and the Council pressed states to catch them. Expert reports had confirmed that genocide and other grave crimes were committed in Rwanda in 1994. Resolution 955 had created an international tribunal to judge those responsible. Resolution 978 was adopted unanimously on 27 February 1995.

States were urged to arrest and hold anyone on their soil against whom there was enough evidence. Such suspects would be held under national law, until the tribunal or a national court could prosecute them. States had to share the suspects' names and the evidence with the Secretary-General and with the tribunal's prosecutor. The Red Cross and the tribunal's investigators had to be given access to the prisoners. The Council also condemned attacks on people in the refugee camps near Rwanda's borders.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1278, adopted on 30 November 1999, is a short procedural text on the International Court of Justice. The Council notes the resignation of Judge Stephen Schwebel, effective 29 February 2000, which will leave a vacancy on the Court for the rest of his term. Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Council fixes the election date. It decides the election will take place on 2 March 2000, at a meeting of the Security Council and at a meeting of the General Assembly during its fifty-fourth session.

As Taliban rule collapses, a path for Afghanistan's future is set out on 14 November 2001. The Council condemned the Taliban for letting the country serve as a base for terrorism and for sheltering terrorist groups. Afghan forces were advancing, and the question of who would govern Kabul was suddenly open.

Talks among Afghan groups toward a new, broad-based government that would represent all Afghans are endorsed. Afghan forces are called on to avoid reprisals, respect human rights and aid law, and keep United Nations and aid workers safe. Member states are asked to give urgent relief aid, help clear mines, and support the country's long-term recovery.

Sanctions on Liberia are renewed and widened on 6 May 2003. Expert panels had found that Liberia's government kept breaching the measures set in 2001, above all by buying arms. Audits had also failed to show timber and shipping registry income being used for proper public purposes.

Liberia is found in breach of earlier demands, and its government and the LURD rebels are pressed toward ceasefire talks under regional mediation. The existing arms, diamond, and travel measures are renewed. A new ban is added: for ten months, states must block imports of round logs and timber products from Liberia, cutting a revenue stream the Council feared was funding arms purchases.

The Golan watch rolled on at the end of 2004. UNDOF troops stood between Israeli and Syrian lines, as they had since 1974. The chief's report of 7 December 2004 found the zone calm but tense. Resolution 1578 passed on 15 December 2004.

The force won six more months, to 30 June 2005. The Council matched the grant with its stock call. Both sides had to act on the 1973 ceasefire text at once. A fresh report was due at the close. It would chart events and steps toward that old text's aims. The file cites a 2000 text on guarding peace staff from disease. By 2004, such health clauses had grown to be a set part of each renewal.

Only until 31 May 2006 is UNMEE, the Ethiopia-Eritrea mission, extended on 15 May 2006. A Boundary Commission meeting in London in March had made some progress, and another was set for 17 May. Full compliance with resolution 1640 is demanded, with a warning: if the parties had not shown the required progress, the mission's mandate and troop levels would be reviewed before the month ended.

A United Nations mission in Chad and the Central African Republic, MINURCAT, is set up on 25 September 2007. Armed groups and attacks in eastern Chad, the north-east of the Central African Republic, and Darfur threatened civilians and aid work across the whole subregion. Both governments asked for help protecting refugees and displaced people near the Darfur border.

The presence would run for one year and pair the United Nations mission with a European Union force. MINURCAT would include up to 300 police and a civilian team to train and support a special Chadian police force for the camps. The European force would handle the wider military protection task. Both parts aimed to keep aid flowing and civilians safe while the Darfur crisis continued.

Gunfire near the village of Bouniak sparked this early Senegal-Portugal clash. Portuguese troops from colonial Guinea had entered Senegalese land. The incident happened on 8 April 1963. Both governments sent speakers to argue their versions. Resolution 178 was adopted unanimously on 24 April 1963.

The Council deplored any incursion into Senegal. It named the Bouniak incident directly. Lisbon was reminded of its own promise to respect Senegal's borders. Portugal had to act to prevent fresh violations. The Secretary-General would keep watching the frontier. Relations in the area were tense, the text warns. One stray patrol could ignite a wider fight. Portugal's African wars made such warnings recur for years.

Rwanda tribunal judges have their terms extended on 7 July 2009. Letters from the presidents of both war crimes tribunals in May and June 2009 set out the staffing needed to finish trials. Several judges' terms were ending before their cases, and the completion strategy was already slipping.

The terms of the permanent and ad litem judges named in the text are extended so they can complete the cases assigned to them. One ad litem judge may also serve past the usual total-service ceiling. The judge appointed to fill a vacancy would serve for the rest of the predecessor's term. The need for further extensions would be reviewed as the tribunal's remaining trials progress.

Congo's sanctions are renewed amid the M23 crisis in Resolution 2078, adopted in late 2012. The Group of Experts' 2012 reports documented embargo violations, and the M23 was committing summary executions, sexual violence, and child recruitment in the east.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the arms, transport, financial, and travel measures of Resolution 1807 (2008) until 1 February 2014. The designation criteria cover anyone who plans, sponsors, or takes part in attacks on MONUSCO peacekeepers, alongside embargo violators and armed-group leaders blocking disarmament. They cover child recruiters, those attacking civilians or blocking aid, and those funding armed groups through illicit resource trade, including gold. The Group of Experts is extended to 1 February 2014. The Council condemns the M23 and demands it and the FDLR, LRA, ADF, and other groups cease violence and lay down their arms. It repeats that external support to the M23 must stop.

Bahrain's future was surveyed in Resolution 278, adopted unanimously on 11 May 1970. Britain was preparing to leave the Gulf, and questions hung over the island's status, including a claim from Iran. The Secretary-General had sent a personal representative to find out what Bahrainis themselves wanted, and his report reached the Council at the end of April.

The Council endorsed that report and welcomed its conclusions. The finding quoted in the text is blunt: a clear, overwhelming share of Bahrainis wanted their identity recognized in a fully independent and sovereign state, free to choose its own foreign relations. The verdict cleared the way for Bahrain's independence the following year and settled Iran's claim peacefully.

Two years after the October War, the Sinai buffer still held. The force there, UNEF, kept Egyptian and Israeli troops apart. Its term was near its end. The chief's report warned of risk if peace work slackened. Resolution 378 passed on 23 October 1975 by thirteen votes to none.

The force gained a full year, to 24 October 1976. The Council matched the move with its stock call. Both sides had to act on the 1973 ceasefire text at once. Faith was voiced that the force would run with care and thrift. A report was due when the term closed. It would chart events and steps toward a broad peace. Such yearly renewals were the norm for UNEF in those years.

Israel's Jerusalem law drew the Council's strongest censure in Resolution 478, adopted on 20 August 1980 with the United States abstaining. The Knesset had passed a basic law proclaiming Jerusalem, whole and united, as Israel's capital, changing the city's status by statute. The Council had warned against exactly this step in resolution 476 weeks earlier, and Israel had not complied.

The Council censured the law in the strongest terms and called it a violation of international law. It declared every Israeli legislative and administrative measure altering Jerusalem's character or status null and void, to be rescinded at once. It also called on states with diplomatic missions in Jerusalem to withdraw them from the city.

Resolution 678 is the UN Security Council authorization for the Gulf War, adopted on 29 November 1990 by twelve votes to two, Cuba and Yemen against, with China abstaining. Iraq had ignored ten resolutions since invading Kuwait, from the withdrawal demand of Resolution 660 to sanctions and embargoes, and the Council recorded its flagrant contempt.

The resolution gives Iraq one final opportunity, a pause of goodwill, to comply fully by 15 January 1991. Failing that, it authorizes member states cooperating with Kuwait's government to use all necessary means to uphold the earlier resolutions and restore peace and security in the area. That phrase became the legal basis for the coalition offensive that liberated Kuwait in early 1991.

More arms paperwork crossed the Council's table in October 1949. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had drafted detailed proposals. They built on the General Assembly's disarmament resolution of November 1948. The commission had adopted its working document on 1 August 1949. Resolution 78 was passed on 18 October 1949, nine votes to none.

The Ukrainian and Soviet delegations abstained, as usual on this file. The Secretary-General was asked to transmit the proposals onward. Discussion records from both bodies went with them. The General Assembly received the full package. These transfers look dull. In truth, they trace how slowly the superpowers circled each other. Neither side would accept limits on conventional forces first.

Genocide suspects who fled Rwanda faced arrest calls from the Council in 1995. On 27 February, it adopted Resolution 978 without dissent. Ten months had passed since the genocide. A UN expert panel had confirmed reports of mass crimes. The Council also worried about attacks in the refugee camps abroad.

The text urges all states to seize and hold suspects on their soil. Proof of crimes within the Rwanda court's reach is the test. Detainees wait for trial by that court or by home courts. States holding such persons must tell the Secretary-General and the court's prosecutor. The call turned the hunt for the killers into a shared legal duty.
wallace-miracles-modern-spiritualism-187:
Alfred Russel Wallace staked his great name on the dark room in Miracles and Modern Spiritualism, out in 1878. Wallace had found the law of life's change by his own work in far isles. Peers who hailed that feat balked when he claimed forms took shape, tables rose, and the dead spoke in his own test rooms.

He prints his tests and dares his peers to match his care. The book is no wild rant; it is a calm, firm brief. It gave the faith its best shield of the age. Rows round it ran for years.
whitehurst-inquiry-original-state-earth-:
John Whitehurst, a Derbyshire clockmaker and naturalist, inquired into the Earth's first state in 1778. His Inquiry treats strata, underground fire, and the Deluge in one scheme. Whitehurst had mapped the layered rocks of Derbyshire with a surveyor's care. Those strata, he argues, record the Earth's formation in stages.

Subterranean heat raises and breaks the crust in his account. The Deluge still plays its part, though nature's agents grow larger beside it. The book bridges the old diluvial theories and the coming geological revolution. Hutton and his age stood not far ahead. Whitehurst's plates of strata served later geologists well. His county pride and exact eye fill the work.
zola-love-episode-1878:
Starkweather's English version of A Love Episode came from a 1905 fine edition with Dantan's pictures. Only five hundred numbered copies were registered for that printing. Twenty-six chapters carry Zola's most delicate novel of 1878.

Helene Grandjean, a widowed mother in Passy, has buried her heart with her husband. Her daughter's illness brings the kind Dr. Deberle into the house. Love ambushes them both before either can guard against it. The slow tale tracks a woman's awakening against the shifting seasons of Paris. No other volume in the saga is so quiet, so tender, or so purely romantic in feeling.
